You should change the domain’s nameservers so the domain points to the new hosting, while keeping the domain registration unchanged.

According to the guidance here, in your GoDaddy account go to Domains > Manage My Domains, tick the domain, then use the dropdown next to Nameservers and choose Set name server. Select Standard and that should be enough to point the domain to the new host.

If you want the domain control to remain with the current registrar, the main thing is to update DNS/nameserver settings only, not transfer the domain.

Changing hosting companies should not affect your SEO ranking by itself.

The main thing to watch is downtime during the move. A smooth, seamless transition is ideal.

The only SEO-related risk mentioned is if the new host is extremely slow, since very slow pages can hurt rankings. If your host is reasonably fast, you should be fine.

Google likely found them because they were exposed through signals that make a URL discoverable, such as being pinged, shared publicly, or linked from a page Google already crawls frequently.

The supported guidance here is:
- Ping the new page when it’s published.
- Share the link publicly on sites like Twitter, Facebook, or YouTube.
- Get a relevant link from another site, especially one with high crawl frequency.
- Link to the new page from your home page or another strong internal page.

So even if the page wasn’t linked in the way you expected, Google may still discover it through these other routes.

If your site is just using jQuery in the browser, changing hosting companies should not affect it. jQuery is client-side, so it runs independently of the web server.

What hosting can affect is server-side scripting, such as PHP, which is used by platforms like WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. For that, you’d want a host that supports the language or server setup you need.

So the closest guidance is: pick a host based on cost, reliability, and the server-side technologies you need, not on jQuery support itself.

The thread does not include a recorded answer, so it doesn’t confirm whether that setup works.

What it does show is the intended approach: one account, one property, and a separate profile for each site under that property, with the default “All Web Site Data” profile implying combined statistics across sites.

It also suggests you would need whatever tracking code is normally used to send data to that property, but it does not say that a special code is required. The closest guidance supported here is that combining stats would be done through the property/profile setup, while individual site views would come from separate profiles.

Google Analytics doesn’t provide a built-in way to simply combine stats from separate, unrelated properties into one total view.

The closest options supported here are:

- Use Universal Analytics with the same tracking code across all sites, which requires creating a new profile and choosing Universal Analytics instead of Classic Analytics.
- For Classic Analytics, use cross-domain tracking if the sites are meant to be tracked together.
- If you want combined totals for all sites, consider a separate web analytics application that can analyze your server logs across all domains.
- For estimating server capacity, it’s better to monitor server resource usage directly with tools like top on Linux or Task Manager on Windows.

If your sites already use separate tracking codes and separate properties, the supported guidance here does not show a way to merge those existing stats inside Google Analytics.

You can check it manually by searching for your own domain name to see whether your site is indexed. If it appears in the results, it’s indexed.

To check ranking, search for the terms you expect to rank for and see where your pages appear. If you don’t find them, that usually means they rank poorly. The answer also notes that there are tools available to automate this process.

Google may have found the domain because it can use registrar-related information to discover new sites to index. The answer provided says Google is a registrar, so it could use that role to find new sites even if there are no public links yet.

It does not say exactly which record or process Google used, only that this is a plausible way it could discover a newly created domain.

Google likely found those old URLs because they were still present somewhere in the cloned WordPress files or database, even if the visible posts and pages were deleted.

The guidance supported here is to search the full site files and database for the old domain or IP address. A text search tool was suggested for this. Be careful if you edit WordPress database data directly, because WordPress uses serialized strings and changing them incorrectly can break things.

So the closest answer is: the old links were probably still hidden in the cloned site’s code, settings, theme, plugins, or database, and Google discovered them from there.

The closest objective check supported here is to see whether Google has manually penalized your site in Google Webmaster Tools. If there’s no message there, then the drop may be from an algorithmic update, and you’d need to review whether your SEO activity follows Google’s guidelines.

So, practically:
- sign up / log in to Google Webmaster Tools
- check for any manual penalty message
- if there isn’t one, investigate possible algorithmic changes and your SEO practices

This doesn’t fully explain a ranking drop, but it’s the objective check mentioned in the answer.

Google can choose to index only some of the URLs in a sitemap, because a sitemap is just a discovery hint, not a guarantee that every listed URL will be indexed. Google decides what belongs in its index based on its own assessment, and may skip URLs it considers thin, duplicate, poor, or otherwise not suitable.

So if Google has indexed more URLs than a sitemap contains, that can happen because Google found additional pages through crawling, links, or navigation outside the sitemap. The sitemap only lists pages you want discovered; it doesn’t limit Google to only those pages.

A sitemap is only advisory, so Google may index URLs that are not in the sitemap, and it may not index every URL that is submitted. The difference can also happen if Google has found URLs through other links or sources, or if it simply hasn’t crawled/indexed all submitted URLs yet.

In the case shown, the sitemap was submitted very recently, so another plausible reason is that Google just hasn’t had time to process all of it yet.

Use an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header with noindex on the CSS, JS, or image responses if you want to keep those files out of search results.

If your goal is only to stop Google from crawling them at all, use robots.txt to disallow those URLs. That prevents crawling and also prevents the files from being used for things like script execution or fetching Ajax content.

If the files are already showing up in search results, the guidance says to fix the HTML pages first if the wrong page is ranking. If you still want the non-HTML files removed, then noindex via X-Robots-Tag is the supported approach.

If you were specifically asking about expiration headers: this material does not say how to set cache/expiration headers for CSS, JS, and images.

Use mod_expires with an active default and type-specific rules, for example:

ExpiresActive on
ExpiresDefault "access plus 24 hours"
ExpiresByType image/jpg "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/gif "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType image/png "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType text/javascript "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 months"
ExpiresByType application/x-shockwave-flash "access plus 24 hours"

This covers CSS, JavaScript, and common image types, and is easier to maintain than setting headers per file pattern.

If you mean the URL in the sitemap `<loc>` value, the safest approach is to generate it dynamically from the current site host rather than hard-coding `http://127.0.0.1/...`.

The evidence only directly covers sitemap change frequency, not host URL generation. It does support the general idea that dynamic values can be generated if needed, but for sitemap metadata it suggests leaving `changefreq` out entirely because it is often not useful or accurate.

So, for the host URL itself, the closest guidance supported here is:
- dynamically generate it if your site can run on different hosts, and
- avoid hard-coding a localhost URL in production.

If you meant the `changefreq` tag, the supported answer is to usually omit it, because dynamic values there rarely help search engines and are often wrong.

This thread doesn’t include an answer, so it only shows that the issue is about setting an expiry date or maximum age in HTTP headers for resources like CSS, JS, and images. It does not explain how to do it.

The closest guidance supported here is that the setting would be in the HTTP headers for those files, not in cookies/sessions. If you want, I can help with the general way this is usually done on a web server or explain what “expiry date” and “max-age” mean in HTTP headers.

Use your hosts file instead. That will let you point the domain to the IP you want without needing to rewrite the Host header in the browser, and it also works for other HTTP methods and other protocols.

You can’t make a dynamic home IP into a static one just by assigning your router the current IP.

The supported options are:
- Ask your ISP for a static IP, usually for an extra fee.
- If you host from home anyway, use a dynamic DNS service so your DNS records update automatically when your IP changes.

If you use dynamic DNS, the main tradeoff is TTL: a longer TTL can leave users pointing at an old IP after changes, while a very short TTL increases DNS traffic and can hurt performance.

Make sure the Analytics tracking script is placed inside the page’s `<html>` and `<body>` structure, not outside them. In the resolved example, the script being outside the `<body>` tag was identified as the obvious mistake.

If you’re also seeing goal conversions attributed to Facebook or accounts.google.com, the closest guidance from this case is to fix the tracking code placement first, since incorrect placement can prevent proper goal registration and lead to confusing attribution.

A self-hosted analytics tool like Urchin’s main advantages are that it runs on your own servers, can be used for intranets, and can process historical logs. It also includes robot/spider reports, status and error code reports such as 404s, and individual visitor history drilldown.

The main downside noted is cost: it’s not cheap, at US$9,995.

The simplest supported approach is to track the form submission as an event and then create a goal in Google Analytics based on that event.

Since the form does not load a new thank-you URL, you should not rely on a destination URL goal. Instead, trigger an event when the form is submitted, then set that event as the goal condition.

I can’t confirm from the provided information how to specifically prevent misattribution to Facebook or accounts.google.com, but the closest guidance here is to use event-based tracking for the conversion itself rather than depending on a changing page URL.

Set the goal using only the path, not the full subdomain URL. With Google Analytics configured to track the main domain and subdomains, a goal like `/conversions/` will be counted whether the visit is on `domain.com/conversions/` or `my.domain.com/conversions/`.

This is the closest guidance supported here: Google Analytics should automatically match the page path across the tracked domain/subdomain setup. There’s no indication in the provided material that you should enter `my.domain.com/conversions/` in the goal itself.

You shouldn’t add a sitewide `NOFOLLOW` meta tag, because it will stop search engines from following links across your whole site.

If you want search engines to crawl and index the internal pages, adding those pages to a sitemap can help. But if those pages aren’t linked anywhere else search engines can discover, they may not rank well.

A better approach is to block only the URLs that depend on the external API using `robots.txt`, if they follow a predictable pattern. Even better, make sure the pages you link to are already generated and stored in your database before they’re requested, so they load quickly for both users and search engines.

No. Based on the AdSense terms quoted here, you may not encourage users to click the ads, directly or indirectly. Phrases like “check out our sponsors,” “support us,” “click the ads,” or “visit these links” are the kind of language that is prohibited if they are intended to prompt ad clicks.

The safest guidance supported by this is to avoid any wording or design that directs attention to the ads or suggests users should click them.

If the links are going to `example.com/en/` and that URL is producing a 404, the only solution supported by the provided answer is to add a server-side redirect in the `/en/` directory, for example with PHP:

```php
<?php
header('Location: /en/home/', true, 301);
```

The evidence does not support a browser-side fix for internal links without server access. It only says that if you can place a PHP/ASP/JSP file in `/en/`, you can redirect `/en/` to `/en/home/`. If you can’t do that, it says you’re “pretty much out of luck.”

If your AdSense ads aren’t showing, the possible causes covered here are:

- your AdSense account may be under review or banned
- the AdSense code may have been copied or pasted incorrectly
- JavaScript may be disabled in the browser
- an ad blocker may be enabled
- you may have more than the allowed maximum of three AdSense ad units per page
- your site content may not be suitable for AdSense
- Google may not be able to crawl or see your site content properly

If you used a website builder or site creator, that could also be relevant, but this only suggests checking whether the code was inserted correctly and whether the platform is blocking or altering it.

The closest guidance supported here is to verify the code, check for account or policy issues, confirm ads aren’t blocked in the browser, make sure you’re within the ad-unit limit, and use Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console to check whether Google can crawl your site.

`.htaccess` is not what makes links `nofollow`, so changing it won’t fix internal links.

What the answer does support is:
- `nofollow` on internal links is not intended for normal internal linking and can hurt SEO.
- If your internal links are showing `nofollow`, the cause is elsewhere, likely in your HTML, CMS, theme, or a plugin/module.
- If you’re using a CMS, check for a plugin or module that is adding `rel="nofollow"` to links.

About adding `http://`:
- The provided evidence does not show that adding `http://` to internal links will remove `nofollow`.
- If your site has both `www` and non-`www` versions, and `index.html` now redirects to the home page, that is separate from the `nofollow` issue.

Closest guidance supported by the evidence:
- Keep one preferred version of the site using redirects, as you already did.
- Inspect the page source and your CMS/plugins to find where `rel="nofollow"` is being added.
- Remove `nofollow` from internal links in the code or plugin settings, not in `.htaccess`.

Hyphens aren’t inherently bad, but domains with multiple hyphens may not get an exact-match keyword bonus, which can hurt rankings a bit.

So based on this, the issue is not that the domain is “bad” or blacklisted; it’s more that the hyphens may reduce any keyword-related ranking advantage.

If you mean your AdSense account was disabled because of invalid clicks, the only guidance supported here is:

- You can try to detect suspicious click activity by temporarily replacing AdSense ads with a simple dummy ad/script that logs IP address, time, and user agent.
- You can report invalid clicks to Google using their invalid clicks contact form.
- As a preventive measure, you can limit ad display to visitors coming from search engines only, though the examples given are just references.

The answer also says that if your AdSense account was already banned, it may never be restored.

It does not give a reliable way to stop all invalid-click attacks, and it says you do not need to know what software attackers use.

Another service mentioned was cdyne’s SMS service.

Hyphens aren’t necessarily “bad,” but the guidance here is to avoid them in domain names unless they clearly improve readability.

The main reasons given are:
- They add noise to the domain itself.
- They are harder to say out loud and spell for someone.
- They can sometimes prevent ambiguity in a multi-word name.

So for something like a multi-word domain, the default advice is to use no hyphen if the name is still clear, but a well-placed hyphen can help when the unhyphenated version is confusing or misleading.

The closest guidance is to use an HTTP-to-SMS gateway service. One example that was used successfully for sending and receiving SMS with PHP is Clickatell, through their SMS Gateway page.

So for your website, you’d typically integrate with an SMS gateway API rather than building SMS handling directly into the site. The provided example covers PHP-based send/receive SMS; it does not include specific ASP code or implementation details for processing incoming SMS beyond using the gateway’s documentation.

The simplest way mentioned is to embed the Google Talk chatback widget on your page using the HTML snippet they provide.

If you mean sending messages in general through the website, this answer only covers direct chat via that widget, not a custom messaging system.

Try searching for “International SMS Gateway.” That’s the term suggested for services like this.

The answer also mentions Twilio as a strong option for support and developer friendliness, and says you can contact Twilio for references. Another service suggested is cdyne’s SMS service.

So, if you want to code against an API to send and receive SMS, the closest guidance here is to look for an international SMS gateway provider, or check Twilio and cdyne.

The provided information says the messages are already handled, and the question is about setting up the subscription service. It doesn’t explain how to send the messages themselves.

For the subscription part, PayPal has a built-in monthly subscription/subscriber service. You can set it up as a product type and configure how often to charge users. It also notes you should make cancellation easy, since complaints to PayPal can cause problems with your merchant account.

It’s not a problem for SEO as long as the snapshot page contains the same content the user would see in the browser.

The key point is that AJAX-crawling pages can look different in the HTML structure and still be fine, including differences like `h1`, `h2`, etc., if the actual content matches. It would only become an issue if the snapshot shows different content from the user page.

Create an XML sitemap of your actual content pages and keep it updated. That’s the supported approach.

It’s generally not worth trying to get Google to index your site’s own search result pages. Google is already meant to index the underlying content directly. If you let it crawl search-result URLs, it can waste crawl budget on a near-infinite number of possible result combinations, and your real pages may get indexed less often or become stale in search results.

So for your AJAX search site, the closest guidance is:
- expose and submit the actual content pages you want indexed
- do not rely on Google crawling internal search results
- keep the sitemap current with your real pages

Google now indexes AJAX pages and can see the page the same way a user does, including interactive JavaScript and AJAX content, without needing special changes for Googlebot.

So if the “Submit to Google index” button isn’t doing anything for an AJAX URL, the closest supported guidance here is that this may no longer be necessary for AJAX crawlable pages. The “Fetch as Google” result working suggests Google can access the page, and Google’s indexing behavior has changed since the original issue was posted.

If the script is not meant to be accessed directly by visitors, don’t try to solve it with bot blocking. Make the main page define a constant, then include the other script. In that script, check whether the constant is defined, and if not, return a 403 error or an empty page.

This only works if you use include rather than file_get_contents, because file_get_contents either just reads the file locally or runs it in a separate process if it’s a URL. Also use a file path rather than a URL, so the PHP code isn’t parsed before your check runs.

If possible, move the script out from under the document root so it can’t be directly requested at all. Whether that’s possible depends on your host’s setup.

You should filter search engine bots by looking at the user agent, not by IP addresses.

That’s the closest guidance supported here. A live, always-up-to-date list of bot IPs isn’t provided, and relying on IPs would require constant updates.

Because Google Analytics treats bounces differently.

If a visitor only views one page and leaves, Google Analytics counts that visit as 0 time on site, even though it can still count the time on that page. So if you have lots of single-page visits, the average visit duration can be pulled down below avg time on page.

In short:
- Avg time on page can include time spent on that page by bounced visitors
- Avg visit duration / time on site counts bounced visits as 0

That’s why avg time on page can be larger than avg visit duration.

This can happen because the two metrics are calculated differently.

“Avg. visit duration” is based on time between hits in a visit, so if a visit has only one tracked pageview or the user leaves immediately after the first page loads, it can show 00:00:00.

“Avg. time on page” is based on time spent on a specific page before the next pageview, so it can be larger if people spend time on a page but still have visits that end too quickly for visit duration to be measured.

In the case you quoted, the 00:00:00 visits are typically users who stayed only long enough for Google Analytics to load, then closed the browser or left right away. That does not necessarily mean robots or a broken script.

You can combat bot/script submissions with a mix of checks and limits:

- Add a fake hidden field that real users won’t see. If it comes back filled in, treat it as a bot and ignore or ban it.
- Use a CAPTCHA such as reCAPTCHA.
- Add a simple human-check question, like “what is 5 + 3?” Bots that auto-fill based on field names may miss it or answer incorrectly.
- Use a per-session token that is also included in the form. If the token is missing or doesn’t match, reject the submission.
- Watch for repeated submissions from the same IP address. If one IP suddenly sends too many requests, temporarily block it.
- Use Akismet for spam detection.

The idea you mentioned about changing cookies with JavaScript and timestamps could help raise the bar, but the evidence here mainly supports the measures above, especially tokens, hidden honeypots, CAPTCHA, and rate/IP-based blocking.

To hide “all traffic” for a specific page, create a filter in Google Analytics for the view:

1. Log in to Google Analytics and select the view you want to change.
2. Go to Admin.
3. Under Filters, click New Filter.
4. Choose Custom Filter.
5. Filter by either:
   - Page Title, if that page has a unique title, or
   - URL, by entering all or part of the page URL.
6. Save the filter.

This will stop Google Analytics from monitoring that page in that view.

Yes. “Avg. time on page” can be larger than “Avg. visit duration” because they are calculated differently.

“Avg. time on page” is based on the time between that pageview and the next pageview on the site. It ignores single-page visits, since there is no next pageview to compare against.

“Avg. visit duration” is based on the time between the first and last pageviews in a visit. Since the final pageview’s time can’t be fully measured, this metric is typically shorter than the real visit length.

So if you want to know how long users typically spend on that specific page before going elsewhere, “Avg. time on page” is the better metric to use.

You can’t really hide the “all traffic” line from that plot-rows graph. The closest workaround is to use the Motion Charts view instead:

1. Set the date range you want.
2. Go to Traffic Sources -> Sources -> Referrals.
3. Make sure the referrers you want are all on the first page by increasing rows per page if needed.
4. Click the Motion Charts icon.
5. On the left side of the graph, change the metric from “Pages/Visit” to “Visits.”
6. Click the line-chart tab/icon in that view.
7. Use the checkboxes to select only the referrers you want to compare.

That gives you the comparison without the big “all traffic” line dominating the chart.

If those 404s have already been fixed on your site, you should mark the errors as fixed in Google Webmaster Tools.

After that, if Google finds the same issue again, it will show up again. If not, the errors are considered resolved.

Those 404s are being caused by a bad link on your site, not by Google.

In the example given, the “want to advertise” banner is linking with a relative URL like `href="_#"`.

That makes the browser and Google crawl a URL like:

`http://yourdomain.com/_`

So every page where that banner appears is generating a 404 for `/_`.

Fix or remove that banner link so it points to a real URL, and the 404s should stop appearing in Webmaster Tools.

Google can report 404s for pages that were never real because it sometimes tries random, made-up URLs to check how your site handles missing pages. That helps it verify that your server returns a proper 404 response instead of treating a non-existent page like a valid one.

So those errors do not necessarily mean someone linked to that page or that it ever existed. They usually mean Google tested a random URL, found it missing, and recorded the 404.

If you’re seeing a lot of them, the main thing to check is whether your site is returning the correct 404 status for missing pages.

For discontinued products, return a 410 Gone for pages that are truly no longer available, so search engines know they no longer exist. On the page shown to users, say the product has been discontinued and provide links to similar products, plus obvious links to the home page, site map, and contact page.

If the items are seasonal and will come back, don’t use 404 or 410. Keep those pages indexed, clearly mark them as seasonal/out of stock, and let users sign up for restock notifications.

That warning usually means Google can’t see one of the required properties on the Product item it is parsing, even if the page visually shows them.

From the code shown, the markup is using `http://data-vocabulary.org/Product`, which is an old, deprecated vocabulary. Also, the snippet shown only clearly includes `name` and `image`; it does not show `price`, `availability`, or `review` actually marked up on the Product item in the part provided.

What this evidence does support:
- Google is complaining because it does not detect a required product property in the structured data.
- The markup format being used is the old data-vocabulary.org format.
- The shown code does not demonstrate `price` or `availability` markup in the excerpt.

Closest guidance supported by this:
- Make sure the product’s `price`, `availability`, or `review` is included as structured data on the same Product item.
- If you are using data-vocabulary.org, update to Google’s current supported structured data format instead, because this old vocabulary is likely the reason Google is not recognizing the fields.

If you want, I can help you rewrite that product markup in current schema.org format.

For removed pages, the guidance here supports leaving them as 404 rather than redirecting them to the home page.

A 404 on a non-existent page is fine, even if another site links to it. Google will not penalize you for that. You just won’t get any Google juice from that link while the page doesn’t exist.

If you later create that page and it starts returning 200, Google should recognize that it now exists and can start treating incoming links to it normally.

A 301 to the closest valid page can pass value sooner, but that only makes sense if you actually want to redirect users and search engines to that other page. Redirecting everything to the home page is not supported by this evidence and would be a less direct fit than returning 404 for pages that are truly gone.

Set removed pages to 404, not 301 to the homepage.

A 301 from a deleted page to the homepage is usually a poor match because it tells search engines and users that the old URL has permanently moved to that specific page, which it hasn’t. A custom 404 page is the better approach, ideally with links to the homepage, search, and relevant category/topic pages so visitors can continue browsing.

If you change many pages this way, also make sure to:
- update your XML sitemap
- remove or fix internal links pointing to deleted pages
- consider notifying sites that link to removed pages

If there’s a closely related replacement page, then redirecting to that specific page can make sense. Otherwise, 404 is the closest guidance supported here.

Google may be able to see the markup, but still not consider it eligible for rich results if the marked-up content doesn’t match the main focus of the page.

From the accepted answer, Google’s testing tool reported that the marked-up content “does not appear to be the main focus of the page,” and the page also had makesOffer specified twice. The guidance supported by that is to:

- make sure the structured data matches visible page content
- ensure the marked-up item is the main focus of the page
- remove duplicate properties like makesOffer if present twice

The warning you mention about needing price, review, or availability usually means the item markup is incomplete for rich snippet display. Based on the evidence here, the closest correction is to include the relevant visible product/offer details consistently in the page and schema, especially price and availability, and avoid duplicated or mismatched fields.

From the SEO perspective shown here, a domain that includes the main keyword is better than one that doesn’t, but the extra words in the domain don’t make a big practical difference.

So between alltogether.com and all-different-words.com, the closer keyword match is likely the better SEO choice. If one of them is a cleaner, more memorable .com, that can also matter for users. The guidance here suggests avoiding overthinking “keyword density” in the domain name itself, since any difference is likely small in practice.

The first option is more SEO-friendly and more user-friendly.

So between alltogether.com and all-different-words.com, the closer match to the SEO-friendly choice would be the cleaner, more compact URL if it reads well. If the words are awkward or overly split up, that is less ideal.

The supported guidance here is:
- cleaner, more readable URLs are better for SEO and users
- you can make a URL look clean while still using parameters behind the scenes with URL rewriting

If you want, I can also help compare those two specific domain styles for branding and readability.

Redirecting a non-existing post to the homepage is generally not a good SEO choice if your goal is to preserve relevance and rankings for that specific URL.

The evidence only directly supports this much: a JavaScript redirect is a bad idea for SEO, and if a page truly needs to move, a server-side 301 redirect is the right approach. It also suggests that if you can, you should replace the page rather than redirect it.

For a non-existing post, the closest guidance supported here is:
- don’t use a JavaScript redirect
- if there is a real old URL that has permanently moved, use a 301 redirect to the new relevant page
- if there is no equivalent page, redirecting everything to the homepage is not ideal from an SEO standpoint

If you want, I can also explain the SEO difference between redirecting to the homepage versus returning a 404/410 for missing posts.

The best practice is to separate the site’s visible structure from the internal file structure.

A redesign or reorganization usually should be handled with a consistent taxonomy and, ideally, a CMS or routing system that lets you change URLs based on the new information architecture. That way you can make the site easier for users to navigate without tying it to a messy folder layout.

For updating links after the redesign, the closest guidance supported here is:

- use the new, more logical URL structure for the updated site
- make sure the routing/file structure is consistent behind the scenes
- avoid redundant or overlapping categories
- base the new structure on how users think about the content, their segments, and common use cases

What this does not specifically cover is the exact migration process for old links. But the practical implication is that if URLs change, you should update links to match the new structure and keep the navigation aligned with the new information architecture.

Redirecting non-existing posts to the homepage is generally not a good SEO practice if the page is simply missing.

The safest approach is:
- If the content used to exist and has a close relevant replacement, redirect to that specific relevant page.
- If there is no relevant replacement, return a real 404 status and show a useful 404 page.

A custom 404 page can still be good for users if it includes search, helpful links, or related content. The important part is that it actually sends a 404 server status.

Automatically sending lots of missing URLs to the homepage can be confusing for users and search engines, especially if the URL was meant to represent a specific page that no longer exists.

The best-supported approach is to use 301 redirects for changed URLs and, if needed, a rel="canonical" signal for duplicate paths.

For a redesign or structure update, it also helps to:
- migrate gradually and keep old and new paths running in parallel where possible
- have the new site structure in place early
- use sitemaps to guide search engines to the new URLs
- avoid making everything switch at once if you can, since that can cause temporary ranking fluctuation
- time the migration so it doesn’t coincide with domain expiry/renewal
- make sure any changed links still point to the most appropriate destination for users

If your structure is changing a lot, the main practical rule is to preserve user value and give search engines clear signals about the new locations.

If you want to redirect www to non-www, the supported options here are:

1. Use two VirtualHost entries, one for the main domain and one for www, then redirect www:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot "/path/to/site"
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.example.com
    Redirect 301 / http://example.com/
</VirtualHost>

2. If you prefer .htaccess, put the redirect in the www site’s .htaccess:

Redirect 301 / http://example.com/

3. If you use one VirtualHost, set the main host plus ServerAlias and use rewrite rules in .htaccess:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    ServerAlias www.example.com
    DocumentRoot "/path/to/site"
</VirtualHost>

Then in .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/$1 [R=301,L]

The example you tried can lead to a redirect loop if the redirect is applied without a separate www host configuration.

To make `example.com` work instead of `www.example.com`, the provided solution uses `.htaccess` with a redirect from the `www` host to the non-`www` host:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/$1 [R=301,L]
```

Put the `.htaccess` file in your site’s root directory.
