- if you want all bots to crawl, you would not use a robots.txt that disallows everything.

No, you don’t need a robots.txt if you want all bots to crawl everything. If it’s missing, that’s generally interpreted as allowing crawling of your content.

A blank robots.txt is still recommended just to avoid unnecessary 404 errors in your stats.

This doesn’t say anything about sitemap.xml, so the closest guidance supported here is that robots.txt is not required for open crawling.

Google may be replacing your page title with the contents of your H1 tag because it couldn’t create a proper title from the text in your title tag, especially if the title contains Danish or other non-English text.

The closest guidance supported here is to:
- make sure your title tag has a clear, language-appropriate title,
- consider using an English title for google.com if that’s the audience you’re targeting,
- and, if needed, provide multilingual versions of the site.

If you want, I can also help you figure out why Google is showing the title twice in the snippet.

Those requests are not from a real Googlebot IP address, even though the IP belongs to Google and the user-agent says bingbot.

The closest explanation supported here is that they were likely made through Google’s PageSpeed service, which can act as a cache/proxy. In that case, a crawler such as Bing or Google may hit a PageSpeed URL, and PageSpeed forwards the request to your site from a Google IP, making it look like the traffic came from Google.

So based on this, it looks like:
- not a genuine Googlebot request
- user-agent alone is not enough to trust
- the Google IP can be explained by PageSpeed forwarding
- it does not directly identify a content scraper

This does not fully explain the huge drop in visits by itself. It only explains suspicious crawler requests and why they may appear to come from Google IPs.

Yes, if you want a proper XML sitemap, it should point to all pages you want search engines to know about, not just entry pages.

For a large site like a social network, the closest guidance here is:
- include each important URL you want indexed
- use the priority tag to indicate relative importance
- if you want it automatically updated, use Google’s sitemap guidance
- if you prefer, use an online XML sitemap generator

This doesn’t say you must include every possible page, but it does say the idea of a sitemap is to point to all pages. For very large sites, you’d follow Google’s sitemap instructions for automatic updating and management.

If you use a sitemap index file, you only need to submit or ping the index file once. You do not need to send separate requests for each sitemap listed in it.

If one of the sitemap files changes, make sure the index file has correct `lastmod` values. Googlebot is expected to use those timestamps and avoid reloading unchanged sitemaps.

If you want to verify what Google actually fetched, you can check your server access logs.

You can’t make Google index every URL in a sitemap.xml. A sitemap is only a discovery signal: it helps Google find pages that might be worth indexing, but Google still decides which URLs to include.

If only some submitted URLs are indexed, the likely reasons are that the others are considered low value or unsuitable for indexing, such as thin content, duplicate content, or poor content, or they are otherwise not being selected by Google’s indexing process.

So the closest guidance supported here is:
- make sure the pages are valuable and unique,
- ensure they’re crawlable and not blocked,
- and understand that even with a sitemap, Google may index only a subset of the URLs.

The closest thing to look for is historical WHOIS registration information: previous owner details and when transfers took place. If you want a record over time for a legacy domain, that kind of history is the main thing to check. One service mentioned for this is whois.sc, though it requires payment for historical access.

You generally want to know how the domain was previously used, because that history may include penalties or other problems that can make it hard to get indexed and rank well.

The main things to look for are:
- signs the domain may have been penalized or used in ways that violated search engine rules
- whether it had real traffic and backlinks
- any indication of suspicious or low-quality past use

In practice, that history is often hard to uncover, so if you can’t verify it, the safest approach supported here is to choose a domain you know had traffic and use a 301 redirect to your main domain.

Look for whether the domain has any current manual actions in Webmaster Tools, because those are shown there even if they were applied when someone else owned the domain.

If you’re worried about Panda or Penguin specifically, those were algorithms, not manual actions, so they wouldn’t appear as penalties you can review in Webmaster Tools.

For a legacy domain, the practical things to check are:
- current manual actions
- the link profile for spammy or paid links
- whether problematic links have been removed or disavowed
- whether settings like URL parameter handling and geotargeting were configured appropriately, since those can affect visibility after a move

If the decline happened after redirecting your old site to the legacy domain, it may take time for cleanup and reprocessing before any improvement shows.

The supported guidance here is to add your sitemap in robots.txt like this:

Sitemap: http://www.mysite.com/sitemap.xml

It also says that, for Google specifically, the best way is to sign up for a Google webmaster tools/Search Console account. Creating a Google Search page there helps ensure the sitemap is read and the site is spidered quickly.

It also mentions Google has a ping utility, but that it assumes a webmaster tools account, so the account route is the clearest recommendation.

You don’t need to create a separate sitemap just for the blog. One sitemap can cover pages across your site, even if different software generates them.

If you already have a Magento sitemap, Google can pick up the blog articles through that as long as the blog URLs are included in it. The key point is that search engines care about the final URLs, not what software created them.

If you want to keep things organized, you can make a separate sitemap for the blog, but that’s mainly for convenience, not because it’s required.

If you want Google Search Console to show your sitemap, report errors, and show index status, you need to submit it there.

If you only upload the sitemap to your server root, Google may still find and use it, but that is not guaranteed and it won’t appear in Search Console’s sitemap report unless you submit it.

You can also add this to robots.txt:

Sitemap: http://example.com/sitemap.xml

That can help Google and other search engines discover it, but it’s not the same as submitting it in Search Console.

Yes, it can happen in the sense that a competitor could point a redirect at your site and potentially cause your rankings to suffer. The provided answer says it’s possible to redirect your domain to a competitor and get them penalized.

It also says that if a site has already been penalized, redirecting it to a new domain won’t fix the problem because the penalty will follow the redirection.

So the closest guidance here is:
- redirects can carry penalties forward
- and, in the situation described, redirects may even be used to harm a competitor’s rankings

Yes, it appears competitors can try to hurt a site’s search ranking by building lots of low-quality, suspicious backlinks with exact-match anchor text. The example here says Google may detect those unnatural linking patterns and issue a warning in Webmaster Tools.

What this evidence does not prove is how reliably that will work in every case. It only supports that it’s possible to create a harmful-looking backlink profile and that search engines may react to it.

Yes, it’s possible for spammy or low-quality backlinks to hurt your site’s performance before Google takes any manual or serious algorithmic action.

What this covers:
- Google may not notify you unless the issue reaches a serious threshold and triggers a manual action or serious algorithmic action.
- A site can still have spammy links in its link profile that negatively affect performance without any notice.
- If your site also has a lot of strong links, the good may outweigh the bad for now.

What it doesn’t fully confirm:
- It doesn’t specifically prove that competitors can successfully get your site penalized.
- It only supports the idea that spammy links, no matter where they come from, can be harmful and may not always lead to a notice.

Closest guidance supported:
- Keep your link profile clean.
- Monitor and address suspicious backlinks, because they can affect your site even if Google doesn’t send a warning.

The best-supported way to find out why a site is being blocked by Websense is to check its category with Websense’s Site Lookup / URL Category tools, but those appear to be available only to paying customers. If you can’t use those tools, the guidance provided says to email suggest@websense.com for categorization-related inquiries and to request a review or category change.

For Sophos, the provided material does not say how to check the block reason. It only covers Websense specifically. So the closest guidance supported here is to identify the category using Websense’s lookup tools if possible, and otherwise contact suggest@websense.com to ask why the URL was categorized that way.

If you want, I can help you draft the email to request the classification and a review.

Yes, if you want Google to crawl and index pages on the social network, an XML sitemap can be useful. But the issue shown here is not really about whether you need one; it’s that Googlebot can’t reach your site’s robots.txt, so it can’t crawl the sitemap.

What this covers is that the problem is likely on the hosting/server side, not that the sitemap itself is invalid. The closest guidance supported here is to check with the site hoster and make sure Googlebot can access robots.txt and the site reliably. If Google can’t reach the site, the sitemap won’t help until that is fixed.

Making more pages public can help attract traffic if they’re pages people are likely to link to, especially player profiles and possibly forum threads. If players can share or embed their profiles on other sites, social networks, or forum signatures, that can bring in visitors. Public game statistics are less likely to help.

If your goal is search engine ranking specifically, the benefit depends on whether the links are followable; nofollowed links won’t help ranking, though they can still bring traffic.

A practical step is to make profiles easy to share or embed in a compelling format so others will want to link to them.

You do not insert the XML sitemap into an HTML page. It is a separate XML file on your server for web crawlers to find.

If you want crawlers to discover it, you can list its location in your robots.txt. There is also a plain text sitemap format with one absolute URL per line, but it has no metadata.

So, if your social network wants search engines or other crawlers to index its pages, an XML sitemap can be used; if not, it is not something you put into the site’s HTML.

You can make your website public by putting it on a web page that anyone can access, or by linking to it from your page.

The guidance here is about a public PGP key specifically: you can either paste the key directly on your page, or upload it to a public PGP key server and then add a link to that key on your website. If you use the same link in your emails and files too, you only have to update the key in one place.

If you want to reduce bots indexing it, you could also use a CAPTCHA or JavaScript to copy the key for the user.

If Sophos is blocking your site and you think it’s a false positive, submit a reassessment request to Sophos here:

https://www.sophos.com/en-us/threat-center/reassessment-request.aspx

Make sure you fill in all the fields.

If you’re not a Sophos customer and only know that someone else reported the block, try to find out which Sophos product alerted on the site, because that helps Sophos investigate faster. If you can’t determine it, enter your best guess in the required “Product” field. Sophos Anti-Virus is listed under “Endpoint Security and Control.”

I don’t have enough information here to say how to check Websense specifically, but for Sophos this is the supported path to find out why the site is blocked and request review.

Google’s +1 count was intended to influence search results in a broader way, not just for your friends and contacts. The accepted guidance says Google indicated that “+1’s can help friends, contacts, and others on the web find the best stuff when they search,” and that counts may be shown in search results even when none of your friends have +1’d a page.

What this supports is:
- +1s could affect how your page is presented in search results
- it may influence clicks by making results look more relevant or trusted
- it was described as impacting global search results, though not necessarily as a direct ranking factor in the same way as traditional SEO signals

It does not clearly prove that +1 count directly boosts rankings in a measurable universal way, only that it can be reflected in search and potentially help visibility and click-through.

Anti-hotlinking is done by checking the HTTP referrer and blocking image requests that come from other sites.

In the example provided, the fix is to escape the dots in the domain name:

```apache
Options +FollowSymlinks
Options +SymlinksIfOwnerMatch

RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^http://(.+\.)?article-stack\.com/ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^$
ReWriteRule .*.(png|gif|jpg)$ - [N,F,L]
```

The key point is that `article-stack.com` should be written as `article-stack\.com` in the regex.

Anti-hotlinking is done here by using an aws:Referer bucket policy on the Amazon S3 bucket instead of serving a separate HTML file to hotlinked image requests.

The available information doesn’t explain the full setup, but it does indicate that the recommended method is to restrict access based on the Referer header using an S3 bucket policy.

For a database-driven site, the important part is that Google can crawl the pages it can reach through normal URLs, not whether the content comes from a database or static files.

What the thread supports is:

- Google’s crawler visits pages over time and fetches pages it can access.
- Content that is only created dynamically in the browser with Ajax may not be understood the same way as content returned in the HTML response.
- If you want Google to see the content reliably, it should be present in the HTML returned for that page.
- You should have unique, crawlable URLs for unique content, such as `http://example.com/thread?id=101`, rather than only a single root page with changing widgets.

So for a database-driven site, the usual approach is to generate a distinct HTML page for each item or thread from the database. Google then crawls those URLs like any other pages.

The thread does not fully explain Googlebot’s internal storage or exact AdSense behavior, but it does support the general idea that Google crawls page URLs, extracts content from the returned HTML, and uses that to index pages.

Google bots work like other normal search-engine bots: they crawl your site, and the good ones obey robots.txt. If your site is database-driven, the main point from the guidance here is that you need to understand and control what the bot can access at the domain/IP and robots.txt level, because bots can be forged and some ignore robots.txt.

So for a database-driven site, the closest supported guidance is:
- allow the major search bots you want, like Google
- make sure they can reach the pages you want indexed
- use robots.txt to control crawling
- don’t rely only on the user-agent name, since it can be spoofed
- watch logs and block bad or stealth bots as needed

This does not give specific details on how Google crawls dynamic database pages, only that legitimate search bots will crawl your site if allowed and that access control matters.

Google bots work by crawling your site like other search-engine bots, but for a database-driven site you usually don’t want to block them with robots.txt if you want indexing and AdSense-related crawling to continue.

The guidance here is to let bots crawl, and instead separate the hits you log from the hits you don’t log. A practical way is to check the visitor’s user agent and only store requests that match the kinds of clients you care about.

So for a database-driven site, the idea is:

- serve normal pages dynamically from your database as usual
- allow search-engine crawlers to access those pages
- identify bot requests by user agent if you need to avoid counting them in your database
- don’t use robots.txt just to stop logging, because that can also stop useful crawling

The closest supported solution is to detect crawler user agents in your PHP code and skip database logging for those requests.

Google does not prefer HTML sites over WordPress sites just because of the platform itself. The evidence only supports that Google can penalize certain page layouts, such as having too many ads above the fold or intrusive pop-ups, especially on mobile.

So for SEO, the important factor is not whether the site is HTML or WordPress, but whether the site has good content and a user-friendly layout without intrusive pop-ups or excessive ads.

There’s no evidence here that Google prefers HTML sites over WordPress sites.

What this does support is that people often believe WordPress may help with SEO because it can make it easier to configure things like meta information correctly, but the thread shown has no answer on record, so it doesn’t confirm that as fact either.

So the closest supported guidance is: Google’s preference is not established here as being about WordPress vs. custom HTML; the main SEO advantage mentioned is easier correct configuration, not a different site type itself.

There’s no evidence here that Google prefers HTML sites over WordPress sites, or that it favors WordPress/CMS sites for local search.

What this does cover is the common rumor that WordPress has “top-notch SEO” and that search engines may be designed to favor WordPress-based or CMS-based sites, but the thread has no answer on record, so that claim isn’t confirmed.

Closest guidance supported by the evidence: there’s no basis here for assuming you should remake a hand-coded site in WordPress just to get better Google rankings.

In general, having keywords in the URL is a plus because it can help SEO and users understand what the page is about.

But in this case, changing the URL structure would be pointless. Your current URL already includes keywords, including the main one you care about. Based on the evidence, changing it now would likely make no difference or could even hurt your rankings.

The easiest approach is to use a small PHP microframework that supports “pretty URLs” through routes, such as Slim, Flight, Limonade, or Glue.

These frameworks typically use Apache rewrite rules in an .htaccess file to send all requests to a single index.php file, where you define the routes. That setup is the front controller pattern.

If you don’t want a framework, you can build your own front controller and rewrite rules, but for a small dynamic site, using one of those microframeworks is the simplest route.

Use 301 redirects and drop the file extensions.

If you’re changing a dynamic PHP site’s URL structure, the safest supported approach here is to make the new URLs permanent with 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new ones. The answer also recommends not exposing file extensions in the URL, since they don’t add value to visitors and make future technology changes harder.

So, the closest guidance supported by the thread is:

- keep a stable, clean URL format
- redirect old URLs to new URLs with 301s
- avoid broadcasting `.php` in the URL unless you have a strong reason to keep it

The thread does not give a detailed implementation plan, but it does suggest that rankings may stay the same, improve, or drop depending on broader search algorithm changes rather than the redirect method itself.

Google crawlers can see PHP dynamic content as long as PHP is processed on the server and the crawler receives the resulting HTML.

What Google sees is not the PHP code itself, but the HTML that PHP generates. So if your PHP script pulls content from a database and outputs normal HTML, Google can read it.

The main caveat from the evidence is that if important things like the page title keep changing without a good reason, that can hurt SEO. If the dynamic content is just how your site generates different pages, that is fine.

Googlebot fetches sitemap files itself, and the fetch frequency seems to depend on PageRank and how often the site changes. So the practical guidance here is: submitting a dynamic sitemap should only help, and if Googlebot finds new URLs in it, it should crawl those URLs right away.

This doesn’t directly explain PHP dynamic content specifically. The closest supported guidance is that Googlebot can discover and crawl URLs it finds in your sitemap, and it also crawls pages on its own schedule based on the site’s characteristics.

Google can crawl PHP dynamic content the same way it crawls any other page: it has to be able to discover the URL, usually by following links.

If the dynamic pages are not linked from your site, Google may not find them even if they’re in a sitemap. Google can look at a sitemap and still choose not to use it, preferring to crawl by links.

So the practical guidance is:
- If those pages matter to users, link to them from your site in a natural way.
- If they’re not linked and not meant for users, Google may not crawl them reliably.
- If they’re already discoverable, Google will eventually revisit them and notice changes over time.

In short: to get Google to see PHP dynamic pages, make sure the URLs are linked in a way Google can crawl, not just generated dynamically or listed only in a sitemap.

You generally can’t rely on search-engine indexing of your own internal search results pages, because search engines tend to avoid indexing search results from other sites.

The closest workable approach is to create crawlable, stable pages that link to those database-generated results pages. For example:

- add a “recent searches” section on the home page linking to the last 10–20 query result URLs
- add “related searches” links on each results page
- add static or semi-static browse pages like:
  - trending searches
  - most popular searches
  - popular tags/categories

Those pages can be generated automatically from your query data, and they give search engines entry points into your content. Once crawlers reach those pages, they can follow links deeper into the site.

So instead of trying to make every possible query URL discoverable in advance, create a smaller set of useful, linkable hub pages that point to your dynamic content.

Create separate, crawlable URLs for each meaningful result or page of database-generated content, and make them accessible with GET rather than only through a form POST.

For example, instead of only showing results after a user submits a form, use URLs like:

example.com/search.php?coatcolor=brown  
example.com/search.php?coatcolor=black  
example.com/search.php?coatcolor=white  
example.com/search.php?coatcolor=black&spots=white

That way, search engines can index those pages directly, and users can also bookmark them, share them, and use browser history properly.

A separate dumped page that redirects to the main page is not the best approach. The better approach is to make the actual result pages available at their own URLs. If possible, use a RESTful, stateless design where each searchable result set has its own address.

If each generated page has enough distinct content, that can be fine for search engines to index. The guidance here is that using a query string instead of rewriting the URL does not really change how Google understands the keywords in the URL; Google is said to treat keywords in the path and in the query string similarly.

So the closest supported advice is:

- It’s okay to have database-generated, categorized pages indexed if they represent meaningful, distinct pages.
- Don’t rely on stuffing lots of keywords into the URL.
- Using only 3–4 relevant keywords in the URL is suggested, with the rest handled elsewhere if needed.
- Query strings are not a special fix for SEO risk; they are still understood by Google.

In short, create clean URLs for pages that correspond to real categories or distinct results, and avoid long spammy keyword lists in the URL.

For an ASP.NET site with a database, the closest guidance here is about deployment rather than SEO.

What it covers:
- Use a hosting company that supports .NET and MS SQL.
- Create the database on the host.
- Use the host’s connection string in your app.
- Upload the site and copy your table definitions/data to the remote database.
- Test that everything works.

It does not explain SEO for database-driven web apps.

If your goal is SEO, the general practical implication is that your database-backed pages still need to be served from a properly deployed ASP.NET site with working remote database access. Beyond that, this material doesn’t provide SEO-specific steps.

For a database-driven site in ASP.NET, the main idea is:

- Make each dynamic page have its own unique `title`, `h1`, and `meta description`, pulled from the database.
- Avoid repeated content across pages.
- Use human-readable URLs instead of query strings or numeric IDs.

For example, instead of:

`http://site.com/page.aspx?id=54637`

use something like:

`http://site.com/cats`

To do that, store an alias/slug field in your database for each item or article, and make sure it is unique.

If you want, I can also show how to implement this in ASP.NET specifically.

Yes, in general people often do see .com as a bit more trustworthy, or at least more familiar. That may be partly because .com is the most widely used and .net has often been associated with sites that didn’t get the .com.

If you already control both domains, it makes sense to use the .com as the main public-facing address and keep .net redirecting to it. Since you own both, the cost of switching is relatively small.

The key thing is to set up a 301 redirect from the old domain to the new one so visitors and search engines are sent to the right place.

If you move to .com, update your site materials and branding so people see the .com going forward. Keep the .net redirect in place so anyone who still types it can reach the site.

`.com` is the most recognized and is generally the best first choice if you can get a good, memorable one.

The rough intended meanings are:
- `.com` = commercial/company presence
- `.net` = network/company web presence; often used by ISPs historically
- `.org` = organization, typically non-profit

In practice, people often use `.net` or `.org` when the `.com` is taken, mostly because they’re also familiar and recognized.

The main advantage of `.com` is recognition and habit: many users will assume `.com` by default. That can make it easier to remember and type.

The main advantage of `.net` or `.org` is that a better-fitting, memorable domain there is preferable to a bad or confusing `.com`. If the `.com` is already taken and not suitable, choosing a good `.net` or `.org` can be the better option.

The drop is most likely because Google is deindexing low-quality or duplicate pages, not because of a server, DNS, or page error issue.

In the case described, the pages were generated by replacing keywords in existing content, which Google treats as low-quality/spun content. The expected behavior is that Google continues removing more of those pages from its index, and it could eventually remove the site’s pages much more broadly.

There isn’t a workaround supported by this evidence other than improving the content quality and reducing duplication.

The main difference is not SEO “power” by itself, but where the domain is considered relevant.

Some domains are treated as country-specific, so they mainly rank in that country. Others are generic and can rank worldwide.

From the evidence provided:
- `.com` is generic and can rank worldwide.
- `.org` and `.net` are not specifically called out in the evidence, but they are generally in the same “generic” category as `.com` in the context of global ranking.
- Country-targeted domains can help you rank better in that country than a generic domain, especially if the site is adjusted for local spelling, prices, and shipping.
- Owning the `.com` version can be advantageous if someone else owns the same name on another generic domain, because they may compete for the same brand name globally.
- Reputation matters: the domain with the most reputation tends to do better in search results.

So the practical difference between `.com`, `.org`, and `.net` is usually branding and availability, not a built-in SEO advantage. If you are targeting a specific country, a country-targeted domain can be better for that market; if you want broad/global reach, a generic domain like `.com` is appropriate.

A sudden drop like that can happen if Google is reporting fewer pages in Webmaster Tools, even while many pages are still actually indexed. In the example provided, it happened to a site affected by Panda, and the reported indexed count fell dramatically before later recovering.

The closest guidance supported by the evidence is to review site quality and crawlability, especially:
- redirecting poor-quality pages to newer, more relevant pages
- fixing broken links
- removing links to poor-quality pages from higher-quality pages

So the decline may reflect Google re-evaluating the site rather than all pages being removed from the index.

The reduction is consistent with Google dropping low-quality, duplicate, or near-duplicate pages from its index.

From the information provided, there’s no sign of a server, DNS, or crawl error causing the drop. The likely cause is the content itself: pages were generated by keyword replacement from existing content, which is the kind of content Google tries to exclude.

Based on that, there isn’t a workaround to keep those pages indexed as-is. The closest supported guidance is to improve the pages so they’re genuinely unique and useful, rather than mass-generated duplicates. If not, the decline in indexed pages may continue.

A sudden drop in indexed pages can happen if Google is having trouble reaching your site or if site configuration changed. In the case described, Googlebot reported DNS lookup errors and trouble accessing the site, which fits the kind of issue that can reduce indexing.

The best next step supported here is to crawl the site yourself with a tool like Xenu’s Link Sleuth to find broken or inaccessible links and pages. Fix any broken links you find, or redirect them to pages that do exist. If you’re using Drupal, there may also be a built-in way to handle redirects.

Also, since the message mentions DNS errors, it would be sensible to check your DNS/server availability and whether the site is overloaded or intermittently unreachable, because that can also cause Google to index fewer pages.
Yes. The information provided says there is an upper bound of 20 properties per account in Google Analytics. Once that limit is reached, additional properties cannot be created.

If the pages are still showing up in Google search, then the issue is likely with the sitemap or Google Webmaster Tools reporting, not necessarily with indexing itself.

What to check:
- Whether Webmaster Tools is showing a sitemap error
- Whether the sitemap passes the “Test Sitemap” function
- Whether the sitemap loads correctly in a browser
- Whether the URLs in the sitemap exactly match the live pages
- Whether anything looks wrong under Index Status / Health

If none of those show a problem, it may just be a temporary reporting glitch in Webmaster Tools and could correct itself within 24 hours.

A big drop in the number of pages reported as indexed can happen even when the pages are still in Google’s search index.

In the example provided, the site had been hit by Panda, and about a month after the initial traffic drop, the reported indexed pages fell to almost zero. After making crawlability improvements, the reported count later returned to normal levels over a few months.

The improvements that were made were:

- Redirecting poor-quality pages to newer, better, relevant pages
- Fixing broken links
- Removing links to the poor-quality pages from higher-quality pages

So the closest guidance supported here is to review crawlability and page quality, especially if the site may have been affected by Panda.

The evidence only says that bounce rate can be affected in Google Analytics by tracking a click as an event, so that action won’t count as a bounce. It does not say anything about Google using bounce rate as a ranking factor.

So, based on this evidence alone, I can’t confirm that a site’s bounce rate influences Google rankings.

No. The information provided only says Google Analytics and Alexa have nothing to do with one another. It does not address Google rankings or whether bounce rate affects them.

The closest guidance supported here is that metrics from one analytics service do not necessarily influence another service’s rankings. But this does not prove anything about bounce rate and Google.

No. The evidence says Google does not use Google Analytics information in its ranking algorithms, and the accepted answer specifically says the answer is “no” when asked whether Google uses that data. So a site’s bounce rate, as measured in Analytics, would not directly influence Google rankings based on this information.

Yes, there can be a trade-off.

With lazy loading via Ajax, search engines may not crawl or index that content unless you make it crawlable by other means, such as keeping it statically available in the page, using an Ajax-crawlable setup, or making it available through a sitemap.

So for content that matters for search visibility, you should be careful about loading it only on scroll. If it’s secondary content, lazy loading can make sense for performance. But it’s not guaranteed to improve overall load time, since the Ajax script still has to run and fetch the content in the background, and that can even make things slower.

In short: lazy load non-essential content when it helps the user, but be careful with anything important for SEO.

Because a meta description isn’t mainly for ranking; it’s for influencing what people see and click in the search results.

If you don’t provide one, Google may show article text instead, but that auto-generated snippet may not be the best summary or the most persuasive one. A good meta description can:

- better describe the page
- attract more clicks from the SERP
- help users understand the page before they click

The best-supported point here is that Google does not use the meta description directly as a ranking factor. But if a better description leads to more clicks, that can indirectly help over time, since user behavior matters.

So the practical reason to use it is not “to rank by existing,” but “to control and improve how your page is presented to searchers.”

Because Google does not always use the article text as the snippet.

The meta description is still useful when:
- the search terms don’t appear on the page, or don’t appear near a good excerpt
- Google wants a clearer, more focused summary of the page
- you want to reduce “click and backtrack” by giving users a better idea of what the page is about

Google can show text from the page if it’s relevant, but it also uses meta descriptions when available, and often prefers them because they can give a cleaner summary.

So the practical reason to use it is: it gives search engines a good fallback snippet and can improve how your result is presented in SERP, even though it doesn’t help rankings.

Anti-hotlinking can be done with rewrite rules that check the HTTP Referer and redirect image requests from other sites.

For example:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  !^$
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  !^https?://www\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  !^https?://subdomain\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule .*\.(jpg|jpeg|gif|png|bmp)$ http://google.com/thief.png [R,NC,L]

If you want to allow people to view images when the referer is empty as well:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  ^$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  !^https?://www\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER}  !^https?://subdomain\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule .*\.(jpg|jpeg|gif|png|bmp)$ http://google.com/thief.png [R,NC,L]

This blocks image requests that do not come from your allowed domains.

If the deleted page is not being replaced by new content, use a 410 GONE response rather than a 301 redirect.

The page can still show a helpful message explaining that it’s gone and provide links to your home page, sitemap, search page, and similar content if available.

A 301 redirect is more appropriate when the old URL has a new replacement destination.

A 301 redirect can point a deleted file to either another file or a web page, including a “pretty URL” with no extension.

Based on the answer shown, the supported approach is to add a separate redirect rule for each old file, for example:

Redirect 301 /fa/home.html http://www.mscaspian.com/fa/
Redirect 301 /about.html http://www.mscaspian.com/fa/about
Redirect 301 /contact.html http://www.mscaspian.com/fa/contact

It also notes that if you’re redirecting to a WordPress URL without an extension, that works as long as the pretty permalink setup is enabled before the redirects.

The answer does not give a method for redirecting all deleted files with one universal rule, only individual redirects like the examples above.

A 301 redirect is generally a bad idea when the old page and the destination page are not relevant to each other.

The guidance here says:

- Redirects are fine when the content is relevant.
- If you redirect deleted pages to an unrelated homepage, that can be a poor user experience.
- It may also carry risk from an SEO standpoint because the links and keywords may not match well.
- In that case, a 410 Gone is sometimes better and safer.

So for deleted pages with unrelated replacement content, the closest supported advice is not to 301 them all to the homepage; use 410 Gone if there isn’t a relevant destination.

Use Google Webmaster Tools to remove pages from the search index for sites you own.

Then use a robots.txt file to ask most major search engines not to index parts of your site. Examples:

Disallow a page:
Disallow: /private_file.html

Disallow a directory:
Disallow: /directory/

This should help prevent indexing of the under-construction or admin areas.

No, repeated blocks like headers, footers, sidebars, newsletter widgets, author blurbs, or featured-item sections are generally not treated as duplicate content by search engines as long as they aren’t the main content of the page.

The concern is mainly when the primary “meat” of multiple pages is the same or very similar. Repeated supporting text across posts is common and usually fine.

A practical way to reduce any ambiguity is to mark those repeated sections with semantic HTML like aside or footer, and optionally add schema.org metadata so search engines can better understand what those pieces are.

To keep Google from indexing pages while your site is under construction, the supported guidance here is to use robots meta tags:

- On the index page, use:
`<meta name="Robots" content="INDEX, FOLLOW" />`

- On other pages, use:
`<meta name="Robots" content="NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW" />`

This would let the index page be indexed while telling search engines not to index the other pages. If your goal is to prevent indexing of the whole site except the domain landing page, this is the closest guidance provided.

No, not if `www.mysite.net`, `www.mysite.net/`, and `www.mysite.net/index.html` all serve identical or nearly identical content and each page uses a canonical tag pointing to `www.mysite.net`.

That said, using only a canonical tag does not really fix the crawl-efficiency issue. Search engines may still crawl all three URLs even though they represent the same content. For simple URL variants like these, a 301 redirect to the canonical URL is usually the better solution.

So, based on the evidence: canonical alone can prevent duplicate-content confusion if the content is the same, but redirects are preferable for URL variants like with/without trailing slash, index.html, or www/non-www.

Do a 301 redirect from the old URL pattern to the new one. That’s the supported way to have Google replace the old URLs in its index with the new URLs over time.

A robots.txt disallow like `Disallow: /search.php?key=*` is not the guidance supported here for solving duplicate content.

Making a word plural in the domain or URL is not especially relevant for SEO. The guidance here is to choose the URL structure that is most logical and readable for users, rather than trying to force both singular and plural forms into the URL.

Google already understands the relationship between singular and plural forms, so “house” and “houses” are closely related in search. Using both in the URL is unlikely to provide much SEO benefit, since keywords in the URL count very little.

A brand should be easily identifiable, so having multiple spellings is likely to create confusion rather than strengthen it.

If you’re targeting both the US and the UK, it’s better to choose a name that works well in both cultures instead of centering the brand around one spelling or trying to make plural/similar variants do the work. That will usually be more cohesive and easier for people to remember.

The main factor is whether people are more likely to search for the plural or the singular form. If the plural gets searched more often, that’s the only real advantage of choosing it.

The closest guidance supported here is to check search demand for both versions. If your budget allows, buying both and redirecting one to the other is suggested so you can avoid losing the other version to a competitor or squatter. If you can’t afford both, then choosing the form people are more likely to search for is the relevant criterion.

404 pages are not covered by the provided information, so I can’t say definitively whether they hurt rankings.

What the provided answer does cover is that shortened outbound URLs generally aren’t considered harmful to SEO in the way the question asked; at most, they may pass a little less link equity than direct links, similar to a 301 redirect.

Closest guidance supported here: if you’re worried about SEO impact from links on your pages, the main issue mentioned is a small loss of link juice from shortened outbound URLs, not a major ranking penalty.

No. Serving a proper 404 for a page that doesn’t exist won’t hurt your site ranking. It’s the correct behavior, and the missing page will be removed from search results, which is expected.

If you want, showing search results or other helpful navigation on the 404 page can improve usability and give visitors another chance to find what they need.

No. Proper 404s are normal and do not hurt the ranking of your site’s other pages. Search engines can tell when a page is gone, and they prefer a proper 404 or 410 response over a “soft 404.”

What this does mean is that the missing URLs themselves won’t rank, but the 404s on removed pages do not affect how your existing pages perform in search results.

If the old Joomla URLs still have links or traffic, the closest guidance supported here is to make sure removed pages return a real 404 or 410, and use redirects only where you have a relevant new page to send users to.

Hiding images on a 404 page would not, by itself, be expected to affect SEO based on the evidence here.

What the evidence does support is:
- 404 pages can be fine for pages that no longer exist.
- Google generally does not treat 404 errors as harmful to ranking.
- The important part is that the page actually returns a real 404 server status.
- Problems arise more if your site keeps linking to lots of non-existing pages.

So if you mean “does making the 404 page visually simpler by not showing images hurt SEO?” the closest supported answer is no, not directly. The more important SEO issue is whether the page is a proper 404 and whether your site is generating or linking to many broken URLs.

Hiding or adding content on a 404 page won’t affect SEO in the way you’re worried about, because Google only looks at the HTTP 404 response, not the page content.

So:
- no PageRank is passed from links on the 404 page
- a 404 page with lots of links is not treated as cloaking or doorway behavior by itself
- redirecting users to a separate `/404` URL doesn’t help SEO and just adds another redirect step
- adding helpful links on the 404 page is fine for visitors

If you mean hiding images specifically on a 404 page, this evidence doesn’t address images directly, but the supported guidance is that content on the 404 page itself does not get SEO value as long as the server returns the 404 status.

If you mean using a URL like `find-new/posts&recent=1` as your homepage, the provided material doesn’t directly address SEO for that setup. It only says you can check Google PageRank for any URL with a PageRank checker, and that there are free SEO-related tools available for evaluating a site.

So the closest supported guidance is:
- You can check the SEO/PageRank status of that homepage URL with a tool like `prchecker.info`.
- You can use other SEO tools to assess whether that page is “SEO ready.”

It does not say whether a URL with query parameters is good or bad for SEO.

A homepage that shows latest posts can be good for SEO, and the cited answer suggests combining freshness with keyword optimization.

The guidance supported here is:
- Google likes fresh content.
- Showing latest posts on the homepage may help search engines crawl it more often.
- If the homepage is also optimized for your primary keyword, that can be a strong setup.

So if your homepage is `find-new/posts&recent=1`, the closest supported advice is to make sure it still includes your primary keyword optimization, not just recent posts alone.

URLs with `?page=something` are not inherently bad for SEO.

From the evidence provided, the key point is that changing the URL format or adding a file-like extension does not itself improve rankings. The same logic applies here: using a query parameter like `?page=...` is not automatically harmful, and there is no SEO benefit just from changing it to a different-looking URL.

If possible, the cleaner approach is usually to avoid unnecessary URL complexity or extra rewriting, since that can add server processing without SEO gain.

URLs with `?page=something` are not inherently bad for SEO based on this. The issue in the example was 404 errors: Google was finding URLs that no longer exist, likely from other sites linking to them.

What the guidance supports is:
- If a URL is genuinely gone, returning a `410 Gone` is better than leaving it as a 404.
- Google may keep trying old URLs if it thinks they should still exist.

So `?page=` itself isn’t shown to be a problem here. If those URLs are valid, they should work normally. If they’re not valid and you want Google to stop checking them, the closest supported advice is to return `410 Gone`.

No. Based on this, query-style URLs like `?page=something` are not described as bad for SEO.

The guidance here is that small URL variations like the order of path parts generally don’t matter enough for search engines to be worth worrying about. The main advice is to pick one URL format and stick with it.

It also suggests avoiding unnecessary IDs in URLs if they don’t serve a purpose, because changing them later can create broken links and re-indexing issues.

You need to use the nameservers provided by Network Solutions, not the FTP server name.

You should enter at least two nameservers, and GoDaddy allows more than three if needed.

Also make sure your website files are uploaded to the new hosting account first. After the DNS changes propagate, the domain will point to the new host.

The best option is usually to change the domain’s nameservers to your web host’s nameservers.

The guidance says that unless you have a static IP, you should point the domain to the web host’s nameservers. Even if you have a unique IP, it can still change if the host moves you to another server or restructures the network.

Manually creating an A record is only the less common choice.

The shorter and closer to the root the URL is, the better. A URL like:

www.example.com/products/page_name/123

is preferable because it gives both users and Google enough context while staying relatively short and simple.

So yes, there is some effect from being deeper in the path, but the advice to reduce it to only 2 elements is too absolute. The best supported guidance here is to keep the URL as short and simple as practical, and prefer a structure closer to the root domain.

If Websense is blocking the site, the guidance here is to have users ask their Help Desk or IT administrator to change the site’s category, since they can override Websense’s categorization. You can also ask Websense to reevaluate the categorization by emailing suggest@websense.com.

This covers Websense. It does not explain how to find the exact reason Sophos is blocking the site, but the closest supported next step would be to check with Sophos’s categorization or filtering support in the same way and request a review/recategorization if it has been classified incorrectly.

If `category` and `subCategory` change what content is shown on `itemList.php`, you usually don’t need to configure anything in Google’s URL Parameters tool. The default setting, “let Google decide,” is generally fine.

Googlebot will understand that those parameters create different content, so it can treat those URLs as distinct pages. The URL Parameters tool is mainly useful for parameters that do not change page content, such as tracking parameters, where you want Google to ignore them.

A couple of important points:
- The settings are site-wide, not per-page.
- If you mark `category` as content-changing, Google applies that understanding across the site.
- That usually isn’t a problem, because Google will only use the parameter where it actually sees it in URLs.

So the closest guidance is: leave URL Parameters alone unless you have parameters that don’t affect content and you want Google to ignore them.

SEO-friendly URLs can help, but they should not come at the expense of readability.

A good URL should make sense to humans at a glance and usually be close to the page or article title. Putting a few relevant keywords in the slug can be fine, but stuffing it with lots of search terms is likely to look spammy and may not actually help if those terms don’t reflect the content.

So the balance is:

- human-friendly first
- include relevant keywords naturally
- avoid keyword stuffing
- keep URLs reasonably short; one recommendation is 10 words or less

In short, SEO is important, but a clear, human-friendly URL is generally the better practice, and the SEO benefit can come naturally when the URL matches the content.

A meta description is still useful because it lets you suggest the search result text instead of relying on Google to choose page content automatically.

If you do not provide a meta description, Google may show article text from the page, but that is not guaranteed and you do not control which text is chosen. The meta description gives you more control over the snippet users see in search results.

What your evidence does cover is a different issue: the text shown before the result, such as a date or other extra information, is not controlled by the meta description. That kind of display is rich snippet data, and the supported way to influence it is with Schema markup, such as BlogPosting schema for an article page.

So:
- meta description: controls or influences the snippet text
- Schema markup: can help Google show extra structured information like dates or other rich results

A human-friendly URL is generally better when you can make it also relevant to the content. URLs that closely match the page title tend to make more sense at a glance, and the same words appearing in both the URL and the page content can help SEO as a by-product.

Packing a URL with only expected keywords can cross into keyword stuffing. That may look spammy and may not help if the keywords aren’t actually relevant to the content. The supported guidance here is to keep URLs understandable to humans and use relevant keywords naturally, rather than prioritizing SEO at the expense of readability.

A practical recommendation given here is to keep URLs fairly short, around 10 words or fewer.

The evidence doesn’t directly compare friendly path URLs against query parameters, but the closest supported guidance is: choose the form that makes the URL clearer and more meaningful, and avoid overloading it with keywords.

From the evidence provided, the main guidance is that if the query string is just for tracking, the redirect should keep the query string on the new URL.

In that example, the recommended redirect is:

So, based on this evidence:

- Friendly URLs without query strings are not shown here as inherently better for SEO.
- The supported advice is to preserve the query string on the new URL when redirecting old URLs.

Using URL parameters or a deeper URL path can matter for SEO, but the effect is not absolute. The closer a page is to the root domain, the more prominence Google may give it, so a shorter, simpler URL is generally preferred.

From the evidence here, a URL like `www.example.com/products/page_name/123` would be better than a longer, more deeply nested path. It does not say that longer URLs are “catastrophically” bad, only that keeping them short and closer to the root is preferable.

So yes, it can be worth simplifying the structure, but the SEO concern seems overstated if the claim is that the current format is inherently disastrous.

http://www.example.com/category/filter?page=1&sort=price-asc&limit=20

That’s preferable to a path structure like `/page:1/sort:price-asc/limit:20`, since it avoids awkward reserved characters like colons and keeps the URL cleaner.

Based on the evidence, it is not a good SEO practice to nofollow internal links. The guidance given says “Don’t nofollow internal links,” and that a flat `#` destination does not really link anywhere, so there’s still no reason to do it.

For labels and tags specifically, the closest supported guidance is:

- if a link doesn’t really go anywhere, it’s better to avoid making it a fake link than to add `nofollow` or `noindex`.

There are many alternatives to AdSense. The best guidance here is to look at competitors’ sites and see who advertises with them, especially ad networks aimed at the same market as your site.

You also don’t need a big-name sponsor. Search Google for ads relevant to your niche and contact those advertisers; if they already advertise on Google, they may be willing to place ads with you too, especially if your content is focused on a niche.

If your site is about a product, affiliate programs are another option. Amazon is a reasonable place to start.

If you want the closest practical answer to “make the most money,” the evidence doesn’t name a single best replacement, but it suggests finding niche-targeted advertisers or affiliate deals rather than relying on a general ad network alone.

The only thing this covers is that AdSense revenue is generally based on ad clicks and/or ad views, and traffic volume can affect total earnings simply because more visitors can mean more opportunities for clicks or views.

It does not say that one click on a higher-traffic site automatically pays more than one click on a lower-traffic site. Based on this, the closest guidance is: revenue depends on how the ad is billed and how users interact with it, not just on the site’s traffic level.

So for a one-time-use high-traffic website, this evidence supports only the general idea that an ad model tied to clicks or impressions is relevant, but it does not identify the best service or guarantee higher per-click revenue because of traffic.

Adbrite is specifically noted as allowing you to put in your own ads, which may help if you want more control over relevance.

For a one-time-use, high-traffic website, AdSense is probably not a good fit unless your traffic is very large and the audience is well matched to the ads. The guidance here suggests that even a site with very high traffic can still earn disappointingly little from AdSense, and that hand-selected ads targeted to the audience may perform much better.

What this does support is:
- AdSense is often weak on relevance and earnings.
- A small site with around 50 visitors/day is not worth it for AdSense.
- Even a very large site can struggle to make meaningful revenue from AdSense alone.

Closest practical guidance: if you want ad revenue, a targeted ad arrangement or manually selected sponsors would likely be a better model than relying on AdSense. If the site is truly one-time-use, the effort to set up AdSense may not be justified unless you expect substantial, sustained traffic.

If the URL is truly gone, a 410 Gone is a reasonable option. The supported guidance here is that you can return 410 and show a page with other similar documents or products the user may be interested in, which may still help convert visitors into sales.

MailChimp is a solid option if you want something simple and affordable. The recommendation here is to use a hosted service rather than running your own, because it tends to give better deliverability and more tools for making newsletters look good.

If the exact search term is “John Smith,” then `/johnsmith` is likely to be more SEO friendly than `/john`, because it matches the full query more closely. The guidance here is that a URL matching the complete search term is generally a better fit for that target search, so the full-name URL would likely have the advantage.

Friendly URLs have these advantages in the evidence:

- Better for users who type URLs by hand.
- More resilient when part of the URL is missing: if the page ID is near the front and the descriptive keywords are later, the page can still load even if the end is cut off.

The evidence does not give direct disadvantages of friendly URLs or direct advantages of query parameters. The closest supported implication is that query parameters are less effective for those user/SEO benefits, while friendly URLs are recommended if you want those benefits.

So, based on the provided text:

- Query parameters: the text does not discuss concrete pros/cons, other than implying they are not as good for keyword-rich, user-friendly URLs.

Yes, it can affect SEO if Disqus creates a large number of internal broken URLs on your WordPress site. The answer here says a large number of broken links can make a site look low quality and may trigger ranking drops and fewer pages in Google’s results.

robots.txt can discourage crawling, but it does not reliably hide a site from search results. Search engines may still list the URL, especially if they already know about it or find links to it.

The closest guidance supported here is:

- Use server-side blocking instead of relying on robots.txt.
- If possible, protect the site with HTTP authentication.
- If you can’t use password protection, restrict access at the web server level with IP allow/deny rules in .htaccess or the main server config.
- Returning a 403 response can help signal crawlers not to access it.
- Blocking known crawler user agents in .htaccess is another option, though it’s less robust than access control.

You don’t rewrite to `.htaccess` in PHP; `.htaccess` is an Apache config file. The likely fixes are to enable Apache’s rewrite module and allow overrides for the directory.

Two things to check:

- Make sure mod_rewrite is enabled, for example with `a2enmod rewrite`
- In your Apache config, allow `.htaccess` overrides by changing `AllowOverride none` to `AllowOverride all`

The `.htaccess` rule you showed is:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule .* index.php/$0 [PT,L]
```

If it still doesn’t work after those server-side settings are corrected, then the issue is not with PHP but with Apache configuration.

Put this in your `.htaccess` file:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^script/(\w+)\.png$ script/image.php?name=$1 [L]
```

This rewrites a request like:

```text
/script/esqew.png
```

to:

```text
/script/image.php?name=esqew
```

It matches only `.png` URLs, and `name` must be at least one alphanumeric or underscore character.

You can’t really “rewrite to .htaccess in PHP”; PHP can only output redirect headers or write a new .htaccess file if it has permission to do so.

For your old links, the closest supported approach is to add a rewrite/redirect rule that catches the old pattern and sends it to the new `1/` path. For example, if you want the old URL:

`/something.htm`

to go to:

`/1/something.htm`

you’d use a rule like:

`RewriteRule ^([^/]+)\.htm$ /1/$1.htm [R=301,L]`

And for the amount variant:

`RewriteRule ^([^/]+)\.htm/([0-9.]+)$ /1/$1.htm/$2 [R=301,L]`

If you also need the new internal rewrites to work, keep your current rules for the `1/` and `2/` paths.

If you meant “write .htaccess from PHP,” that would require PHP code that opens `.htaccess` and writes the rewrite rules into it, but the evidence here only supports the redirect/rewrite rule approach above.

To keep Google from indexing a subdomain, place a robots.txt file in the subdomain’s root with:

- Use .com/.net/.org if the site is intended to be global.
- A ccTLD hack like .re is mostly a marketing choice, not an SEO advantage.

If .com or .net are unavailable, it’s reasonable to choose another available name rather than rely on a ccTLD trick for a global site.

Country-specific domains do not, by themselves, seem to get special weight in search results. A site on a .cn domain can still rank in English results, and .us domains can contain content in other languages.

What matters more is the locale of the content and the branding/vanity value. A country-specific domain can help signal “this business is in this country,” but it is not inherently required for search visibility.

They can also be useful for organizing infrastructure, for example using different hostnames by country and redirecting users based on geography.

For the page path itself, it can stay in one language if you want. That is supported as a workable option. Keeping the URL path unchanged is simpler and is not penalized by search engines, but using separate URLs per language is the more SEO-friendly approach overall.

So the closest answer is:
- different URL for each language: yes, recommended
- different URL for each page: yes, each translatable page should have its own URL per language
- the visible path/name of the URL can still stay in one language if needed

For each page, it also makes sense to have separate URLs per language version so search engines and users can clearly distinguish them.

Yes, if the pages are meant for different languages or language variants, the closest guidance here is to use separate URLs for each localized version.

For pages that are only slightly different for a locale, the guidance says that this kind of subtly localized content is exactly what you should be doing, and that search engines can be helped to understand it with:

- separate locale targeting, such as ccTLDs or language/location directories
- correct language codes like en-GB, en-CA
- rel="alternate" hreflang="x" to show the equivalent versions across languages or regions

So the supported answer is: separate URLs are appropriate for localized content, especially when using hreflang to connect the versions. It does not say every minor page change must have a separate URL, but it does support separate URLs for each language/variant and each localized page version.

If you want to offer a cookie opt in/out, the usual approach is to make it optional and explain what it’s for before setting it. The evidence here mainly says that some users do disable cookies, especially third-party cookies, while first-party cookie blocking appears much lower. It also suggests that cookie rejection rates have varied a lot across studies.

A practical way to handle it is:

- Tell users what the cookie does and why you want to use it.
- Let them choose “Allow” or “Don’t allow.”
- If they decline, use another method if possible, or degrade gracefully.
- Don’t assume cookies are always available, because some users do turn them off.

If you’re asking about prevalence, the closest guidance supported here is that disabling all cookies was reported as low in some studies, while third-party cookie blocking was notably higher.

If there’s any chance you’ll send marketing emails later, the safest guidance here is to get opt-in authorization from the start, usually during new member registration. If you already have members, add it as a checkbox in their profile so they can change their status.

For email content, marketing emails must follow CAN-SPAM rules. Transactional emails are different. If you mix marketing content into a transactional email, it can get into a gray area.

I don’t have evidence here specifically about cookies, but the closest supported approach is the same kind of consent flow: present the choice at signup or in account settings so users can opt in or out.

The guidance in the thread is to set a preferred URL with a canonical link element. In practice, that means marking the page you want search engines to treat as the main version as the canonical URL, and putting that on pages that are duplicates or near-duplicates.

What this covers:

- Canonical tags are the supported way to indicate the “master” copy.
- This is especially useful when similar content exists on multiple pages.

Use a canonical URL on the duplicate pages and point them to the preferred version.

Put this in the `.htaccess` for the old domain:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.newdomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

This will redirect requests like:

- `www.domain.com`
- `www.domain.com/folder`
- `sub.domain.com`
- `sub.domain.com/folder`

to the same path on `www.newdomain.com`.

Use a rewrite rule in Apache, not in Django, if you want the old URL to redirect before it reaches the WSGI app.

The working pattern from the thread was:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} sid=([0-9]+)
RewriteRule ^/modules\.php /news/story/%1/? [R=301,L]
```

The key fixes were:
- include the leading slash in the pattern: `^/modules\.php`
- stop Apache from appending the original query string by ending the target with `?`

That setup redirects legacy URLs like:

`/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=600`

to:

`/news/story/600/`

If you want, I can also help translate that into a Django `urls.py` pattern for the new `/news/story/<id>/` route.

- chicagos.com.co is the one that Google indexes

If you want URLs like `example.com/course-compilers` to serve `course-compilers.html`, the .htaccess rule from the thread is:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME}\.html -f
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ $1.html
```

What it does:
- turns rewriting on
- makes sure the request is not a directory
- checks that a matching `.html` file exists
- rewrites the request to that `.html` file

So a request for `/course-compilers` would load `/course-compilers.html` if that file exists.

If you want it to work with a different extension, replace `.html` with that extension.

If you want, I can also help adapt this for a navigation setup like `courses/compilers`.

As long as the issuing certificate authority is trusted by the client’s browser, the certificate will typically appear trusted. EV certificates mainly mean the organization’s identity has been more strictly verified, not that the technical security is fundamentally stronger.

Based on the example given, there doesn’t seem to be any practical difference in the verification process or the certificate itself when buying through a reseller versus buying directly from the original seller. In that case, the only change was that payment went through the reseller; verification and everything else still went through the original certificate seller.

So, if your situation is similar, the main supported conclusion is that using a well-known reseller can be a valid way to buy the certificate, and the brand/source of the reseller did not affect the process in that example.

If you want the simplest low-cost option, the accepted answer says GoDaddy’s Standard SSL certificates are inexpensive and fast to acquire, and they work in every browser without untrusted-certificate warnings.

From that, the main thing you can count on with a basic cheap certificate is browser trust and standard SSL protection. The evidence does not compare safety levels between cheap and expensive certificates, so it doesn’t support saying the cheapest ones are less safe.

It also doesn’t support any difference based on whether the provider is European or not. Based on the answer, location doesn’t appear to matter for browser trust; the certificate was chosen because it works everywhere. If you’re deciding purely on what this thread supports, a low-cost standard certificate from a known provider is a reasonable choice.

A leading slash means the URL is rooted at the site’s top level, not relative to the current page path. So `/somedir/somepage.html` would resolve to `www.mysite.com/somedir/somepage.html`.

Without the leading slash, the link is treated as relative to the current directory. For example, if you’re on `/cream-cakes/`, then `blah.html` would point to `/cream-cakes/blah.html`, while `/blah.html` would point to the site root.

If you meant a double slash in a URL like `//example.com`, the provided material doesn’t cover that.

Use `rel="canonical"` on the paginated component pages to point to the version you want search results to show, if that’s the preferred page.

The guidance here says Google allows canonicalization for pagination, including using a canonical on component pages to indicate a View All version. It also notes that this can apply even when the paginated pages differ by sort order, not just when they are exact duplicates.

So, for a paginated series:

- put `rel="canonical"` on page 2, 3, etc.
- point it to the main or View All URL if that is the page you want indexed
- this is an accepted use, even though the pages are not strictly duplicate content

In the example given, the page is also sorted differently, so page 2 can represent a different set of answers over time. That still fits the broader canonicalization use described here.

If you want, I can also show what the HTML tag would look like on page 2 and what the target URL should be.

Use `rel="canonical"` on a link element to indicate the preferred URL for a page when there are multiple equivalent or duplicate URLs.

The accepted guidance here says the set of `rel` values is not one single exhaustive list in one place:

- For HTML 4.01, the W3C defines the official link types.
- For HTML 5, link types can be registered through the microformats rel registry.
- IANA also maintains a registry of link relations, which points to RFC 5988.

So for `canonical`, the closest supported answer is:

- it is a valid link relation,
- it belongs in the `rel` attribute of a link tag,
- and the registries above are the places to look for what values exist.

Example usage:

```html
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/preferred-page" />
```

If your question is about whether `canonical` should be used on `a` tags, this material only supports it as a link relation generally, and the common canonical use is with a `<link>` element in the page `<head>`.

Visits and pageviews are different measurements, so there is no exact one-to-one relationship.

In the usual interpretation, each visit starts with one pageview. If the bounce rate is 54%, that means about 54% of visits end after that first pageview, and the remaining 46% continue to other pages.

So, using your numbers as an approximation:

- 30,000 visits would generate at least 30,000 pageviews
- about 16,200 of those visits would bounce
- about 14,800 visits would continue and account for the rest of the 86,000 pageviews
- that means the non-bounce visits would average about 3.78 pages each

There is no exact way to say “only 15,000 users generated the 86,000 pageviews” from those stats alone, because visits and pageviews are not the same thing.

Also, Alexa ranking is relative to other sites. Even if your pageviews stay the same, your ranking can worsen if other sites are getting more pageviews or otherwise performing better in Alexa’s system.

Google can take a while to reflect changes after it crawls your site. Even if you’ve removed the noindex/nofollow and Googlebot is visiting now, the search results may not update immediately. The update timing can vary: sometimes it happens within minutes, other times it can take about a week.

Based on the information provided, the best guidance is to wait and be patient.

Google’s cached version and the search result snippet are updated separately, so having the latest page in cache doesn’t guarantee the new meta description will show in search results right away.

The evidence says this can take days or even weeks, depending on how important Google considers the site. Resubmitting the page in Webmaster Tools does not necessarily speed this up.

So the closest supported answer is: Google has likely crawled the page, but the indexing/snippet update hasn’t caught up yet.

- XML sitemaps
- RSS feeds

But the strongest signal described here is the date that appears on the page itself. In the example given, the date shown in Google’s search results matched a date found in the page content, even when it did not match the sitemap’s `<lastmod>` value. If the date is not visible on the current page, Google may use a date found in its cached version of the page.

So the closest supported answer is: Google seems to infer publish date mainly from the page content, and possibly also from sitemap and RSS data, but the on-page date often takes precedence.

Google/PageSpeed Insights doesn’t use a real device; it uses a WebKit renderer that emulates mobile and desktop. So it should react to your CSS media queries based on the emulated viewport, not an actual phone screen size.

For common mobile targeting, the provided guidance suggests using breakpoints like:
- max-width: 479px for portrait smartphones
- 480px to 800px for landscape smartphones / portrait tablets / narrow desktops

If your CSS uses `display: none` inside a media query, Google’s renderer should apply it the same way a normal mobile browser would, as long as the viewport conditions match. In short: if it hides correctly in mobile browsers, it should also hide in PageSpeed Insights.

A viewport meta tag like this is also recommended:
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1>`

The loss of Facebook likes, Google +1s, and tweets should not affect PageRank. PageRank is based on inbound links, not social signals.

With a 301 redirect, Google passes most or all of the PageRank to the new page. The exact amount has historically been described as “all or most,” but the key point is that the loss of social counts itself is not what affects PageRank.

You can only drill down to the social network and action in the standard Social reports. The `opt_target` value passed to `_trackSocial` is not available there as a report breakdown, based on the information here.

If your rankings dropped after a wave of spammy links, the closest guidance here is that this can happen to weaker sites with thin link profiles, especially for certain keywords. It may not be a manual penalty, so a reconsideration request may not help.

What you can do is focus on strengthening the site’s link profile with better, stronger links. That makes the site less vulnerable to this kind of attack.

If the problem is that another site is mirroring your content and outranking you, the supported steps here are to add canonical URLs to your pages so Google can recognize your site as the original source, submit a DMCA request to Google, and disavow the links from that domain.

Blocking the users may not help much. The closest guidance supported here is that showing a clear message on your pages identifying your site as the original may be more useful than just blocking them.

You can’t block or redirect those hotlinked .ru images with .htaccess, because the image requests are made by the spammer’s browser or elsewhere, not by your server.

What the evidence does support is filtering the comments themselves: add a comment filter that checks for .ru and blocks the comment, or use spam filtering code/plugin for comments.

So the closest supported guidance is:
- use a bulk email provider or hosted SMTP relay,
- send only to properly opted-in subscribers,
- throttle delivery if needed to avoid immediate spam flags,
- don’t rely on gradual sending to bypass anti-spam systems.

If you hide an image with `display:none`, it is still downloaded and still works. So for a Google Analytics tracking gif, `display:none` does not stop the request or the tracking.

The closer caution is that if the image `src` is blank, then nothing is downloaded and the `onload` event will not fire. If you only use `display:none`, the download still happens.

So the supported guidance is: `display:none` does not prevent the image from being requested; it just keeps it from being shown.

Google may look at the sitemap and still choose to crawl your site by following links instead. If the pages aren’t linked from anywhere, Google may not find them even with a sitemap.

The closest supported advice is:
- If the pages are important for users, link them from the site in a human-friendly way.
- Include them in the sitemap if you want search engines to know about them.
- If they are mainly “spider food” and not meant for users, it may be better not to rely on a sitemap for them.

So the count shown is for that exact address. If the page now lives on HTTPS, you need to make sure the Like button uses the new canonical URL consistently across the site, and understand that the counts may still be split between HTTP and HTTPS versions rather than merged.

- Use the exact URL you want Facebook to count.
- Don’t expect likes to transfer automatically when the URL structure changes.
