The meta description does not directly affect page ranking, but it can affect click-through rate, so it is worth using. Keep it relatively short, around 160 characters or less.

Meta keywords are no longer useful for SEO.

Other meta tags like author, robots, and copyright may be appropriate for your site, but they are not presented as important ranking factors here. The robots tag can control whether search engines index a page.

A practical approach is to use the meta tags that fit your site, especially title and description, and test changes by observing whether rankings or clicks change.

That meta robots tag is likely inside the AdSense iframe, not on your actual page. If so, it won’t affect your site’s SEO. It’s there so search engines don’t crawl or index the ad content inside the iframe.

No. Meta keywords are not obsolete in the sense of being removed; they still exist in the HTML5 specification.

What has changed is that search engines no longer use them for ranking, because they were too easy to abuse. So they have little or no SEO value.

They can still be useful for other applications that want a set of keywords for a page without extracting them from the content, especially when manual keywords are more accurate. Meta descriptions are similar in that they can be used by search results, social sharing tools, browsers, and screen readers as a summary or description of the page.

So the closest accurate answer is: meta keywords are still valid HTML metadata, but they are generally obsolete for SEO.

Meta keywords are effectively obsolete for search ranking.

The evidence says Google and Bing do not use meta keywords at all, and while some other search engines may still index them, their impact on ranking is very low to negligible. So it is generally not worth spending time maintaining them for SEO.

If you do use them, they’re only potentially useful when they’re specific to each page, not reused site-wide.

Meta keywords are not the right way to mark content as obsolete. The evidence supports using visible dates and clearly stating on the page that the information is outdated or may be outdated, ideally with a link to a newer version if one exists.

It also supports using structured data/microdata such as RDFa or Schema.org to describe dates or validity, which may help search engines and user agents in the future.

So, for “obsolete” content, the closest supported guidance is:
- show the publication date and any other relevant dates
- add a notice that the content is outdated if appropriate
- link to a newer version when available
- optionally use microdata/structured data to expose that information

If you’re seeing visits with fewer than 1 page per visit, the closest explanation supported here is that some of those “visits” may be bots or very short visits where the Google Analytics JavaScript didn’t fully load, so no pageview was sent.

- If many sessions have page depth under 1, bot traffic is a likely cause.

A dedicated server gives you full use of the hardware. A VPS gives you root access and a private software environment, but the underlying physical machine is shared with other customers.

In practice, the biggest differences are:

- Performance consistency: with a dedicated server, the CPU, memory, and disk are yours. With a VPS, what you get can vary depending on how heavily the host has oversold the machine.
- Overselling risk: VPS providers often place many virtual machines on one physical server, assuming not everyone will use their full allocation at once. That can make a VPS much cheaper, but also less predictable.
- Disk I/O: VPSes are often more variable in storage speed than dedicated servers. If your workload depends heavily on disk access, this matters a lot.

If your application is not very disk-I/O bound and you just need root access and a private environment, a VPS may be perfectly fine. If you want guaranteed access to the full hardware and more consistent performance, dedicated hosting is the better fit.

A hosting package gives you basic web hosting features like uploading files, creating databases, and installing common software. You usually do not get full control over the server environment, so you can’t easily change things like the PHP or Perl version. You also share disk space and CPU with other users.

A virtual private server acts like its own server, but it is actually sharing one physical machine with other VPSs. It has its own resource limits, such as memory and CPU, and you can install and configure software more freely.

A managed dedicated server is a real server used only by you.

For ASP.NET, C#, and MS SQL Server, the choice depends on how much control and how many resources you need. If you need more control over the server environment and more resources, a VPS or dedicated server is a better fit than a basic hosting package.

You can usually start by checking the domain’s WHOIS record, since the DNS server entries may give clues about the host. A WHOIS lookup is available through services like whois.net.

If that doesn’t identify the host, trace the site’s IP range with an IP WHOIS search. Starting with the ARIN WHOIS Database Search can tell you who owns the netblock, or route you to another registry like APNIC. Netcraft’s “What’s that site running?” lookup can also show the netblock owner and related details.

Another possible clue is the domain’s MX (mail server) DNS entries. These are less direct than they used to be, but they can still help. You can query them with NSLOOKUP, either locally or with an online tool such as Kloth.Net, using the domain name without “www” and choosing an MX query.

A useful place to look is the list of cPanel Partners, since it includes many reseller hosting options for different locations.

If you want UK-based choices, searching for “United Kingdom” turns up more results than searching for “UK” alone.

One important caveat: “unlimited” disk space or bandwidth is usually just marketing. You’ll likely be better off choosing a host that is clear about its policies and limits.

The main drawback of hosting at home is that typical home internet service is asymmetrical: the download speed is much higher than the upload speed. Since a website mostly sends data out to visitors, your upload rate becomes the bottleneck. Also, residential connections often have terms of service that prohibit running public web or FTP servers, partly because the upload side may be shared and one user can degrade service for others.

You do not necessarily have to be a company to have such a connection, but business-grade service is often what providers offer for this purpose.

The main issues to watch for are shared state and shared files.

If sessions are stored on the web server, both machines need access to the same session storage. Otherwise users can lose sessions or appear to get multiple sessions as requests bounce between servers. Sticky sessions may help if your load balancer supports them.

Any temporary files used during requests should also be available to both servers, such as files in a shared temp directory.

If you use SQLite, be careful about locking, especially if the database is shared over NFS. That setup can be slow and problematic.

For SSL, it’s often better for the load balancer to handle the SSL handshake and then pass requests to the backend servers.

More generally, any shared files should live on network storage rather than on a single web server, so one server going down does not take the site’s shared state with it.

To point `support.example.com` to a public IP address, use an A record, not a CNAME.

Example zone entry:

`support    14400   IN   A   xx.xx.xx.xx`

Replace `xx.xx.xx.xx` with the actual IP address.

You can add the A record either in the domain’s zone file or in your registrar’s DNS panel. If your domain uses your server’s nameservers, add it on the server; if it uses the registrar’s nameservers, add it in the registrar panel.

You don’t need to set DNS servers on your PC. What you need is a DNS entry for your domain that points to your home/public IP address, ideally using dynamic DNS if your IP changes.

To make your site reachable from outside your LAN, you also need to:

- make sure your ISP allows hosting from home
- check whether your internet upload speed is sufficient
- account for your IP changing over time, which is why dynamic DNS is often needed

There isn’t a single minimum bandwidth for a website. It depends on how much traffic the site gets and when people visit it.

A few useful rules from the answer:

- 125 GB per year is not much.
- 125 GB per day would need about 12.5 Mbit/sec if the traffic were spread perfectly evenly.
- A 1000 Mbit/sec uplink means a 1 gigabit per second connection, which is about 120 megabytes per second in theory.

For a 1 Gbit/sec connection:
- In theory, you could handle about 80 sites each using 125 GB per day, but that would fully use the connection.
- In practice, because traffic is uneven and peaks happen, it would probably struggle with even 20–40 such sites.
- If 125 GB is per month per site, then a 1 Gbit/sec link could likely handle around 1000 sites, since that is under 0.5 Mbit/sec on average.

So the real answer is: bandwidth needs depend on total traffic and peak usage, not just how many websites you host.

“Server-Client Authentication” means the certificate can be used not only to authenticate the server to the browser, but also to authenticate the client to the server.

In practice, that usually means the website can require users to present a personal client certificate installed in their browser. If client authentication is enabled, the server checks whether the client’s certificate chains to a trusted CA, and if no valid certificate is provided, the server can reject the request, for example with a 403 response.

So the added benefit is client certificate support for mutual TLS, not something that a basic server-only SSL certificate provides.

`<Directory />` refers to the filesystem root `/`, not `/var/www`.

Its purpose is to set default Apache options for that virtual host. Since Apache applies `<Directory>` settings from the shortest matching path outward, a `<Directory />` block provides a base configuration that applies to all directories under that virtual host unless a more specific `<Directory>` block overrides it.

For a general-purpose website, this is commonly used as a stable default because it works no matter where the site’s document root is placed later. In contrast, using `<Directory /var/www>` would only cover that specific path.

Cloud hosting, web hosting, and VPS are related, but they’re not the same thing:

- Web hosting is the broadest term. It usually means hosting a website on a server managed by a provider. It can be very simple/shared, where multiple customers use the same machine and you have limited control.
- VPS (virtual private server) means you get your own virtual machine with root access, but it still shares the underlying physical hardware with other VPS customers. In practice, the main differences are how much hardware resource you can reliably get and how much the provider oversells the machine.
- Cloud hosting is a marketing term that often refers to hosting built on a pool of virtualized resources rather than one fixed physical server. In many real-world cases, it behaves a lot like VPS hosting, but the provider may be able to move, scale, or balance resources more flexibly.

From the information here, the practical point is that VPSes can be cheaper because providers often oversell the host machine: they pack more virtual machines onto one physical server, assuming not everyone will use all their CPU, memory, and disk I/O at once. That means a VPS may not always have full guaranteed performance, especially for disk I/O. A dedicated server gives you the full hardware, while a VPS gives you root access on shared hardware.

So, the closest guidance supported here is:
- use web hosting for basic website hosting needs,
- use VPS if you want root access and more control, and your workload is not heavily bound to disk I/O,
- expect cloud/VPS-style hosting to vary by provider, especially in how much they oversell resources and how consistent performance is.

Yes. With a front controller setup, static files like images should be allowed to bypass the controller if they actually exist on disk.

The rewrite rules shown are intended to do that: if the requested path is an existing file, symlink, or directory, Apache stops rewriting; otherwise it sends the request to index.php.

A common version of this is:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-s
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-l
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule ^.*$ index.php [NC,L]

So if img/image.jpg exists in the public web root, it should be served directly rather than routed to ImgController.php. If it is still being sent to the front controller, the issue is likely with the rewrite setup or the file path/location, not with the front controller pattern itself.

A 301 redirect should pass link value from the old domain to the new one, so the new domain can benefit from the old backlinks. But it may not pass 100% of that value; there’s a dampening factor, so rankings may not carry over perfectly.

Best case, try to get the sites linking to you to update their links directly to the new URL. That gives the cleanest signal and avoids any loss from the redirect.

A 301 redirect will pass the old domain’s signals to the new domain, so if the old domain has bad links, those can carry over and affect the new site too.

- if they can’t be removed, consider disavowing them

So in general, redirecting an old domain to a new one can affect rankings positively or negatively depending on the old domain’s link profile. If the old domain has problematic links, they may continue to influence the new domain after the 301.

If the pages are actually the same content, Google is often able to recognize that and group them together, but the safest way to avoid confusion is to choose one preferred version and use a canonical tag pointing to it, usually the lowercase one.

The evidence doesn’t directly answer the trailing-slash question. It only covers duplicate pages with different URLs and says the fix is to use a canonical link to indicate the preferred/original page.

So, if your concern is that `mysite.com/category1/product` and `mysite.com/category2/product` show the same content, the closest supported guidance is to choose one canonical URL and point the others to it with a canonical link.

There’s no difference between `http://example.com/` and `http://example.com`.

The only caveat is that this is about the homepage/root URL. For links into a directory, the presence or absence of a trailing slash can matter. For absolute homepage URLs, either form is fine; being consistent is a good idea.

There’s no meaningful SEO difference by itself.

Traditionally, a trailing slash meant “directory” and no trailing slash meant “file,” but that distinction is mostly obsolete now. For practical purposes, the important point is consistency: use either the version with the trailing slash or the version without it, and stick to one.

If both versions are accessible, they can be treated as duplicate content unless you handle them consistently. The closest guidance supported here is to keep internal linking consistent and avoid mixing:

http://www.example.com/page/
http://www.example.com/page
http://www.example.com/page/index.htm

So the difference is mainly in URL structure and consistency, not SEO ranking.

From the evidence provided, the main point is that the domain choice itself is said not to make much difference for search rankings. The ranking impact is described as being driven more by actual page content and social presence than by the domain name.

So the closest guidance supported here is: when internationalizing, don’t rely on the domain alone for SEO. Focus more on high-quality localized content and presence. The evidence does not cover other common international SEO pitfalls, so I can’t confirm specifics like hreflang, duplicate content, or geo-targeting from this source.

A main pitfall is assuming that duplicate content across regions will automatically hurt SEO. For the same language across different geo-targets, duplicate content is not considered a problem.

The supported guidance is:
- If you use subfolders for geo-targets, add each subfolder in Google Webmaster Tools and set the geographic targeting there.
- Use language tags like `<html lang=en>` for the document language.
- Use `hreflang` link tags to indicate alternate language versions.

Those tags are for language versions, not for geo-targeting with the same language.

The evidence doesn’t address internationalizing a website or SEO pitfalls specific to that. It only covers guest blogging, where the main points are:

- You may get a backlink and possibly some reputation/traffic from a host site.
- The benefits depend a lot on the host site’s rules and what links or other perks they allow.
- If your goal is just backlinks, commenting on similar blogs might be just as effective.
- If your goal is feedback or testing your writing on a larger audience, guest blogging on a high-traffic site can help.

So the closest guidance it supports is: define your SEO goal first, and watch out for relying on guest blogging mainly for backlinks, since the payoff may be limited and highly dependent on the host site.

Use Google Webmaster Tools’ “Fetch as Googlebot” feature and test the affected URLs.

That will tell you whether Google can actually reach those pages from its own servers, or whether the problem only happens for Googlebot / from Google’s network, even though the pages load normally for you in a browser.

If Googlebot fetch fails while your browser gets a 200, that points to a connectivity, crawl, or user-agent-specific issue rather than the pages truly being 404s.

Try using Google Webmaster Tools’ Fetch as Google on one of the URLs marked “Access Denied.” If it fetches successfully and returns 200 OK, Google can re-crawl and submit the URL for indexing.

If it still returns 403, then the problem is likely on your server side: the server may be denying Googlebot access or may be misconfigured and returning 403 only for Google. In that case, you’ll need to check why the server is blocking those requests.

Fix the 404s on your site first. Then mark those errors as fixed in Google Webmaster Tools.

If Google finds the same 404s again later, it will report them again. If it doesn’t find them again, they’re considered fixed.

Yes, it’s generally safe to remove them if those URLs no longer need to exist and they’re still just old crawl errors.

The guidance here says Google treats 400 and 405 like other 4xx errors, and Google Search Console can be very slow to clear crawl errors. If the pages should stay inaccessible, a 401 Unauthorized may be more appropriate for signed-in-only pages.

If the URLs are gone permanently, 404 or 410 are the usual choices; 410 is often used when you want to signal they’re intentionally gone. If they still return a 4xx or 5xx, Google may keep retrying them for months.

Yes, it’s generally safe to remove them if they’re old 404s and those pages no longer exist.

The guidance here is to either:
- 301 redirect the old URLs to the most relevant equivalent on the new site, or
- if there isn’t a good match, redirect them to the home page.

The main concern is human visitors landing on broken links. Search crawlers will eventually stop requesting the old URLs.

If you might need some of those URLs again in the future, removing them now doesn’t prevent you from creating them later, but if that happens you’d need to restore or redirect them appropriately.

Yes, based on the answer provided, it’s safe to remove them. The guidance says 404 pages “will get removed from the index faster than blocked pages,” and that the errors “will disappear” over time.

The closest supported advice is:
- use 301 redirects for any pages you can preserve or map to relevant new URLs
- let the remaining old URLs return 404 rather than blocking them
- optionally use a custom 404 page for better user experience

So if those 400 old URLs are genuinely gone and you can’t redirect them appropriately, leaving them as 404s is acceptable.

Yes, a new domain that only redirects is likely to get its redirect target indexed, and in the scenario described it can create a mess of indexed URLs like `new-domain.com/old/`.

The guidance here is to avoid redirecting `old-domain.com` until `new-domain.com` is ready. Keep the old domain active while you build the new site, then when everything is ready, use a 301 redirect from `old-domain.com` to `new-domain.com` and set up page-specific redirects if needed.

If you already use the temporary redirect to `new-domain.com/old/`, search engines may index that folder URL, and you’d then have to deal with traffic and indexing there later.

A new domain that just 301-redirects to the main site generally will not index as its own result. A 301 tells search engines the page has permanently moved, so the old URL is typically dropped from the SERPs and the destination page is the one that matters.

The closest exception mentioned is a 302 redirect: those pages often stay in the SERPs, but that usually requires the domain to exist and get indexed first, and it may be seen as suspicious. It also likely would not rank well for searches.

So: yes, search engines may follow the redirect and pass value to the main site, but the new redirecting domain itself usually won’t appear as an indexed result if it’s only a permanent redirect.

A 301 permanent redirect to a different site/domain is treated the same as other 301s: search engines associate the old URLs with the new URLs, carry over links and PageRank to the new URLs with a small loss, and eventually replace the old URLs in search results.

So if you redirect each old page to the corresponding page under the new domain/subdirectory, it should generally work out SEO-wise in the same way as any other properly mapped 301 redirect.

Yes. If a new domain only redirects some URLs, search engines can still index other URLs on it.

In the example shown, the redirect was only for the home page, not the whole site. So if search engines find links to deeper paths, they may still index those pages on the main domain.

To make the entire domain redirect, the rule needs to pass through the full path, like:

RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://subdomain.website.com$1 [R=301,L]

If you want, I can also explain why a 301 redirect may still leave old URLs in search results for a while.

A 301 redirect to a new URL/domain can preserve most SEO value, but each extra redirect can slightly reduce trust and authority passed along.

So if you’re redirecting to a different site/domain:

- Best case: one direct 301 from the old URL to the final URL
- Less ideal: a redirect chain, because every additional 301 can weaken the ranking value a bit
- Two redirects is usually only a small issue
- Three or more redirects is where it becomes more concerning

The safest approach is to make it a one-to-one 301 redirect straight to the final destination, and then verify that the response is actually a single 301 leading to the final URL.

Use a 301 redirect from the old domain/page to the new domain/page.

That tells search engines and users that the content has permanently moved, and it signals Google to treat the new URL as the permanent one and transfer incoming links to it. In the provided answer, this is described as the right way to move content so the stronger domain can benefit from the links and SEO value.

For example:

domain1.com/example.html → 301 redirect → domain2.com/example.html

This also helps because keeping all content under one domain supports cleaner internal linking and a better content structure, which is beneficial for SEO.

Heading tags like `<h1>` and `<h2>` do matter for SEO, but not in a “big difference” way by themselves.

They are a ranking factor, but the main value is using them properly so users and search engines can understand your page better. A common guideline is to use only one `<h1>` per page, then use `<h2>` and `<h3>` in order, almost like a table of contents.

So: yes, they help, but their biggest benefit is structure and clarity rather than a huge direct ranking boost.

A keyword in the domain name can help a little, but only slightly. It usually is not the main reason one site ranks above another.

From what’s shown here, the other site is likely ahead for other reasons, especially the number and quality of backlinks pointing to it. Having 30 backlinks is not necessarily enough, and a single link from an important site can be worth more than many links from low-value sites. It also matters whether those backlinks are actually indexed by Google.

Changing your URL to include the keyword, or creating a subdomain with it, is not shown here as a guaranteed fix and may not improve rankings much.

The closest supported guidance is to focus on stronger, higher-quality backlinks and overall SEO rather than relying on the domain name alone.

Yes. A page with a non-keyword domain can outrank a keyword domain. The domain name is only one ranking factor, and it does not make ranking impossible.

A year may also not be enough time if the keyword is competitive. The main guidance supported here is to make sure your optimization is strong across all ranking factors you can control, and be patient for results.

The thread does not provide an answer.

It only shows that the question was about finding keywords with high Google SERP rankings for a domain using services/tools, but no solution or method is recorded.

Closest guidance supported by the thread: if you want to discover successful keywords for a domain, you would need a tool that checks a domain’s rankings for specific keywords; the thread does not say how to find the keywords themselves from only the domain.

It’s not likely to make much difference based on the information provided. The answer available says search rankings are now weighted more toward actual page content and social presence than the domain name itself.

So having multiple domains that redirect to your main domain should not, by itself, be a major ranking factor according to that guidance.

Yes, multiple redirects can have a small negative impact on rankings because some trust and authority is lost with each 301 redirect.

If you can, it’s better to do a direct one-to-one 301 redirect from each old domain/page to the final destination on your main domain, rather than chaining redirects through multiple steps.

One redirect is usually not a big deal. Two is only slightly suboptimal. Three or more can become risky.

Yes, it can have an impact if multiple domains are serving the same content without proper redirects. The guidance here says Google may treat that as duplicate content and decide which domain is authoritative.

The closest supported advice is to use 301 permanent redirects so search engines understand the content has moved. If the extra domains are just redirecting to your main domain, that is the safer approach.

If the exact domain you want is taken, the suggested alternatives for SEO-friendly naming are:

- add a secondary keyword
- use a synonym
- add an “s” or another applicable suffix
- add “the” or another applicable prefix
- use an alternate TLD like .net or .co
- use a dash if the domain has two words

I can’t determine from this whether an add-on domain specifically improves SEO, but these are the closest domain-name alternatives recommended here.

Use a 301 redirect from the add-on domain to the main domain. That sends users to the main site and signals search engines to index only the main URL, which is the closest fit to avoiding the second domain appearing in SERPs.

You need both.

The CNAME is the DNS record that makes `www.example.com` point to the same server as `example.com`, so browsers can find it. The rewrite rule in `.htaccess` is what tells the server to redirect requests for the non-`www` version to the `www` version.

So if your goal is to use `www` consistently, the supported approach is:
- create the `www` CNAME
- add a server-side redirect from `example.com` to `www.example.com`

That is the closest guidance supported by the evidence.

Not really as a long-term strategy.

A 301 redirect from an old domain to a new one may temporarily pass some value like indexed age or link equity, but Google is expected to treat normal redirects as standard behavior and to ignore attempts at link spamming. The benefit appears to fade over time as the new site is evaluated on its own merits.

So buying abandoned domains just to funnel “link juice” to a new site is unlikely to be a reliable or lasting technique. If the old domains still get traffic, you may benefit from redirecting that traffic, but the better way to help a new site is to improve its content and earn links from authoritative, relevant sites.

Not reliably. The guidance here says buying expired domains may not have the PageRank benefit you’re hoping for, and if the domain was penalized before, it may be hard to get it indexed and ranking well.

The closest supported advice is to buy domains you know have traffic and 301 redirect them to your main domain, so you can capture that traffic without hosting content on a potentially penalized domain. But even then, there isn’t concrete information on exactly how search engines handle it.

Using abandoned domains just to get link juice is not something this evidence supports as a good technique.

What it does support is that if you want to move value from one domain to another, a 301 redirect is the preferred approach. The accepted answer says Google prefers 301 redirects, and that cross-domain canonical tags are tricky and not something they really believe in for passing juice reliably. It also says canonical tags are mainly for fixing duplicate-content issues.

So the closest guidance here is: if the goal is to make a new domain rank as well and as fast as possible, use 301 redirects rather than relying on abandoned domains or cross-domain canonical tags.

No, not necessarily.

A VPS is not guaranteed to handle the traffic any better than your current shared hosting. The key point is that all servers have limits, and if the spike hits those limits, the site can slow down or fail regardless of whether it’s shared hosting or a VPS.

What matters most is:
- whether the traffic is mostly reading or mostly posting
- how well your forum scales
- whether the server has enough resources for the load

If the spike is mostly people browsing, a CDN or caching service may help a lot. If a lot of users will be posting at once, then you’d need testing to know whether your current plan or a VPS will handle it.

So the closest advice supported here is: don’t assume you must pick a VPS; instead, judge based on the expected load and whether the activity is read-heavy or interactive.

The closest supported guidance is to use one main domain and create separate location landing pages for each city, like mycompany.com/my-company-cleveland and mycompany.com/my-company-columbus, with content specific to each location.

Redirecting the city domains to the main domain is not likely to get those redirected domains indexed highly, so it would not be a strong SEO strategy. Having multiple identical sites on separate domains is also not a good idea because the content is duplicated and the traffic gets split.

If the business really has branches in those locations, setting up proper location pages and using Google Places may help those pages rank well. If there is not actually a location in a city, using city-specific pages could be seen as spammy.

`example1.mysite.com` and `example2.mysite.com` are subdomains of `mysite.com`.

“Multi-domain” means a site can be accessed by more than one domain name, such as when two different domains point to the same website. They are not interchangeable terms.

Since all the sites are WordPress sites, each domain would be configured as its own virtual host pointing to the appropriate WordPress files.

If you’re just forwarding one or more newly registered domains to a single domain, that is unlikely to provide any SEO benefit. The forwarded domains themselves won’t help the destination rank just because they contain keywords.

The only case in the evidence where forwarding helps is when the old domain was already established, indexed, and had backlinks, and you use a 301 redirect to move that site to the new one. In that situation, some SEO benefit can pass along.

So, forwarding multiple top-level domains to one domain is not inherently bad for SEO, but it usually does not help SEO unless those domains already had their own value and you use a proper 301 redirect. The registrar-style “framed forwarding” shown is unlikely to have any SEO benefit.

A 301 redirect from one domain to another is the right approach, but based on the evidence, 10 days is too soon for Google to fully recrawl and reflect the change.

Google may take about 30 days for full recrawling. If the situation still hasn’t changed after about a month, then the next thing to check would be whether the redirect is set up correctly.

So for a .com or .org redirecting to a country-specific domain like .am, the supported guidance here is: use a 301 redirect, then give Google time to process it, and if rankings/indexing still don’t move after roughly 30 days, review the redirect setup.

Yes, it can be bad for SEO if you 301 redirect multiple top-level domains into one domain, especially when those domains already had rankings and backlinks.

The evidence here says redirects from one domain to another “usually give terrible results,” and that rankings can drop after the merge. It also suggests that old domain names won’t help the new one much, and may even hurt it.

What it supports most strongly is:
- domain-to-domain redirects often cause SEO loss in the short term
- merging sites this way can make previously ranking pages plummet
- the safer SEO approach would have been to keep the domains/content separate while serving them through the same application, rather than consolidating everything by redirect

So, based on this evidence, forwarding multiple domains to one domain is not a good SEO strategy in general.

The available information only says that the domain extension is a matter for SEO, but it does not provide any answer about redirecting from .com or .org to a country-code domain like .am.

The closest guidance supported here is that domain extension can matter for SEO, so choosing a domain ending should be considered as part of your SEO setup. But there is no recorded answer here about whether a .com or .org should redirect to a country-specific domain.

Yes. You can compare hosting speed with tools like WebPageTest, Gomez, Fiddler, HTTP Watch, and the Net tab in Firebug or the Resources view in Chrome/Opera’s developer tools.

Use heading tags to describe the specific page’s content, not keep them the same sitewide if they don’t fit every page.

If a static h1 is relevant to every page, it may be acceptable, especially if users can add specific h2 subheadings, but that’s unlikely to be true for every page. So the best-supported guidance here is to vary the h1 based on what’s actually on each page and make it relevant and succinct.

The answer supported here is no for subdomains being separate entities in general, though Alexa/traffic ranking may consolidate them under the primary domain.

Do a 301 redirect from the parked domain to the main domain. That tells search engines which domain is the canonical one and helps eliminate duplicate-content confusion, which is likely why the old URL is showing in SERPs.

If you’re using Apache, you can set up a redirect in your `.htaccess` file. The example given is:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^(www\.)?newdomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.existingdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]

This should make users and search engines consistently reach the same domain.

If two domains point to the same website content, search engines may still choose different snippets or titles in SERP depending on the page and how they index it, but the provided material does not give a specific method for making each domain show a different meta description and title.

What it does cover is that changing title, description, and keywords meta tags frequently is possible, but it may affect ranking, and no minimum or maximum safe frequency is given.

Closest guidance supported here: avoid changing `<title>`, description, and keywords meta tags daily without a clear reason, because frequent changes can affect how search engines evaluate and display the page. If your goal is different SERP titles/descriptions for two domains, this evidence does not provide a direct solution.

If the two domains are treated as separate websites, duplicated meta descriptions on one won’t affect the other.

The evidence says subdomains like `a.example.com` are considered different websites from `example.com` for this purpose. So duplicate meta descriptions on the subdomain can be a problem for the subdomain’s SEO, but not for the main domain.

It also says having the same meta description on two different websites is not a problem by itself.

If you want different titles and descriptions in SERP, that’s something search engines may choose based on the page and site they index, but the provided evidence only covers that duplicate meta descriptions on one site do not affect another separate site.

- you can try to encourage them

- Keeping the site full of strong, useful content
- Marking up your navigation with semantic HTML
- Using an `id` like `nav` or `navigation` on your menu so Google can identify it as navigation

No. Hosting on Amazon EC2 is not, by itself, adequate protection against DDoS.

- present a human-readable message and an unlock CAPTCHA on that page

Take screenshots and save other proof first. Then send the parties involved the documents they require to remove the copied content, focusing on the plagiarism of your copyrighted images and product descriptions.

The steps supported here are:
- Send the site owners a cease-and-desist letter.
- Send the web host a DMCA takedown notice; WHOIS can help identify the host.
- Send DMCA takedown notices to search engines under their procedures, including Google, Bing, Yahoo!, and AOL.
- If that doesn’t work, involve lawyers.
- Set up Google Alerts for your unique search terms so you’ll be notified if the content appears elsewhere.

The main practical point is to document the copying, then pursue removal through the host, the site owners, and search engines.

Based on the evidence, the most supported steps are:

1. Do a WHOIS lookup for the site owner.
2. Contact the hosting company’s abuse department as soon as possible.
3. Provide supporting documentation, including proof that you own the code/materials.
4. Include evidence that you already tried to contact the offender.
5. Send a DMCA takedown notice.
6. Send a cease and desist letter, ideally from a lawyer if you can get one.
7. Send copies of those notices to both the host and the site owner, preferably by certified mail.
8. Also contact the domain registrar and PayPal, since they are involved in hosting and payment processing.

The evidence does not say exactly how likely a takedown is or what the laws are in your jurisdiction, but it does support these as the practical next moves.

If the copied material is being used on a spammy site and it’s not just a legitimate quotation, the options supported here are:

- File a complaint with AdSense if the site uses it.
- File a Google Content Removal Request.
- Report the site to Google as a content scraping/spam site.

The answer also indicates that in the U.S. partial copying can sometimes be covered by fair use if it’s a real quotation that adds value and is related. But if the site is mostly spam and scraped content, that cuts against it being a legitimate quote.

What this does not fully settle is exactly how many paragraphs is enough for a DMCA takedown. The guidance here supports that full copies are clearly actionable, and that even partial copy/paste on a spam site may still be worth reporting through Google’s complaint and removal processes, especially if it’s hurting your rankings.

Usually, when a domain name reaches its expiration date, the registrar puts it into a hold period for a while, typically around 90 days. During that time, the domain is locked so the original owner can still recover it, but usually only by paying a recovery fee. After that hold period, the domain may be unlocked and made available again, or in some cases the registrar may keep it and resell it through its own auction process.

The exact timing can vary by registrar, but the evidence supports that it is often at least a month or two and commonly around 90 days.

When a domain name reaches its expiration date, it usually does not become available to others immediately.

Typically, it goes through these stages:

- Grace period: often about 30 days. You can usually renew it for the normal renewal price, and others cannot register it.
- Redemption period: if not renewed, it often enters a redemption period of about 40 days. It is still not available to others, but renewal usually costs more.
- Pending delete / dropped: if it still isn’t renewed, it can eventually be deleted and become available for registration by someone else.

So, reaching the expiration date does not mean you lose it right away. In the situation described, a transfer can still be processed even if the domain expires during the transfer window, and expiration alone is not a valid reason to deny a transfer request.

You can rewrite the friendly URL to a PHP page that looks up the profile by username.

If usernames are unique, a simple approach is:

```apache
Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule profile/(.*)/ profile.php?username=$1
RewriteRule profile/(.*) profile.php?username=$1
```

Then a request like:

`website.com/profile/kevinlee`

will internally load:

`profile.php?username=kevinlee`

The general idea is to replace `?id=24` with the username in the URL, and use rewrite rules to map that friendly URL to your PHP script.

- whether the important content is only accessible through JavaScript,
- whether bots can reliably see the same content users see,

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="http://en.example.com/" />

This is the closest supported fix in the evidence. It suggests Google should be able to understand and index the Italian, German, and English versions properly when each page references the others with hreflang.

It does not directly answer which domains to add in Webmaster Tools, but it does show that you should make sure all language versions are connected with these alternate hreflang tags so Google can associate the subdomains/mapped domains correctly.

You can’t force Google to show your site with a preview image in search results. Based on the information provided, it’s up to Google whether it embeds videos or images in the SERPs.

- The logo in the header is usually treated as layout/decoration, not the kind of image image sitemaps are meant to highlight.
- If the logo is important, the closest supported approach is to include it only on the home page, or on a page specifically meant for brand assets.
- There isn’t a known official or widely supported method in that answer for telling Google about the logo image directly.

So the closest guidance is: put the logo on your homepage, and if you have a brand-assets page, include it there too. Don’t try to list the included header file in the image sitemap, and don’t add the logo to every page just because it appears there.

Bing indexing and crawling your sitemap does not guarantee the pages will appear in results. The evidence here points to a crawl/indexing problem on the site itself rather than just a sitemap issue.

What it supports:
- A sitemap is not strictly required for indexing if the site is crawlable.
- Pages that should be indexed need to return 200 OK.
- Old URLs should return 301 redirects to the new URLs.
- If new pages are still showing 404s or 500s, Bing may crawl them but not index them properly.
- There may be redirect or server-response problems causing Bing to find the old URLs or treat the new ones as unavailable.

Closest guidance supported:
- Check the HTTP response codes for both old and new URLs.
- Make sure the new URLs return 200 OK.
- Make sure old URLs redirect with 301 to the correct new pages.
- Use a crawl tool to find 404 and 500 errors on the site.
- If the sitemap links point to pages that are not returning 200 OK, Bing may not index them.

So the likely issue is not “Bing crawls my sitemap but doesn’t show pages,” but that the pages Bing finds are not responding correctly or are not reachable in the way Bing expects.

If your robots.txt was empty, Google may treat that as a temporary error and not immediately trust that crawling is allowed again. A safer setup is:

User-agent: *
Disallow:

After that, it can still take at least a week and sometimes up to a month before Google indexes the site.

Google can index pages it has already crawled even if it has not finished crawling the whole site, so you do not have to wait for every page to be fetched first.

If you want to speed up crawling, the main thing supported here is improving the site’s reputation with more high-quality inbound links. Crawl rate is largely governed by PageRank.

If Bing is crawling your sitemap but pages aren’t showing in results, the closest guidance from the available information is that crawl/index data can lag behind what you see elsewhere.

- Bing may have crawled the sitemap, but its index/reporting can still be behind.
- Crawling a sitemap does not guarantee immediate appearance in results.
- It may simply need time for Bing to update and surface the pages.

What this does not confirm is whether Bing has fully indexed your specific pages or whether there is another indexing issue. The evidence only supports the idea that delayed reporting/index updates can happen, so the first thing to do is allow more time before assuming there is a problem.

```apache
RewriteCond /your/web/directory%{REQUEST_URI}\.html -f [OR]
RewriteCond /your/web/directory%{REQUEST_URI}\.php -f [OR]
RewriteCond /your/web/directory%{REQUEST_URI}\.cgi -f
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ /$1/ [L,R=301]
```

But the answer also warns that forcing trailing slashes on all URLs can break relative links and change the meaning of the URL. It suggests that if your goal is only to remove file extensions, a simpler approach is:

```apache
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.html -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.html [L]

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.php -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.php [L]

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILE}\.cgi -f
RewriteRule (.*)$ $1.cgi [L]
```

If you specifically want to remove trailing slashes from URLs, the provided evidence does not include a complete working rule for that. The closest supported guidance is that rewriting slashes should be done carefully because it can break links and file resolution.

Use a rewrite rule that either expects the trailing slash or allows it optionally.

For example:

RewriteRule ^first-page/$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^second-page/$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=2 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^third-page/$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=161 [QSA,L]

Or, if you want both versions to work:

RewriteRule ^first-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^second-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=2 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^third-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=161 [QSA,L]

The `(/)?` makes the trailing slash optional, so `/subdir/first-page` and `/subdir/first-page/` both match, but nothing else after that.

For the domain root, no extra redirect is needed: `http://www.domain.com` and `http://www.domain.com/` are treated the same.

For other URLs, the trailing slash can matter. File URLs like `page.htm` or `file.php` should not have a trailing slash. Directory URLs generally should have one, and Apache will usually 301 redirect to the slash version automatically.

So the closest rule is:
- root domain: slash and no slash are equivalent
- files with extensions: no trailing slash
- directories: use trailing slash, and Apache often handles the redirect for you

Use redirects, typically in the site’s `.htaccess` file if the server supports it.

If many old URLs follow a pattern, you can group them and redirect a whole section at once instead of creating one rule per page. For example, instead of redirecting:

`/news_article/01` → `/news/01/`  
`/news_article/02` → `/news/02/`

you can redirect the whole old folder:

`Redirect permanent /news_article http://www.mydomain.com/news/`

If the goal is to stop a PHP script running under Apache from connecting to a specific site, the closest guidance here is to block that destination at the network level, for example with an iptables OUTPUT rule aimed at that domain’s IP address.

If the script’s target comes from a URL parameter, another option is to rewrite or intercept requests in Apache/.htaccess so the script is not allowed to proceed for that input.

A code change in the PHP script itself is also a straightforward fix: add a condition to refuse or skip execution when the requested host is the one you want to block.

If you can identify a simple signature for the bad requests, the best place to stop them is as far out in the network as possible, ideally at the external or “choke” router before they reach Apache.

If the requests are varied and don’t share an easy signature, you’d need something more intelligent, such as a firewall that can do deeper inspection and translate your Apache-style blocking rules into network-level filtering.

iptables is not described as very intelligent here, so if you were going to use it to drop packets, the better place would still be at the router rather than deeper inside the server.

If you can only block them in Apache, you could suppress logging for those specific requests, but that’s not recommended because it removes useful data for later analysis.

If Apache/PHP has already started sending the page body, it’s too late to change the HTTP status to 404 or 410. Status codes have to be sent in headers before any HTML is output.

The practical fix is to check whether the content exists first, then either:
- send a 404/410 header and display the error page, or
- redirect to a 404 page, which is common but not as ideal as returning the status directly.

If a 301 or 302 redirect can still be sent, then a 404 header could usually have been sent too, because both must be sent before any HTML.

So the closest guidance is: restructure the page so existence is determined before output begins. If that’s not possible, redirecting to a 404 page is an acceptable fallback and commonly used, though it’s not the best possible setup.

If the usernames are unique, the basic approach is to rewrite the friendly URL to a PHP page that looks up the profile by username.

For example, instead of using `/profile/?id=24`, you can make `/profile/kevinlee` map to something like `profile.php?username=kevinlee`.

One way to do that is with mod_rewrite in `.htaccess`:

```apache
Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule profile/(.*)/ profile.php?username=$1
RewriteRule profile/(.*) profile.php?username=$1
```

Then in `profile.php`, you read `$_GET['username']` and query the database for that user.

- accessibility problems
- responsiveness problems
- slower page speed

- don’t rely on pixel-perfect text rendering
- if exact appearance is critical, use an image instead of live text

The answer also says canonical URLs act like a 301 redirect for SEO purposes, so links to the secondary domain count toward the primary domain.

It does not confirm a clean way to do this without iframes or similar hacks.

No, cloaking/domain masking is not needed for this.

You can buy the domain from any registrar and point it to your web host’s DNS servers. If your host allows it, you can then add that domain to the same hosting account as an alias or a separately hosted site.

Domain/url masking is a different thing: it hides the real destination in the browser address bar by using a third-party redirect, often with an iframe or proxy-style setup. It’s generally a clunky solution and usually used when you can’t properly configure the domain through the host.

It’s generally better for the homepage to be at the root domain rather than in a sub-folder.

The guidance here says that pages closest to the root are typically treated as more important by search engines, so keeping the homepage at www.domain.com is preferable from an SEO perspective. It also notes that placing the site in a folder can create extra redirect and link-handling issues later if the structure changes.

From a user-experience standpoint, it’s also considered less ideal to open the main site in a folder, especially by modern expectations.

So while it’s not described as catastrophic, the supported recommendation is to use the root domain for the homepage if possible.

No. The information here is about folder visibility to crawlers, not about whether a homepage should live in a sub-folder.

What it does support is this: if a directory is browsable in a browser, then robots or anyone else can likely find its contents. If you don’t want a folder’s contents listed, you can disable directory listing with:

Options -Indexes

That said, this doesn’t indicate that having your homepage in a sub-folder is inherently a bad idea.

Grouping your navigation pages in a public sitemap won’t have a known SEO effect in Google search.

The guidance here is that the order URLs appear in a sitemap, or how they’re grouped, does not affect SEO, and it also doesn’t affect public-facing site maps. So for Google search, there isn’t a recommended “best” organization like alphabetical vs. by filter vs. every filter combination based on SEO alone.

If your goal is SEO, this evidence only supports using a sitemap to list pages, not expecting the structure of that sitemap to improve ranking or crawl value.

Google won’t “organize” navigation pages for you in search in any special way from the information here. The guidance it supports is to create and fill out a Google Places listing for your business so Google has better location data on hand. That can help with local search results and map display, but it doesn’t specifically describe how to make site navigation pages appear or be organized in Google search.

If your goal is better location-specific visibility, the closest supported step here is to set up and complete a Places listing.

Use clear, keyword-relevant navigation and page structure, with meaningful headings on the pages themselves. The guidance here is that search engines like Yahoo place more emphasis on in-page factors such as headings, while Google places more emphasis on the anchor text of incoming links and also gives more weight to keywords in the URL.

So for your site’s navigation pages, the closest supported advice is:
- make the page titles and headings descriptive
- use keyword-relevant internal navigation text
- keep the URL keywords meaningful
- make the layout and structure easy for search engines to understand

If you want, I can help turn that into a practical navigation-page structure for Google specifically.

Use a progressive JPG for the image you want to show. That will display a low-detail, blurred version first and then refine into the full image as it loads.

Keep in mind the drawback: if a browser doesn’t support progressive JPGs, it may wait until the whole file is downloaded before showing anything.

If you want to show a “coming soon” placeholder during redevelopment, a progressive JPG is the closest approach supported by this information.

Instead of showing only a “coming soon” or “under construction” notice, it’s better to make the page a little more informative.

You can explain what is coming soon and why visitors should come back later. It also helps to include a short about section, contact information, and even a simple email subscribe option so people can be notified when the site is ready.

Try not to add unnecessary redirects or unrelated content that wouldn’t match what the finished site will actually offer.

The closest supported guidance is that the date shown with an image in Google results may be coming from the image’s EXIF metadata. If so, you can view the EXIF data with an online EXIF viewer and use an EXIF editor to change the date fields to a more recent date, such as 2014.

It also suggests checking whether the image is already cached in Google Image Search. If it is, you can try uploading it via the camera icon and, if found, request removal using Google’s image removal process.

What this does not confirm is a reliable way to show an image with no date at all. It only supports trying to change or remove the date source, especially in the image metadata or cached image result.

The closest guidance here is:
- an empty robots.txt file is also fine
- you can simply not use one at all
- if you do use one, it’s useful for pointing search engines to your XML Sitemap
- without it, your web logs may show a lot of 404 entries for robots.txt requests

No. If you want all bots to crawl everything, you do not need a robots.txt file; a missing file is interpreted as allowing crawling of all content.

If you want to avoid unnecessary 404 errors in your stats, you can create a blank robots.txt.

Shorter URIs are not inherently better for SEO. What matters more is that the URL is user-friendly: short and easy to remember, free of strange characters or query strings, descriptive of the content, and reflective of the site structure.

A short URL can be good if it still describes the page well. If shortening just means hiding useful information or adding extra redirects, that is not an SEO advantage. In particular, using a URL shortener outside of special cases can interfere with proper PageRank flow unless it uses a 301 redirect.

The closest practical guidance supported here is: use a clean, descriptive slug generated from the page title, rather than adding unnecessary numbers or making the URL short at the expense of clarity.

No. From an SEO perspective, shorter URIs are not inherently better.

What the evidence supports is that you should prefer the original, direct URL over a shortened/redirected one when possible, because:

- redirected URLs can pass a little less link equity
- they may be slower for users and bots
- the original URL is usually more descriptive and can include keywords
- URL shorteners can disappear, breaking links
- shortened links are often less trustworthy to users

So the closest supported guidance is: use the original URL, and focus on making it descriptive and direct rather than just short.

Not necessarily. From the SEO guidance here, the important factor is not URI length, but which domain is the main one and whether you use a 301 redirect when changing names/domains.

If `companyx.com` is already indexed and you want to preserve its search visibility, the supported approach is to 301 redirect it to `businessy.com` so the new domain becomes the primary one. The CNAME itself isn’t the key SEO issue in this guidance.

So, based on this, shorter URIs are not described as better for SEO; the domain change and proper redirect setup matter more.

If Google knows about the URL through links from elsewhere, it can crawl it.

In the evidence here, the answer says Google will certainly grab the linked images because they’re linked from the main domain. It also suggests Google may not actively crawl the subdomain as a separate entity if it’s only serving resources.

So for a static HTML file with no pointing link, this doesn’t fully confirm whether Google would discover it on its own. The closest supported guidance is: without a link pointing to it, there’s no indication Google will necessarily find or crawl it, but if it is linked from somewhere Google knows, it can be crawled.

Yes, Google can crawl it if it knows the URL somehow. But if the page has no incoming links and isn’t listed in things like an XML sitemap or otherwise exposed, it typically won’t be found and crawled.

So the closest answer is: Google can crawl an unlinked static HTML page, but it generally cannot discover it on its own without some kind of hint.

If you want the closest guidance supported here, the main point is to choose one delimiter and use it consistently, and keep the title concise. Google may still rewrite the title if it thinks it’s better for search results.

So, based on what’s provided, there’s no support here for choosing between `|` and `-` in a title. If you’re asking about the visible page title format, that answer isn’t covered by this evidence.

Use the pipe (`|`).

The guidance here is that if you’re choosing only between a colon and a pipe for a meta title, the pipe is preferred because:

- a colon can already be part of the page title, which can make titles confusing if you use another colon to separate site and page text
- the page title should come first, and the site name after it, so the separator should work with that order

So a better pattern is:

`Top 10 list of stuff | Example.com`

The best approach supported here is not to rely on special characters in the content. Instead, create a separate page for each tag, using a clean URL like `/tagged/mytag`, and make sure each tagged product or document is accessible under that tag path, for example `/tagged/mytag/myid` or `/tagged/mytag/mydocument`, with a canonical URL set.

Then, when searching, use a query like:

`inurl:/tagged/mytag`

So for product pages, the closest supported guidance is to structure tags in the URL and search by URL pattern, rather than trying to make Google search special-character wrappers around the tag text.

For product page URLs, the safest practice is to stick to a-z, A-Z, 0-9, underscore, and hyphen. Other special characters can cause problems, sometimes only with certain browsers or devices, and may get URL-encoded in ways that look messy.

If you’re considering special characters in product names or page text, that’s a different issue from the URL itself. The guidance here only supports avoiding special characters in the URL slug/path, especially for SEO and reliability.

No. The provided information only says that robots.txt should be placed in the root directory, at http://www.example.com/robots.txt. It does not say robots.txt is necessarily required.

Local SEO, based on the evidence, is about creating pages or site sections that clearly identify each local business with location-specific details like address, phone number, and other vendor information. The example given suggests using markup for customer pages and organizing them as sub-directories or sub-domains under one site.

It differs from general website SEO in that simply making a generic site and changing the domain, logo, title, or header text is not enough for local SEO. Search engines can detect duplicate or very similar content, and that can hurt rankings. So local SEO here is more about unique, location-relevant content and structured business details, while website SEO in this case would be the broader optimization of the site itself.

There isn’t an answer in the thread, so I can’t say for certain why Google would treat one site author differently from another.

Local SEO is for getting found in a specific language/region market, while website SEO is broader and tied to the site itself. From the information here, the main distinction supported is that if you have separate domains for different languages or countries, you generally do not need hreflang; hreflang is mainly for a single multilingual site on one domain.

So, in practice:

- Local SEO: aimed at a local audience, and you can also set geotargeting for each site in Google and Bing.
- Website SEO: optimizing the site content and structure more generally.
- Difference: a translated German site and English site on different domains are not treated as duplicate content just because they cover the same subject, and hreflang is not required in that setup.

The closest guidance supported here is that each site should be translated by a human and tailored to its language users, rather than just using machine translation.

Being in the top 5 for a keyword does not mean your Google impressions will match the local search volume.

The supported explanation here is that search results can vary by person because of personalization/filtering, so your site may rank differently for different users even for the same query. Also, Webmaster Tools data is not real time and can lag behind actual search activity.

So the closest guidance is: low impressions can happen even when you see yourself ranking well, because rankings are not identical for everyone and the reported data may be delayed.

Google appears to determine those important links by analyzing the breadcrumbs on the page — the navigational links that show where the user is in the site hierarchy, like “Home > Toys & Games > Robots.”

According to the cited information, Google’s bot reads those breadcrumbs from destination pages and uses them to generate the hierarchical links shown in search results. It’s not described as a guaranteed or fully documented process, but breadcrumbs are the supported explanation given here.

The evidence only says that Google Custom Search results can be displayed on your site by hosting them as an iframe, using the Custom Search Engine support link provided.

It does not explain how Google determines important links on a website for display in search results.

Google can show a link’s text and snippet in search results in a way that reflects the page’s title and description, and using keywords that match what users are searching for can make the result more likely to be clicked.

The evidence also says Google can attach tracking parameters to result links, so it may know when a result is clicked for a particular search term.

What it does not fully explain is how Google decides which links are “important” on a website overall. The closest supported guidance here is that making your title and description match what searchers want can help those results attract clicks, and Google may use that title text as the displayed link text in search results.

Create or claim the Google Places listing for each location, and point each one to the matching city-specific page on your site. Make sure the name, address, and phone number are exactly consistent across the Places listing, the page, and any city directories.

For the pages themselves, avoid making them only a city name swap. Add unique local details such as area-specific specials, photos of the store and staff, a Google Map, and directions. That helps reduce duplicate-content concerns and gives each page more value.

Also try to get reviews from customers in each area, since that can help local search visibility for those cities.

This covers the strongest guidance supported here: local landing pages plus matching business listings and unique city-specific content.

If you operate in multiple counties but only have offices in two towns, you can still tell Google that you serve those broader areas. That can help with local results, but it does not guarantee rankings in every county.

What the guidance supports is:

- Businesses with a physical address tend to rank more easily in local search than businesses that only serve a service area.
- You should tell Google the areas you serve.
- If you have multiple real offices where customers are served, multiple addresses can help you rank more easily in those locations.
- If you do not have offices in all the counties, ranking there usually takes more effort, such as citations, social mentions, backlinks, and overall authority.

So the closest practical answer is: add and verify the listings for your actual offices, make sure Google knows the service areas you cover, and understand that appearing in counties without offices is possible but harder and not something a listing alone will ensure.

It’s hard to rank in local results for cities where you don’t have a physical location. The closest guidance here is:

- create unique landing pages for each city/location
- include the full address and phone number on the relevant pages
- use relevant internal links
- get inbound links from locally and topically relevant sites
- generate positive reviews for each relevant location page
- if possible, have a location closer to the area you want to rank in

Google’s local results are address-based, so if you have an office in one city, you can usually target that city well, but ranking strongly in a neighboring city is much more difficult without a physical presence there.

Google local/map results are ranked by relevance, prominence, and proximity. That means even if your listing is claimed and complete, it may not appear in Google Maps or local search if the search terms, the viewer’s location, or the map area being searched don’t match well enough.

Closest guidance supported here:
- Make sure the listing details are accurate and complete.
- Keep in mind that search results can vary based on where the search is being done from.
- Adding location-specific terms to the search can affect whether your listing appears.

The evidence doesn’t show any separate “Google Places” listing type that needs to be transferred from a local listing.

Map listings are ranked by your search terms plus proximity, relevance, and prominence.

Proximity can depend on:
- your location
- the part of the map already being shown before you search
- your search terms, especially if they include keywords plus location

So the main way to improve your position is to strengthen those ranking factors as much as possible, especially making sure your listing is relevant to the search terms and well established/prominent. If your listing is far from the searcher or the search is pulling results from another area, it may still not appear high even with a complete, claimed profile.

To improve your position, focus on overall SEO rather than just the Google Maps listing.

What the answer supports:
- Ranking depends on many factors, not just the amount of information in the listing.
- Backlink quality matters more than backlink quantity.
- The other site may have stronger links than yours, even if it looks weaker.
- A search-friendly URL structure can help, including having keywords in the domain name.
- The fact that their domain includes “sprinklers” could be helping them.

Closest guidance supported by the evidence:
- Review and improve the quality of your links.
- Make sure your pages and URLs are optimized for the target keywords.
- Keep researching SEO factors beyond the listing itself, since Maps rankings are influenced by many signals.

Set up a Places listing yourself. That gives you more control over the business location data Google has on hand, which can help Google understand your location better and may improve how your business appears in map-related search results.

The answer also suggests that filling out the listing more completely can affect how some information is used, but it does not give any guaranteed method for improving ranking in the map listing.

Submit your site in Bing Webmaster Tools if you haven’t already. If you have, check the crawling stats there to see whether Bing is having trouble accessing or indexing your pages.

Also, focus on getting quality backlinks to important pages and make sure your internal navigation lets crawlers find them. Search engines may index pages more readily when they discover them through links.

Things that can affect indexing include duplicate content, site navigation, page size, and load time. Review any errors or issues shown in Bing Webmaster Tools and fix them.

This doesn’t specifically address a “localized view” of your data beyond improving crawl/indexing, but the guidance here supports making your pages easier for search engines to discover and index.

Use Google’s alternate language markup.

That lets you tell search engines about the language or country variants of each page, either on the pages themselves or in your XML sitemap. It can also be used for alternatives in the same language aimed at different countries.

It’s better not to rely on automatic redirection based on the user’s perceived language, since Google recommends against that. A better approach is:
- mark up each localized version as an alternate of the others
- link the sites together clearly
- make each localized page well optimized for its target audience

That should help search engines crawl the site and surface the right localized version in local searches, while still letting users navigate to the correct content if they land on the wrong site.

A practical URL strategy is to use separate language sites, such as en.example.com, fr.example.com, and so on, rather than forcing automatic redirection.

Automatic detection based on Geo-IP or browser language can be unreliable, so a safer approach is to let users choose and optionally suggest a language using Geo-IP or the Accept-Language header. You can also reorder the language menu or show a “translate to [language]” link.

If you want search engines to handle discovery, separate language subsites is the supported approach. Any hosted CMS that supports multilingual sites can work for this, but if you need to read Accept-Language or do Geo-IP in a custom way, you usually need server-side scripting access, which most hosted CMS platforms do not provide.

The closest guidance supported here is to follow Google’s “Working with multi-regional websites” guidance, since that is cited as covering URL structure for multilingual sites in detail.

From the question itself, the directory approach like:

- `www.yoursite.com/sv/...`

is presented as a valid option, and the answer does not prefer subdomains over directories. It only points you to Google’s best-practice guidance for the detailed recommendation.

The answer in the thread is that the subdirectory form is generally preferred: domain.com/language/page.

It suggests choosing the structure that best fits your content, but for language specifically it gives the example of Wikipedia using a language path and says this seems to be the standard, recommending it.

So, based on that guidance, domain.com/language/page is the better choice.

You’re unlikely to be “penalized” just because the site has multiple languages or two domains pointing to the same hosting.

What matters for SEO is that each language has its own unique URL. Search engines need separate, crawlable URLs for each language version. It’s fine to use separate domains, subdirectories, subdomains, or URL parameters, as long as each language version lives at a distinct URL.

What’s problematic is keeping the same URL and changing only the language through sessions, cookies, or request headers. In that setup, search engines may only see one version, not all the language variants.

So the closest guidance is:

- make sure users end up on language-specific URLs when they switch languages
- don’t rely only on sessions/cookies to serve different languages
- real translations are fine; avoid automatic translated duplicates
- if you use two domains, each should clearly serve its own language version

In short: separate URLs per language, and redirect or link users to the correct language URL after switching.

A workable approach is to preprocess the site before it’s sent to the client, for example with PHP conditional includes. That way, each language can be served as a clear copy of the site in that language, which should let search engines index the site separately for each language.

What this supports is the idea that you can keep one underlying codebase and generate language-specific output at request time, rather than manually maintaining fully separate copies of everything. It does not confirm whether this is the “best” SEO approach overall, only that this method can produce language-specific pages for indexing.

The evidence suggests choosing the language in the path rather than on a subdomain, so domain.com/language/page is recommended over language.domain.com/page.

It also says you should decide based on your content and points to an article discussing subdomains vs. subdirectories, but the direct recommendation given is that the path-based version seems to be the standard and is preferred.

A .fr domain is not, by itself, hurting your SEO. The main point is that Google.fr is localized to France, so you’re competing in a smaller, more French-focused search environment, while Google.com is much broader and more competitive.

For a multilingual site, switching to a .com or .org would not, on its own, improve rankings. The TLD is not a ranking factor here. So if your site is already on .fr, that domain is just as good as .com or .org for SEO.

What this does not fully answer is how to increase English traffic specifically. Based on the evidence, the closest guidance is: your site is more likely to be discovered by French users through Google.fr because of localization and competition differences, not because of the domain name.

There isn’t a big SEO advantage to choosing one setup over another. Using separate top-level domains, subdomains, or subdirectories is generally about structure and operations more than search ranking.

What matters most from the provided guidance is:

- You can improve response times by hosting content closer to users, which can help usability and SEO.
- Subdomains and subdirectories can share cookies, which helps with login and tracking across languages.
- Getting country-specific top-level domains can be difficult, time-consuming, and expensive.

So if you’re deciding between one domain with both languages or separate sites, SEO alone doesn’t strongly favor either. The closer guidance supported here is to choose based on practical factors like hosting location, cookie sharing, and the cost/effort of managing multiple country domains.

GET variables do not inherently have bad effects on a page. In the example given, Google can recognize and index URLs with GET variables as different pages.
