A shared host usually means your files live on one physical machine, and you typically get FTP details to upload them there.

Cloudfront is different: the files live on many servers around the world, and a user gets the file from the nearest server, so it is designed to be quicker for the user.

The evidence does not fully compare all “cloud hosting” options with web hosting, because Amazon’s other cloud services do different things. It only clearly supports this comparison:
- shared hosting: one physical machine, FTP upload
- Cloudfront: distributed across many servers, optimized for speed

If you mean a specific cloud service other than Cloudfront, the closest guidance supported here is to compare that service separately, since not all cloud services work the same way.

To influence how Google shows your pages, make sure each page has proper HTML metadata and real page content.

Use tags like these in the page:

```html
<meta http-equiv="content-type" content="text/html; charset=utf-8" />
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow" />
<meta name="keywords" content="keyword1, keyword2" />
<meta name="description" content="description." />
<title>My Page title</title>
```

The title and description help search engines understand the page, and `robots` tells them whether to index it and follow links.

This alone won’t guarantee Google will display exactly what you want. The page should also have valid content and SEO-friendly URLs. If Google is showing something like “Index of ~/user,” that usually means it’s finding directory-style content rather than a properly titled page, so fixing the page title, description, and page content is the closest supported guidance here.

If you want Google to discover and index pages, the simplest supported way is to have a page that links to them. Google’s crawlers can follow those links and find the pages.

That said, this does not guarantee Google will crawl or index them, and there’s no simple way to force Google to scan a list of URLs or make it show pages in a specific way just by submitting them. If you control the pages yourself, the closest reliable option is still to make them easy to crawl by linking to them and, where possible, using normal indexing tools like sitemaps or URL submission.

Using traffic exchange programs like paid-to-click, paid-to-surf, autosurf, and click-exchange programs can put your Google AdSense account at risk, because AdSense specifically prohibits sites displaying Google ads from using third-party services that generate clicks or impressions.

The evidence only directly confirms this for Google AdSense. It does not say that every pay-per-impression ad program has the same rule, but it does support the general guidance that you should check each ad network’s policy before using traffic exchange traffic.

If you move the Crown Heights content from the root to /crown-heights, the main thing is to keep the important content and links in place so the new page still clearly represents Crown Heights.

- link to it using “Crown Heights” as the anchor text
- include that link in navigation and/or a widget on the site
- have a clear “Locations” section or menu with both “Crown Heights” and “East End”
- make sure your sitemap reflects the new structure

One thing to keep in mind is that if Google can’t clearly decide, it may still prefer the domain root over an interior page.

If your goal is to keep a particular page from being indexed, the guidance here does not explain a specific noindex method. It only supports that search engines can index distinct URLs and content. The closest practical takeaway is to avoid exposing the page through crawlable links if you do not want it found, or use standard SEO controls such as `noindex` if your setup supports that.

If your goal is to hide a page from users but still have search engines crawl it, that’s generally not a good idea. Showing different content to users and search engines is usually treated as black-hat SEO.

Also, if the page is messy or not useful to users, search engines likely have no reason to crawl it, and it could even hurt your site’s overall ranking if it gets indexed.

The closest guidance supported here is: don’t try to conceal content from users while exposing it to search engines. If you don’t want a page indexed, it’s better not to make it look like crawlable content intended for search engines.

Use an HTTP `X-Robots-Tag` response header on the file, for example:

```http
X-Robots-Tag: noindex
```

For PDFs and other non-HTML files, that’s the supported way to tell search engines not to index them. If you can set headers on your server, you can do it like this in Apache:

```apache
<Files ~ "\.pdf$">
  Header set X-Robots-Tag "noindex, nofollow"
</Files>
```

A few important points:

- This works only if you can modify the HTTP headers for those files.
- `robots.txt` does not stop a file from appearing in search results if other sites link to it.
- If you block a file in `robots.txt`, search engines may not crawl it and therefore won’t see the `X-Robots-Tag` header, so don’t use `robots.txt` to block it if your goal is indexing control.

If you need to hide only specific files, apply the header only to those file types or paths.

You can block the file from being indexed by adding a rule to your robots.txt file.

For a specific file extension, you can use something like:

User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow: /*.pdf$

If you want to block all search engines rather than just Google, use:

Disallow: /*.pdf$

If you only want to block one specific file, use the full path to that file instead:

Disallow: /path/to/pdf/thefilename.pdf

Be aware that blocking by file extension will also block any PDF files you do want indexed, so a file-specific path is the safer option if you only want to hide certain files.

You can limit scrapers by rate-limiting and blocking abusive request patterns at the web server level.

The options mentioned are:

- mod_security for request limiting and filtering
- mod_evasive to detect and temporarily block an IP that:
  - requests the same page too many times per second
  - makes too many concurrent requests
  - keeps requesting while blacklisted
- mod_qos to control:
  - concurrent requests per URL or virtual host
  - requests per second
  - bandwidth limits
  - connection limits per source IP
  - request/header filtering

So a good approach supported here is to use Apache modules rather than relying only on a daily hit cap per IP. The guidance here does not specifically validate a “1000 hits per day” threshold, but it does support per-second, concurrent-request, and connection-based limits as a better fit for scraper control.

A practical approach suggested here is to use a spider trap: create a URL like `/spider-trap/somepage.html`, disallow that path in `robots.txt`, and place a link to it that is hidden from human visitors. If a crawler or scraper reaches it, you can block that IP from accessing anything on the site and show a human-readable page with a CAPTCHA or unlock step.

This doesn’t fully solve “too many pages too fast” rate-limiting by itself, but it does give you a way to identify and stop abusive crawlers/scrapers and then gate access with a CAPTCHA.

A # at the end of a URL is the fragment/hash part. It’s commonly used for:

If you’re seeing the page “redirect” to the same URL with just # added, the most likely cause is a link or script using href="#" and an onclick handler. That often happens when JavaScript is attached to a link but the click handler doesn’t prevent the browser’s default action, so the browser appends the hash.

To find it, look for:

- links with href="#"
- JavaScript click handlers on those links
- missing return false or equivalent preventDefault() in the handler

The behavior you described is consistent with an incorrectly configured link or script rather than a server-side redirect.

Set each virtual host’s ServerName and DocumentRoot to separate directories, and don’t place one site’s files inside the other site’s document root.

For example:

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
  ServerName serverA.com
  DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverA"
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
  ServerName serverB.com
  DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverB"
</VirtualHost>

With this setup, serverB’s files won’t be reachable as http://serverA.com/serverB/ because serverA is serving from its own document root. The key is that ServerName and DocumentRoot must be different for each vhost.

Place a rewrite rule in the /shop/ directory so requests to mydomain.com/shop/ are redirected to the subdomain you want to use.

For example:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteBase /

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^shop\.mydomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^shop/$ http://shop.mydomain.com [L,NC,R=301]
```

This allows the files to stay in /shop/ but prevents direct use of mydomain.com/shop/ by sending visitors to shop.mydomain.com instead.

If you have two subdomains pointing to the same /shop/ directory, you can’t keep both accessible from the main domain and also block direct access to that same path without choosing a preferred subdomain to redirect to.

It’s worth it, but the importance depends on what the errors are.

If the errors are broken links, they should be fixed because they can hurt search ranking. If they’re missing CSS or JavaScript files, they can make a site look unsafe in some browsers and worry users. If the DOCTYPE is wrong, pages may render incorrectly in some browsers. General HTML/CSS errors can also cause display problems and even slow rendering because the browser has to compensate for broken code.

So 27 errors isn’t automatically “bad,” but the goal should be to reduce them, especially if they affect usability, rendering, or trust. Some errors may be unavoidable, but a no-error site is better for the best user experience.

- valid or invalid CSS has no effect on SEO

So, if the validation errors are only because of prefixed CSS3 properties and your site behaves correctly, it’s reasonable to ignore those validation warnings.

Valid HTML probably is not a direct ranking factor for SEO. But it is still recommended, because valid code helps ensure your content can be properly crawled and indexed. Invalid HTML can break a crawler the same way it can break in a browser.

So, yes, it’s worth it as a best practice for reliability and crawlability, even if it doesn’t appear to directly improve rankings.

An XML sitemap is generally good, not bad.

For a small site with mostly static content, there’s probably very little functional difference between an XML sitemap and a simple text sitemap. A text-only sitemap has no fundamental disadvantage.

XML sitemaps can be more useful on larger sites with a mix of frequently and infrequently changing pages, because priority and last-modified data can affect crawl frequency. They can also include media information, like video sitemap data, which plain text sitemaps can’t.

The main downside is that if you include extra metadata, it adds a chance for mistakes, but that’s not inherently worse than making a mistake in a text sitemap URL list.

An XML sitemap is generally good, especially when you have many URLs or want to include extra information like last-modification dates, images, or videos.

A simple text URL list is easier to make by hand and easier for humans to read, but that advantage mostly matters only for very small sites. Once you need a generated sitemap, XML becomes more useful because it can carry more than just URLs.

So the closest answer is: XML sitemaps are good, and often better than plain text sitemaps for anything beyond the simplest use case.

RewriteRule .* http://mysite.com/mypage.html [R=301,L]

This redirects requests for `mysite.com/?page_id=1103` to `mysite.com/mypage.html`.

Use an `.htaccess` rewrite rule in the main domain’s document root to return a 404 when someone tries to access the add-on domain’s folder through the primary domain:

```apache
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^exampleB/ - [R=404,L]
```

For your case, replace `example.com` with your main domain and `exampleB/` with the add-on domain’s root directory name.

This blocks access via the main hosting domain path, while still allowing normal access through the add-on domain itself.

```apache
</VirtualHost>
```

If you already have a wildcard DNS record covering that level, the subdomain will normally resolve without adding a separate DNS entry. In that case, you would still configure the Apache virtual host for `sub.domain.com`, but you would not need extra DNS changes for the name itself.

So the rule is:
- DNS must provide an address for the hostname, either explicitly or via wildcard.
- Apache virtual hosts then map that hostname to the right site/folder.

If the wildcard exists but points elsewhere, or if the hostname is not resolving to your server, then the Apache config alone will not make it work.

```apache

RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} ^ref=(.+)$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^index.php$ /? [L,R=301,NC]
```

- If it’s a domain name, resolve it with nslookup to get the IP, then decide whether blocking that IP is appropriate.
- Be careful: if the source is part of a shared pool or generic host range, blocking it may affect valid users.
- If this is happening automatically, your protection script may be working correctly, but it could also be blocking legitimate users.

So the practical way to “solve” it is to locate the offending address in the logs and block it if it’s clearly malicious, while checking whether the block is too broad. If the rejection is from rotating IPs in a pool, there may be little you can do except keep the protection in place and monitor/log more closely.

```sql
CREATE USER 'something'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'yourpassword';

```

Or otherwise add matching privileges specifically for `localhost`.

That’s why the error says:

`Access denied for user 'something'@'localhost'`

Use a condition that checks both HTTPS and the host, then redirect to the non-www host:

```apache
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} ^on$
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www\.x\.co\.uk$
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://x\.co\.uk$1 [L,R=301]
```

This redirects `https://www.x.co.uk` to `https://x.co.uk` and leaves `http://` requests alone. If you want the same pattern for a different domain, replace `x\.co\.uk` with your domain.

It sounds like your domain’s DNS is not being managed at the place where you’re trying to edit it.

To point `host.com` to `www.host.com`, you need to add the DNS record in the system that controls the domain’s nameservers. Your registrar may own the domain, but if it says it has “no access” to the nameservers, then it cannot add the record there.

What to do:
- Check which nameservers your domain is using.
- Go to the provider that controls those nameservers.
- Add the needed DNS record there.

For a `host.com` to `www.host.com` setup, that usually means creating a record for `host.com` that points to `www.host.com` using the DNS panel that actually manages the nameservers.

If you want, I can also tell you the usual record type to use for this in a control panel like DotNetPanel.

In DNS, you can’t “route” one name to a different website the way you’re describing if both names end up resolving to the same target. An A record for `@` points a name to an IP address, and a `www` CNAME or A record will just resolve `www.host.com` to whatever target you set.

If your goal is:

- `host.com` → one server
- `www.host.com` → another server

then you need separate DNS records for each name, each pointing to the correct IP or hostname. If your panel is automatically making `www.host.com` follow `host.com`, then that behavior is coming from the DNS setup or panel defaults, not from routing itself.

If what you actually want is to show content from another server while keeping `www.host.com` in the browser, the closest supported approach is a reverse proxy. DNS only gets the visitor to a server; the reverse proxy then forwards requests to the other server.

So in dot net panel, check whether you can create independent records for:

- `@` → IP of the main server
- `www` → IP of the other server

If the panel forces `www` to mirror the root domain, then you’d need to change the DNS configuration at the provider that hosts the zone, or use a reverse proxy instead.

A practical way to judge needed connection speed is to estimate:

expected concurrent users × expected traffic per user

For example, if pages are about 200 KB and 100 users may be active at once, you’d need around 20 MB of bandwidth at that moment. In reality, not everyone requests a page at the exact same time, and page generation time also matters, but this gives you a rough idea.

Signs that you may need to upgrade include seeing the network interface near its limit during busy periods. If you can monitor bytes sent per second and it’s consistently high, that’s a good indication. If visitors report slow downloads at peak times, that can also point to insufficient bandwidth.

If your goal is to have Google and other search engines drop those pages, a 410 Gone response is the better fit than redirecting everything to /index.html.

A 301 says “this page moved,” so search engines may keep the old URL around for a while and treat the destination as the replacement. A 410 says “this content is gone,” which is the clearer signal for removal.

For your case, the suggested approach is:

- keep /index.html accessible
- keep static files like css, js, images accessible
- return 410 for other .html and .php pages
- optionally serve a custom 410 page with a link back to the homepage

Example:

```apache
ErrorDocument 410 /error-docs/e410.html

RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !^/error-docs/
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !=/index.html
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} !\.(gif|jpe?g|png|css|js)$
RewriteRule . - [G]
```

This does not redirect users to the homepage. It tells clients and search engines that the requested page is gone, while still letting your homepage and assets work normally.

A point-scale system gives you more information than a binary system, so it’s generally more useful if you want to capture how strongly people feel about content. A binary upvote/downvote system is simpler and can still reflect community consensus well, and it’s also easier if you later want to use the votes in a collaborative-filtering style system.

The main caution with 5-star systems is calibration: if users tend to be extreme, the scale can still work, but you need to account for the fact that the average rating may not be centered where you expect. In that case, you’d compare ratings against the actual distribution and adjust the scale so the midpoint and spread make sense for your audience.

If your only goal is “good content rises, poor content falls,” all three approaches can work. A binary system is the simplest. A 5-star system is richer if you want more nuance. An upvote-only system is the least informative, but can still work for ranking content if you just want positive reinforcement.

So the closest guidance supported here is:
- use binary if you want simplicity and consensus,
- use a point scale if you want more nuanced data,
- don’t dismiss star ratings just because some users are extreme raters; calibrate them instead.

If you change the static IP of a nameserver, you update the IP address of that nameserver host at your domain registrar, and the registrar updates the authoritative DNS server for the TLD.

The registry stores both the nameserver hostname and its IP address when the nameserver is registered. If the IP changes later, the registry does not “detect” it automatically; it has to be updated through the registrar.

So, in short: you don’t change a static IP “to a domain name” automatically. You register the nameserver hostname with its IP, and if that IP changes, you manually update the nameserver’s IP at the registrar.

If you want your domain name to follow a changing IP address, the DNS provider has to update the A record dynamically. A CNAME can point `www.domain.com` to `domain.com`, but the root domain itself (`domain.com`) cannot be a CNAME.

The guidance supported here is:

- use a dynamic DNS service to update the A record for `domain.com`
- set `www.domain.com` as a CNAME to `domain.com`
- if your current service can’t update the root A record, it may not be sufficient
- if dynamic DNS is too limiting or paid, a static IP may be simpler

A 301 redirect from the root to `www` may help with web traffic, but it doesn’t replace DNS for pointing a domain to an IP address.

Your site working at `www.example.com` but not `example.com` usually means the web server is only configured for the `www` host name. `www` is just a subdomain, so the server needs to be told what to do for the non-www version too.

The usual fix is to either:

- configure the server to answer for both `example.com` and `www.example.com`, or
- redirect one version to the other, which is often the simplest solution.

For Apache, one common way is to add a separate virtual host that redirects the non-preferred version, for example:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.domain.com
    Redirect permanent / http://domain.com/
</VirtualHost>
```

If your site works with www.domain.com but gives a 400 bad request on domain.com, the provided solution is to redirect the non-www version to the www version using an .htaccess file.

If you’re using Apache, create a file called .htaccess in your website root and add:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^yourdomain\.com [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.yourdomain.com/$1 [R=301,NC,L]

This will send visitors who enter the non-www version to the www version.

Your pattern is matching only one character at a time because of `(.)`, so it won’t capture a full path segment. If you want to redirect everything under `a3ff/` to the same path on the target domain, use `(.*)` instead.

For example:

`RewriteRule ^a3ff/(.*) [DOMAINNAME]/$1 [R=301,QSA,L]`

That would handle things like:

- `/a3ff/X` → `http://domainname/X`
- `/a3ff/ABC` → `http://domainname/ABC`

If you want `/a3ff/` itself to redirect too, you’d need a separate rule, since `.*` can match an empty string but your current rule structure may not cover every case cleanly.

`RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [OR]`
`RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !on`
`RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://www.example.com/$1 [R,L]`

This will redirect:

- `http://example.com`
- `http://www.example.com`
- `https://example.com`

to `https://www.example.com`.

If you have other subdomains like `forum.example.com`, keep the host match as shown. If not, you could instead use a negative match against `www.example.com`.

Use a full URL in the target, including protocol and domain. For example:

RewriteRule ^(\S+)/directory/(\d+)/(\d+)/entry/(\d+)/?$ http://www.example.com/directories/index.cfm?sFuseAction=XXX.YYYY.ZZZZ&nDirectoryID=$2&nEntryID=$4&nCategoryID=$3&sDirectory=$1 [NC,L]

If your goal is specifically a 301 redirect, that answer only shows the full-URL syntax needed.

Use a rewrite rule that matches the path and checks the query string, then redirects to the new URL:

`RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING}  ^q=customer%20reference&f= [NC]`
`RewriteRule ^dyn/$ /customer-references/? [L,R=301]`

That is the solution that worked for this case.

A 301 redirect can only send one old URL to one new URL. If your old dynamic URL pattern now maps to multiple different static URLs, you need a rule that determines the correct destination based on the query string or path values.

The guidance supported here is:

- Keep the old `product.php` working if it still needs to serve those products.
- Add the new friendly URLs and map them back to the right product in your application.
- If you want old requests to go to the new URLs, use logic that inspects the incoming URL and redirects to the matching new URL, for example based on `type` and `id`.
- If IIS only lets you set one redirect target, that alone isn’t enough for a one-to-many case; you’d need conditional routing/rewrite logic rather than a single static redirect.

So, for your case, you should not redirect all old dynamic URLs to one single page. Instead, create per-product/per-URL redirect rules or application code that reads the old parameters and sends each old URL to its corresponding new static URL.

The response also suggests that if you want `/category/product` URLs to work, you can rewrite them internally to something like `product.php?categoryname=$1&productname=$2`, or use PHP to detect old `product.php` requests and redirect them to the new friendly URL.

Yes. Entire folders can be redirected, not just individual files.

If you rename a folder and the URL changes, you can use a 301 redirect in `.htaccess`, for example:

`Redirect permanent /OLD http://example.com/NEW`

That will redirect everything under the old directory to the new one, such as:

- `http://example.com/OLD/page_one.html` → `http://example.com/NEW/page_one.html`
- `http://example.com/OLD/page_two.html` → `http://example.com/NEW/page_two.html`
- `http://example.com/OLD/an_image.png` → `http://example.com/NEW/an_image.png`

So this is not limited to pages moved to another folder; it also works for a renamed folder.

If your site serves the same content at both `mydomain.com` and `www.mydomain.com`, and you can’t set up a 301/permanent redirect from one to the other, then add both versions in Google Webmaster Tools and set your preferred domain there.

If you can redirect visitors from the non-canonical version to the canonical one, register the version you want to use as the main domain.

To use the www version with Google, point `www.mydomain.com` to `ghs.google.com` in GoDaddy DNS.

If `mydomain.com` does not go to `www.mydomain.com`, that is not controlled by DNS. You need to set up a redirect/forward from `mydomain.com` to `www.mydomain.com`.

GoDaddy offers domain forwarding for free. Use their forwarding setup instructions for `mydomain.com` so visitors to the non-www address are sent to the www address.

To make it a 301 redirect, the rule needs to point to the full URL, including the protocol and domain, not just the internal path.

For example:

RewriteRule ^(\S+)/directory/(\d+)/(\d+)/entry/(\d+)/?$ http://www.example.com/directories/index.cfm?sFuseAction=XXX.YYYY.ZZZZ&nDirectoryID=$2&nEntryID=$4&nCategoryID=$3&sDirectory=$1 [NC,L]

That is the syntax supported by the provided answer.

`RewriteRule (.*) http://www.blog.mysite.co.uk/$1 [R=301,L]`

If that still fails, the issue is likely with server configuration rather than the redirect target itself.

Use a 301 redirect.

That’s why the URL in the address bar doesn’t change when you click links.

If you want the page URLs to appear normally, you’d need a real redirect or to host the site directly rather than using GoDaddy’s masked redirect.

Yes—if you set GoDaddy’s forwarding to “Forward only” and choose redirect type “301 (Permanent),” that is the search-engine-friendly 301 redirect.

“Forward with masking” is different; it uses a frame-based redirect, not a true 301. So for a real permanent redirect, switch to “Forward only” with 301 selected.

The cases where subdomains are suggested are when you’re running separate servers under the same domain, or when the site is more like a portal for many separate websites, such as each user having their own blog.

So in this case, unless you have that kind of separation or portal structure, folders are the safer choice.

and the thread itself doesn’t resolve which should be chosen.

So, based on the evidence, both methods together are effective for preventing duplicate indexing, and that combination is what should be preferred.

No, blocking `/content/` in `robots.txt` should not affect crawling of your real pages, as long as your important pages are not under `/content/`.

`Disallow: /content/`

Google may try to crawl subdirectories based on links it finds, including paths like `/content/foo/foo.html`, but if your real pages are elsewhere, they should still be crawled normally.

You can’t submit a wildcard de-index request like `http://www.mysite.com/file.php*` to remove all those URLs at once.

What the answer supports is:

- the removal tool is meant for emergencies, not bulk cleanup
- Google should be allowed to recrawl and discover the URLs are no longer valid
- if those pages should not exist, return `410 Gone` for them
- if the issue is duplicate or changed URLs, use canonicalization and proper redirects so Google keeps only the correct versions

So for PHP pages that were indexed with different query strings or path variants, the supported approach is to fix the server responses and let Google clean them up over time, rather than trying to de-index them with a pattern.

A few keywords in a URL can help a little bit, but only as a very small SEO factor. They may also make the link clearer to users.

It’s not a major ranking signal compared with great content, titles, and link text. So keywords in URLs are not needless, but they’re only mildly useful.

If you already have a URL structure in place, the guidance here suggests not changing it just to add keywords. A readable, natural URL is fine if it makes sense to users and includes relevant terms.

Repeating the title in a forum post and having the same phrase appear in the meta title, actual title, and post content is not automatically keyword stuffing.

The key point is whether it reads naturally and is used in context. If the page is very short and the keyword makes up a large share of the visible text, that could be a concern. But on a forum, repeated topic titles and related terms are common, and Google is generally understood to handle that.

So the closest guidance supported here is:
- if the repeated keyword phrase is natural and contextual, it’s probably fine
- if the page is thin and the keyword dominates the text, it may look like stuffing

In other words, repetition alone isn’t the issue; unnatural, excessive repetition without context is what would be problematic.

Putting the same “ratings-reviews-prices” part in every product URL would probably be seen as spammy or keyword stuffing, especially if it appears on all pages without variation.

The guidance here is:
- If you use those words in the URL, make sure the page actually contains ratings, reviews, and prices for that product.
- Even then, it’s not necessary to stuff the URL with those terms.
- A better approach is to include those words naturally on the page itself, and vary the title and description where possible.

So the closest supported answer is: it’s safer to avoid repeating that fixed keyword bundle in every URL. Use a cleaner unique product URL, and let ratings/reviews/prices appear naturally in the page content.

If the page represents a real, distinct result with enough different content, then having keywords in the URL is generally okay. The answer says Google can understand keywords in the URL and in the query string as essentially the same thing.

It also says that in this case, because these are categorized/generated pages, that’s acceptable.

For SEO, though, the answer suggests you usually don’t need to stuff lots of keywords into the URL. A few keywords are fine, but 3–4 is probably enough. If you want to use keywords, putting them in a meta tag is also recognized by Google, so you don’t need to pack them all into the URL.

So the closest guidance supported here is:
- Don’t worry too much if the URL is keyword-based, as long as it points to a meaningful, distinct page.
- Avoid excessive keyword stuffing in the URL.
- Query strings are not a special fix; Google can treat them similarly.

Google no longer supports Google Authorship, so there’s no need to add multiple rel="author" links for Google.

What the provided answer does support is:
- rel="author" can still exist as a microformat for other applications
- Google now encourages structured data instead
- Google can still recognize authorship through structured data, bylines, and citations

So for Google specifically, multiple rel="author" links are not something you need to worry about anymore.

Google’s guidance here says rel="author" is an HTML5 relation and does not have to be tied to a Google profile. The evidence does not specifically address whether Google is okay with multiple rel="author" links on one page or site.

What it does support is that rel="author" can be used to identify authorship, and Google may use it for authorship display if it’s associated with a Google profile. It also says structured data authorship can be interpreted.

So the closest supported answer is: there’s no evidence here that multiple rel="author" links are prohibited, but this thread does not confirm Google’s position on multiple author links.

It also says PageRank’s influence on rankings is now very small, so a 1-point increase would not usually explain a 300% traffic jump by itself. The traffic change could come from other factors such as new links or other ranking changes.

A single 301 redirect is generally fine, but multiple 301 redirects can have a negative effect on ranking because some trust and authority is lost with each redirect.

If your goal is only to send human visitors to the new site, the closest supported guidance here is to use a 301 for visitors but keep search engine crawlers from being redirected. The caveat is that this can be seen as cloaking, so it needs caution.

A date in the URL segment can be useful because it gives each day’s content a stable, shareable permalink. For this case, that’s the main benefit: users can bookmark or share a specific day, and old days remain directly accessible.

The downside is that if `/index.html` is only a 302 redirect to the current date, the home page may not show up in search results; search engines may instead surface whatever dated URL they last crawled. Because of that, the safer option is the first structure: keep `/index.html` as the main page, and link from it to `/2013-06-30.html` for today’s content.

- update the article content,
- change the publish date if appropriate,
- keep the same URL rather than adding/changing date segments in it.

A date in the path is useful when the URL represents a hierarchy, not just a list of parameters.

For example, `www.magic.com/date/2010/02/02` can naturally fit with broader pages like:

- `www.magic.com/date/2010`
- `www.magic.com/date/2010/02`
- `www.magic.com/date/2010/02/02`

That makes sense if the site offers year, month, and day views.

By contrast, `date=2010-02-02` is better when `date` is just one independent parameter among others. It’s a more natural fit for unordered query values.

So the benefit of date in URL segments is not that search engines “understand” it better in some magical way, but that the URL structure is cleaner and more suitable for hierarchical content. If the date is just a filter, query parameters are fine. If it’s part of a nested structure, path segments can be more elegant.

The closest guidance here is that moving a single page from one domain to another is generally not the ideal SEO approach if you can avoid it. The supported approach shown is to use IIS/web.config rewrite rules so that requests for `domain.com` are redirected to `www.domain.com`.

Example:

```xml
<rewrite>
  <rules>
    <rule name="Redirect domain.com to www" patternSyntax="Wildcard" stopProcessing="true">
      <match url="*" />
      <conditions>
        <add input="{HTTP_HOST}" pattern="domain.com" />
      </conditions>
      <action type="Redirect" url="http://www.domain.com/{R:0}" />
    </rule>
  </rules>
</rewrite>
```

Or with regular expressions:

```xml
<rewrite>
  <rules>
    <rule name="Redirect domain.com to www" patternSyntax="ECMAScript" stopProcessing="true">
      <match url=".*" />
      <conditions>
        <add input="{HTTP_HOST}" pattern="^domain.com$" />
      </conditions>
      <action type="Redirect" url="http://www.domain.com/{R:0}" />
    </rule>
  </rules>
</rewrite>
```

So the closest guidance is: configure the redirect on IIS using a rewrite rule.

Soft 404s in GWT can happen when a URL rewrite or redirect succeeds at the URL level, but the platform-side route or page generation fails and returns a page with little or no real content. In that case, Google may treat it as a soft 404.

What to do:
- Check whether campaign or referral tags are being rewritten correctly.
- Log requests and rewrites to see whether the tagged URL is reaching the expected page.
- Look for cases where the page loads only a header/footer with a blank body, or otherwise returns content that looks like an error or empty page even though it isn’t a real 404.
- If the redirect is being broken by the software layer, fix the route/query handling so the page resolves normally.

So, campaign URL tags themselves can contribute to soft 404s if they trigger a bad rewrite or a failed platform-side redirect.

It also notes that automated rank-checking tools may violate a search engine’s terms of service.

If you mean checking where your site appears in search results, that’s the closest objective method covered here, but it doesn’t provide Yahoo-specific instructions.

That can happen if the sitemap includes URLs that redirect. Google may not count the sitemap URLs themselves as indexed pages; instead, it indexes the final destination URLs after the 301 redirects.

So Google can show more indexed URLs than are listed in the sitemap if:
- some sitemap URLs are old or non-canonical,
- those URLs redirect to other pages,
- Google has indexed the redirect targets instead.

The closest guidance supported here is to regenerate the sitemap with only live, canonical URLs and remove redirected URLs from it. Also make sure robots.txt is set up correctly. If you check the redirected destination URLs, those are the ones Google should show as indexed.

Adding `http://` to internal links is not shown here to provide any SEO benefit.

The closest supported guidance is that internal links in a menu can help by strengthening internal linking, but the format of the link text or adding extra description is not indicated as having SEO value.

If a page is indexed, it can still fail to appear for the keywords you expect because it may simply be ranking poorly or not ranking for those terms.

A practical check is:
- Search for your domain name to confirm the site is indexed.
- Then search the terms you want to rank for and see whether your page appears.

If it shows up for your domain but not for keyword searches, the page is indexed but not ranking well for those search terms.

Hyphens aren’t necessarily bad for domain names, but the guidance here is to avoid them unless they clearly improve readability.

In general:
- They add noise to the domain.
- They are harder to say out loud and spell.
- They can help reduce ambiguity in a multi-word name.

So the default advice is to use no hyphen if the name is still clear, but a well-placed hyphen can be useful if the unhyphenated version is confusing or misleading.

Google can index a page and still not show it for searches. The closest supported explanation here is that Google may not trust the page enough to rank it, especially if the site looks spammy or low-quality because of unrelated links and content.

What this covers:
- The page can be indexed.
- `site:` results can show it’s in Google’s index.
- It still may not appear for keyword searches if Google sees it as irrelevant or low quality.

Closest guidance:
- Remove unrelated links.
- Make the content focused and useful for the page topic.
- Improve overall quality and relevance.
- Be patient, since newer sites can take time to build reputation.

Google is likely reporting no authorship because the `rel="author"` link is hidden from users. Based on the guidance here, Google won’t show authorship information that isn’t visible to humans, and hiding the author link with `display:none` or similar CSS is not expected to work.

So the supported fix is to make the author link visible on the page if you want authorship to be shown. The evidence doesn’t say that `nofollow` is the problem; it points to the hidden markup as the main issue.

Don’t redirect removed pages to the home page by default.

The closest guidance here is:
- Use a 301 to the most relevant replacement page when there is a clear match.
- If there isn’t a good replacement, let the page return 404.
- If you have lots of removals, use redirect patterns where possible, and if not, handle unmatched URLs through a redirect list and otherwise return 404.

So: 301 to a relevant page when appropriate; 404 when there’s no good equivalent.

If you have a choice, it’s generally better to avoid hyphens in the domain name because they can make it less user-friendly when spoken or typed out loud.

That said, if the hyphen makes the name clearer or prevents confusion in an exact-match or ambiguous multi-word domain, it can be worth keeping. So you usually wouldn’t change it just because it has hyphens; only change it if removing them would make the domain clearer and more natural for users.

No. The supported guidance is to disavow the spammy or unnatural links pointing to your site, not automatically every link from spammy directories.

If a directory link is clearly part of the spammy backlink profile, it fits what Google is asking you to disavow. But the evidence does not support disavowing all directory links by default.

For a site moving to site-wide HTTPS, the closest supported guidance is to make sure search engines can clearly identify the original version of each page. Using hard links that point to the original article helps indicate which version is authoritative.

This does not fully cover every step of an HTTPS migration, but it does support the idea that clear canonical/original links can help reduce duplicate-content confusion.

Switching from HTTP to HTTPS by itself does not automatically fix duplicate content issues in Google.

Based on the case you provided, Google may treat the HTTPS pages as duplicate content if the same content is also available elsewhere, and it may choose to show the other version instead. The issue described was not HTTPS itself, but that the site content was a copy of another site.

So the closest supported guidance is:
- make sure the HTTPS version is the only version you want Google to index
- avoid or remove duplicate copies of the pages elsewhere

If you want, I can help you think through what to check when moving a site from HTTP to HTTPS.

If Google is choosing the non-HTTPS pages instead, the supported guidance here is that it may be treating the HTTPS site as duplicate content if the same pages also exist elsewhere.

The closest advice supported is:
- make sure the HTTPS version is the only place hosting that content, and
- remove the duplicate pages from the other domain so Google no longer sees two versions of the same content.

There’s no indication here that you need to do anything special in GoDaddy’s domain manager just because the site uses HTTPS.

Google can index a page without necessarily showing it for any search terms. Google doesn’t always index everything on a site, and it may choose not to surface some pages if it doesn’t consider them relevant enough.

You can check for crawl errors in Webmaster Tools and make sure robots.txt isn’t blocking the page. You can also use the diagnostic tool to view the page as Google sees it and, if that works, manually submit it for indexing. Even then, Google still decides whether the page is worth indexing and showing in search results.

The supported fix is to have the hosting provider reconfigure the Apache SSL/virtual hosts correctly so the HTTPS version is handled properly.

It may also be possible to add an .htaccess rule on the SSL site to block access when the domain name doesn’t match. If the host won’t or can’t do that, changing hosts may be the practical option.

What this does not support is a complete self-service fix without help from the host.

If HTTPS is creating duplicate versions of the same pages, the main thing is to make sure only one version is treated as the preferred URL.

What to do:

- Pick one preferred version, usually the HTTPS URL.
- Make sure the other version is not publicly indexable if it shows the same content.
- Add a canonical tag on duplicate pages pointing to the preferred URL.
- Use redirects where appropriate, especially if the non-preferred URL should not exist for users.
- Make sure internal links always point to the preferred HTTPS version.

If the pages are really just one page with different in-page states or navigation, use one canonical URL for that content rather than letting each variation be indexed separately.

If you share the URL pattern, I can help narrow down whether redirects, canonicals, noindex, or URL cleanup is the best fix.

Use a 301 redirect from the old HTTP URLs to the new HTTPS URLs. That is the supported way to get Google to replace the old URLs in its index and to stop the old and new versions from being treated as separate pages over time.

It won’t happen immediately, but it will happen.

A robots.txt Disallow on the old URLs is not the right fix here, because blocking crawling does not replace indexed URLs with the new ones.

If the same pages become accessible under both http and https, the supported approach is to make search engines understand which version you want indexed.

The guidance available here supports:
- using rel=canonical on each duplicate page to point to the preferred version
- or, if you do not want the duplicate version indexed, using a noindex, follow robots meta tag on those duplicate pages

It does not indicate an automatic SEO penalty; it says duplicate access can create indexing issues unless you manage it deliberately.

So for a site-wide move to https, the closest supported guidance is to have each http page point canonically to its https equivalent, or noindex the duplicate version if you are intentionally keeping it accessible but not indexed.

Fixing the duplicate URLs should remove the issue, and there usually isn’t a special SEO penalty that keeps lingering just because the same content was available on multiple URLs.

For an existing site moving to site-wide https, the closest supported guidance is:

- Make sure the preferred URL is clear by using redirects, rel=canonical, and internal links.
- If both http and https versions are accessible, search engines may choose a different URL to show.
- If duplication is widespread, it can slow crawling or delay discovery of updates.

So the main goal is to consolidate the site onto one preferred version, usually with redirects and canonical signals. If rankings are still down after that, the cause is likely something else rather than the duplicate content itself.

Moving the site to https site-wide should not create a duplicate-content SEO problem by itself. Search engines are concerned with duplicate content across different URLs, not repeated content within the same page.

If the same content is available at both http and https, the main concern is making sure one version is treated as the canonical version and the old one is redirected or otherwise not indexed. The evidence here does not go into those technical steps, but it does support the idea that repeated HTML or layout differences within a page, such as separate mobile and desktop menus, normally do not cause SEO issues.

So the closest guidance supported is:
- use one preferred URL version for each page
- avoid having both http and https indexable as separate pages
- repeated page elements themselves are not usually a duplicate-content penalty unless they look spammy or like keyword stuffing

Search engines index pages by URL, so the main duplicate-content concern is when the same content is available at more than one URL.

If you enforce https site wide, the safest approach is to make sure each page has only one preferred URL and that all links, internal references, and redirects point to the https version. That way, search engines see the https page as the canonical version instead of treating http and https as separate URLs with duplicate content.

The evidence also indicates that repeated content on the same page is not normally a duplicate-content SEO issue by itself, unless it looks spammy or like keyword stuffing.

So the closest supported guidance is:
- use https as the single preferred version of each page,
- redirect other versions to it,
- and avoid having the same content accessible at multiple URLs.

If you want, I can help you with a practical migration checklist for switching an existing site from http to https.

To improve the chance of your business showing in the right-hand side of Google search results, make sure you’ve given Google the right signals:

- Keep your business Name, Address, and Phone number consistent everywhere
- Add your business to quality citation sites and local directories like:

It may take some time to appear, roughly 7–21 days in the described process, because Google may need to confirm your address. It is also not guaranteed, since Google does not show this for every business or search result.

To get a business to show up in the right-hand side of Google search, the closest guidance here is to create and verify a local business listing.

What to do:
- Sign in to Google+
- Go to Pages under Home
- Click Create a page
- Choose Local Business or Place
- Enter your business name or address and select it if it appears
- If it doesn’t appear, choose the option that says it’s not listed or that you entered it correctly

  - accurate street address
  - phone number that reaches the business directly
- Submit the page
- Complete verification, or skip it and finish later from the dashboard

The guidance also supports linking your Google+ page and website. It does not fully explain every factor that affects whether Google shows the map box, but a verified local business listing with accurate address and phone details is the supported path.

Put this in the `.htaccess` for the old subdomain:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.newdomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://www.newdomain.com/subdirectory/%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

This is the closest supported pattern from the provided case: it redirects the incoming request to the new domain while preserving the requested path. Adjust `subdirectory/` to the target subdirectory you want on the new domain.

Yes. Google does not inherently treat .php pages differently from .html pages just because of the extension. What matters more is the URL and the content.

So a PHP-generated main page can be indexed by Google as long as it is reachable and indexable like any other page.

If each URL really leads to a distinct page of content, using the same keywords in many URLs is acceptable. Google can understand keywords in the path and in a query string as effectively the same thing, so changing the URL structure does not remove the keyword value.

The main point is that the pages should have enough different content behind them. If they are just categorized or filtered result pages, that is okay as long as each page is meaningfully distinct.

It also suggests that stuffing lots of keywords into many URLs is not necessary. A few relevant keywords are fine, but packing as many as possible into the URL is not needed for SEO.

Yes. Google can index a PHP-generated main page.

The best-supported approach here is to make sure the preferred URL is clear. A 301 redirect from `page.php` to `page`, along with a canonical tag pointing to `page`, helps Google treat `page` as the main version and avoid duplicate indexing.

No clear evidence says these are good for Google ranking. What the provided information does say is that traffic exchange programs like paid-to-click, paid-to-surf, autosurf, and click-exchange can put a Google AdSense account at risk, because Google AdSense prohibits using third-party services that generate clicks or impressions.

So the safest guidance supported here is: don’t rely on text ad exchange, traffic exchange, or auto surf websites for SEO or ad traffic, and check the policy of each ad network you use.

A dash is technically fine in a domain name. The provided text does not show that it has any specific SEO benefit or penalty. So the closest supported answer is: you can include a dash, but there’s no evidence here that it will help or hurt SEO.

Usually, no. A dash in a domain name does not generally help SEO.

It can be useful if it makes the name easier to read or helps protect your brand, and it may help a little when the words in the name are otherwise ambiguous. But the SEO impact is limited, so the main decision should be based on readability and branding rather than search rankings.

Start by checking whether the drop is only in Google impressions or whether traffic from other sources also fell too. If other sources are steady, the site itself is probably not broken.

The most likely place to look is Google-side changes: algorithm updates, crawling, indexing, or ranking fluctuations. Those can change often and cause impressions to go up and down.

If the issue seems to be only Google impressions, the closest supported guidance is to keep improving the site with more content, since that can often help.

Google rankings can change suddenly because Google is constantly updating its index. A sudden drop or jump can be a normal fluctuation, with the site briefly re-evaluated and then settling back.

If you recently resubmitted a sitemap, it may have prompted Google to recrawl, but it’s not possible to say that caused the ranking change directly. Google may simply have refreshed the index after your changes and then reverted to its earlier assessment.

The main advice is not to make more major changes right after a sudden ranking shift, since that makes it harder to tell whether the change was temporary or caused by edits. If you had just made a change right before the drop, rolling that change back would be the clearest exception.

A sudden drop in Google position can happen for several reasons:

- competing sites may have gained stronger or more relevant links
- you may have lost some quality links
- competitors may have improved their SEO and content
- a small algorithm change may have favored other sites
- a small algorithm change may have affected weaknesses on your site
- normal ranking fluctuation can also cause temporary drops

What to do:
- check whether the sites that moved ahead of you are new or recently changed
- undo any recent changes on your site if you made any
- wait and see whether rankings recover
- keep building quality links
- don’t make lots of changes at once, because that can make things worse

If you want, I can also help you make a short checklist to diagnose the drop.

Adding a dash in a domain name generally does not help SEO. If the words are already clear, the dash won’t make search engines understand the keywords better.

A dash can be useful for readability or to protect a brand, especially if the name is ambiguous. But in terms of SEO impact, it’s not likely to provide a benefit.

If traffic suddenly became very low after a website problem, the most likely causes here are:

- your page URLs changed and 301 redirects were not set up
- your page content, title tags, or other meta tags changed in a way that hurt rankings
- Google still needs time to re-index the updated pages

If the URL stayed the same, old links or robots are not the reason traffic dropped.

Closest next steps:
- check whether the URLs changed
- set up 301 redirects if they did
- review any changes to titles, meta tags, or page content
- wait for Google to re-index the site

A sharp drop in keyword rankings can happen for a few reasons: competitors may have improved their SEO or gained stronger links, you may have lost good links, or a small search engine algorithm change may have affected your pages or helped others. Rankings also naturally fluctuate, so a temporary drop can sometimes recover on its own.

The closest practical checks are:
- See whether the pages now ranking above you are new or recently updated.
- Review whether you lost quality backlinks.
- Think about any recent changes you made and whether reversing them changes rankings.
- Check for recent search engine algorithm updates.
- If nothing obvious changed, avoid making major edits too quickly and monitor while continuing to build good links.

A sharp decline in website statistics could be consistent with the site running slowly, which can frustrate visitors and cause them to leave sooner. That would lower pageviews per visit and could reduce overall visitor counts.

What this does not confirm is the exact cause of the decline. It does not show that a JavaScript change or any other specific change definitely caused the drop, and it does not provide a way to determine the “real” stats.

The closest supported guidance is to check server performance reports or other signs that the site slowed down around the time the decline started.

You can’t directly choose or fully control which Google sitelinks appear for your site.

What you can do is:
- build a site with substantial traffic,
- keep creating good content,
- use semantic HTML for your navigation so Google can recognize your menu links,
- avoid using JavaScript for links and menus.

If sitelinks already appear, Google may let you influence which ones show through Google Webmaster Tools, but that still doesn’t let you force sitelinks to appear in the first place.

You can’t directly choose which Google sitelinks are shown. Google decides whether to show a sitelinks search box, and the exact criteria aren’t public.

What you can do is make sure your site has clear structure and built-in search functionality, since that may help Google show sitelinks or a search box, but there’s no guaranteed way to force it.

You can’t directly choose Google sitelinks from your site. The best you can do is improve the chances of Google showing the links you want by:

- getting more traffic and publishing high-quality content
- using semantic HTML for navigation
- marking your menu with an id like `nav` or `navigation`
- avoiding JavaScript for links and menus
- being patient, since sitelinks are rare and there isn’t a known public algorithm for getting them

If you already have sitelinks, Google Webmaster Tools lets you control which links may appear there.

You can’t directly choose which Google sitelinks appear for your website. Google selects them automatically.

The only control mentioned is that, if you use Google Webmaster Tools, you can demote specific sitelinks so they rank lower in preference. That may cause them to disappear, but Google still decides what to show. Demotions last 90 days.

So you can:
- not choose only your preferred sitelinks
- demote unwanted sitelinks in Webmaster Tools

Hyphens aren’t inherently bad, so there’s no need to change it just because it has hyphens. The main downside is that multiple hyphens may reduce any exact-match keyword advantage, so it could hurt rankings a bit.

If the domain is otherwise working for you, this evidence does not suggest it is “bad” or blacklisted.

If you want a bot to follow every link, the main requirement is that it can actually reach your site and access robots.txt. If Googlebot can’t reach robots.txt, it won’t be able to crawl the sitemap either.

An XML sitemap can be useful for helping Google crawl and index pages, but it won’t solve an access problem. So the closest supported guidance is: make sure the site host/server is reachable, robots.txt is accessible, and then use a sitemap if you want help with discovery.

Hyphens aren’t necessarily bad, but the guidance here is to avoid them unless they clearly improve readability.

If your exact-match domain is already clear without the hyphen, the closest guidance supports changing it to the cleaner version. If removing the hyphen would make the name confusing or misleading, keeping the hyphen can be reasonable.

Changing the title and meta tags with jQuery is not covered directly by the provided material, so I can’t confirm crawler behavior from this evidence alone.

What it does support is that search engines may choose different snippets or titles in SERP even for the same content, and that frequent changes to `<title>`, description, and keywords can affect ranking or how search engines evaluate and display the page.

Closest guidance supported here: if your goal is to influence what appears in search results, relying on frequent client-side changes is not a guaranteed solution, and this evidence does not give a direct method for making crawlers use jQuery-updated title/meta tags.

Create a normal XML sitemap file, place it in your site’s root directory, and make sure it opens directly in a browser at a URL like www.domain.com/sitemap.xml.

Then submit that sitemap URL in Google Search Console. If Google says the sitemap is empty, first verify that the file is actually accessible at that URL and that it contains valid URLs, then resubmit it there. Also check for broken links before generating the sitemap.

Google may be treating two versions of the same page as separate URLs, such as lowercase and CamelCase versions, which can cause the title to appear twice in search results.

The recommended fix is to set a canonical URL for the preferred version of the page, for example:

<link rel="canonical" href="/deutschland/Bayern/Camping-Allweglehen-19062">

This tells Google which URL version should be considered the main one.

If Google is showing your meta title twice, it usually means the page title tag is being repeated or not set correctly in the page’s head section.

Make sure your page has a proper title tag and meta description tag, for example:

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<TITLE>This will be your site title</TITLE>
<META Name="Description" Content="This is the description of your site.">
</HEAD>

If Google is showing something unexpected like “IIS7,” that can mean the title and description tags are missing or not configured correctly.

The evidence only supports that a blocked or penalized site is generally affected at the domain level, not the whole server. So other sites on the same VPS or IP would not be expected to be blocked just because one site was.

It does not directly say whether competitors can cause your website to be penalized.

Use human-readable, unique URLs instead of query strings or numeric IDs.

For database-generated content, store an alias/slug for each item in your database and make sure it’s unique. Then use that slug in the URL, for example:

`http://site.com/page.aspx?id=54637` → `http://site.com/cats`

Also make sure each dynamic page has its own unique `title`, `h1`, and `meta description` pulled from the database, and avoid repeated content across pages.

The evidence doesn’t directly explain how Google bots work on database-driven sites. What it does support is that database-driven sites are heavier than static sites and that performance depends on how many simultaneous requests they get, plus the server software and database you run.

So the closest guidance is: Google bots will still crawl sites that are database-driven, but the practical impact on your server depends on how “heavy” those pages are and how much traffic/crawling they receive. For lightweight database-related pages, a 1 CPU-core / 1 GB RAM server may be suitable only for simple, low-traffic use.

Google crawlers can index PHP dynamic content if each page has its own unique URL. The supported guidance here is:

- make each dynamic page accessible at a distinct URL
- use GET parameters in the URL rather than POST for pages that vary by content
- include the AdSense code on each page you want indexed for relevant ads

If your PHP pages are generated from database content, Google should still be able to target each distinct URL. The main issue mentioned is when many different pages are served from the same URL via POST; in that case, changing to GET-based URLs is recommended.

For a database-driven site, the material here only says that the site still needs to be properly deployed and able to connect to its remote database. It does not explain how Google bots crawl or index such sites.

The closest guidance it supports is:
- make sure the site is hosted on a server that supports your stack,
- create and connect to the database correctly,
- upload the site and database content,
- verify the pages load and work.

So, if Google bots are to access the pages, the pages must be served correctly by the deployed site with working database access. Beyond that, this doesn’t provide specific SEO or crawling steps.

Use URLs with parameters if the content is generated dynamically on each page load from those parameters. Those URLs can be indexed and returned in search results, and they should behave normally when clicked.

The main thing to avoid is exposing the same underlying content through multiple parameterized URLs, because that can create duplicate-content issues. If the page is just hidden content being shown or hidden based on parameters, search engines may treat those as multiple URLs for the same content. In that case, a canonical URL can help, though then only one URL is likely to appear in search results.

So, for database-generated content you want indexed, the closest guidance here is:
- generate the content dynamically for each parameterized URL
- make sure each URL represents distinct content
- use canonical URLs if duplicate versions exist

The most likely explanation is that Google is dropping low-quality, duplicate, or near-duplicate pages from its index.

There’s no indication here of a server, DNS, or crawl error causing the decrease. The kind of content described before was generated by keyword replacement from existing content, which Google often excludes.

So the supported guidance is to improve the pages so they are genuinely unique and useful. If they remain mass-generated duplicates, the number of indexed pages may continue to decline.

A big drop in indexed pages does not, by itself, explain a drop in impressions. The supported explanation here is that Google may have changed how your pages rank or show in search results, such as after a Panda-type update, which can reduce impressions even if the site still has many pages indexed.

So the closest guidance is: the issue may be less about the size of the index and more about reduced visibility or ranking in Google.

The most likely cause is that Google is deindexing low-quality or duplicate pages, rather than there being a server, DNS, or page error problem.

If the pages were created by swapping keywords into existing content, Google may treat them as spun or low-quality content. In that case, more pages can continue to drop from the index, and the removal could eventually become broader across the site.

The only supported guidance here is to improve content quality and reduce duplication.

A meta description is still useful because Google does not always show page text instead of it. Google may use the meta description, a snippet from the page content, or no description at all.

So the meta description helps because it gives you a short, page-specific summary that Google can choose to show in search results. For best results, it should be unique to the page and accurately describe the content. If there is no meta description, Google may pull text from the page itself.

If you do not want any snippet shown, you can use `<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet">`.

Meta descriptions are also typically kept around 145–150 characters to fit common display limits.

A large drop in indexed pages can happen even when pages aren’t blocked by `robots.txt` and don’t have a `noindex` tag.

The guidance available here suggests checking Google Search Console/Webmaster Tools stats and comparing the number of URLs in your sitemap with the number Google has indexed over time. That can help you see when the drop started and whether it affected only certain pages or the whole site.

Possible causes mentioned include duplicate content, weak content, copyright concerns, outside spam links, non-family-friendly content, deceptive ad placement, or sometimes no obvious reason at all.

If you can’t find a clear issue, the closest supported advice is that there may be little you can do to restore the exact pages, and rebuilding the pages in a different form was suggested.

Use a meta description because it is one possible source of the search snippet, but not the only one. Google may use it if it is valid and matches the page content; if not, it may show text from the page itself or another source instead.

So even though Google can generate a snippet from article text when there is no meta description, the meta description still gives you a chance to provide a concise, controlled description that Google may choose to display.

A 301 to the start page is usually not the right choice for deleted files.

If a removed file has a relevant replacement, redirect it to that equivalent page instead. For example, redirect `/page.html` to `/page`.

If there is no clear replacement, the evidence does not support sending all deleted files to the home page. It’s likely too broad.

So the closest guidance is:
- redirect each old file to the most relevant new page if one exists;
- don’t use the start page as a blanket target for unrelated deleted files.

Use a maintenance mode that returns HTTP 503 Service Unavailable and includes a Retry-After header while the site is under construction. That tells Google the site is temporarily unavailable and to come back later.

Password-protecting the folder is also fine. If you do that, put up a static HTML page with some content so search engines still have something to crawl and can start indexing when you’re ready.

I can’t confirm anything about specific setups like preview DNS, static IPs, or a /dev/ subdirectory.

No, not directly. A proper 404 page is generally fine and is not treated as harmful to ranking by Google. The more important SEO point is that the page should return a real 404 server status, and your site should avoid linking to lots of non-existing pages.

If you mean the 404 page itself, making it simpler or hiding images would not be expected to hurt SEO based on this information.

If images are hidden on a 404 page for a legitimate reason, that’s different, but if the hiding is meant to deceive search engines, it can be treated as cloaking and may lead to penalties.

If different URLs show the same or very similar content, the safest approach is to make sure only one preferred version is treated as the main page.

What to do:
- Keep only one canonical URL for that content.
- If the URLs are just variants of the same page, add a canonical tag to the preferred URL.
- If the alternate URLs don’t need to be indexed, use redirects or noindex where appropriate.
- Make sure internal links consistently use the preferred URL.
- If the page is actually one page with in-page navigation or state changes, avoid creating separate indexable copies for each section.

In short: if the content is duplicated across URLs, consolidate it to one indexable URL and point everything else to that version.

Using `?page=something` isn’t inherently bad for SEO, but simpler URLs are generally preferred.

SEO-friendly URLs are somewhat important, but not for everyone.

Some users do notice and prefer descriptive URLs before clicking, and search engines like Google give them some weight. At the same time, many users don’t care about the URL at all. So they’re a good choice because they can help both the people who pay attention and search engines, while not really affecting users who don’t care.

SEO-friendly URLs are important if you want the benefits described here: better SEO, easier manual entry by users, and more resilience if part of the URL is missing. The evidence says keywords in the URL are one of the more important ranking factors, so friendly URLs are recommended for that reason.

It does not provide direct disadvantages of SEO-friendly URLs or direct advantages of query parameters. The closest supported guidance is that query parameters are less suited to those SEO and user-friendly benefits.

They are not important if they mean stuffing in keywords or making the URL awkward. The best-supported guidance here is to keep URLs human-friendly, use relevant words naturally, and keep them fairly short — around 10 words or fewer.

If you’re choosing between friendly URLs and query parameters, the closest guidance is to pick the form that makes the URL more understandable and meaningful, rather than optimizing for SEO alone.

Using a query parameter like `?page=something` is not inherently bad for SEO. Based on the evidence, the main point is that changing the URL format by itself does not improve rankings.

So the closest supported guidance is:

- Query parameters: are not automatically harmful for SEO.
- Potential downside of “friendly” rewrites: if you add extra rewriting or complexity just to change the URL style, that can add server processing without any SEO gain.

So, from the evidence, the practical pro of cleaner URLs is readability, not SEO; the practical con is possible added complexity. Query parameters are acceptable and not inherently bad for SEO.

Friendly URLs are mainly better for search rankings and usability.

Pros of friendly URLs:
- Keywords in the URL can help SEO.
- They are easier for users to read and understand.
- They can still remain useful even if part of the keyword text is missing, as long as the page ID is near the front.

Cons of friendly URLs:
- The provided evidence does not mention specific downsides compared with query parameters.

Pros of query parameters:
- The provided evidence does not describe any specific advantages over friendly URLs.

Cons of query parameters:
- The provided evidence does not mention specific SEO or usability drawbacks, but it does say friendly URLs are worth doing if better search rankings are the goal.

So, based on the evidence, the strongest guidance is that friendly URLs are preferable when SEO and clearer, more user-friendly links matter.

Using path-style or “friendly” URLs is generally preferable when the URL represents site structure or a resource hierarchy. They give a cleaner, clearer URL, make the hierarchy obvious, can improve navigation for users, and can make routing and controller design cleaner during development.

Query-string parameters are still handled well by search engines, so they’re not bad. They’re a better fit when you’re passing variable data to a page rather than describing structure.

So, in practical terms:
- Friendly/path URLs: best for site structure and resource hierarchy; clearer and cleaner.
- Query parameters: best for variable data; perfectly workable and search-friendly.

If you’re starting a new site, clean URLs are a good choice.

Gmail usually puts mail in spam because of message content, recipients marking it as spam, or a poor reputation for the sending server IP.

Using a shared server IP by itself is not usually the reason, even if other domains on the same IP send mail from different addresses. Gmail’s guidance is to keep the From address consistent for bulk mail.

What you can do:
- Check whether your server IP is blacklisted or has a bad reputation
- Use a reputation checker like senderscore.org or senderbase.org
- If the IP reputation is poor, the host or server admin may need to fix it
- If the IP is fine, look at the content and sending patterns of the emails

Common reasons from the previous case were:

- The SMTP server may be configured as an open relay, so that should be tested first.
- If Gmail already marked messages from that sender as spam, later emails may keep going to spam even after changes. Try marking an old message as “Not spam” and test sending to multiple Gmail accounts to see whether it’s account-specific.
- Make sure the sender address matches the domain used in the links in the email.
- Reduce the number of links in the email.
- Remove link target attributes if they are not needed.
- Include a clear unsubscribe option and a physical mailing address.

Also check the new sending IPs against blacklists, and make sure the reverse DNS for those IPs matches the domain sending the mail.

To reduce the chance of spam placement, you can also:

- verify the new outgoing servers are not blacklisted
- consider third-party certification/whitelisting help if needed

To prevent a specific file from being indexed, add a rule to your robots.txt file.

If you want to block one file, use its full path, for example:

Disallow: /path/to/pdf/thefilename.pdf

If you want to block all files of a certain type, you can block by extension, for example:

Disallow: /*.pdf$

If you only want Googlebot to respect it, you can use:

User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow: /*.pdf$

Blocking by extension will also block any files of that type you may want indexed, so a file-specific path is the safer choice if you only want to hide one file.

If the duplicated part is something like a slideshow or other heavily text-based repeated block, a possible approach is to place it in an iframe and use a canonical link so search engines know which URL should be indexed.

Visits and pageviews are related, but they are not the same.

A visit creates at least one pageview. With a 54% bounce rate, about 54% of visits end after the first page, while the rest continue to other pages. In the example given, that works out to roughly 16,200 bouncing visits and 13,800 visits that go deeper into the site.

So:
- visits = visits/session count
- pageviews = total pages loaded across those visits
- bounce rate = percentage of visits that end after one page

That means you can’t convert visits to pageviews exactly from bounce rate alone. In the example, 30,000 visits and 86,000 pageviews suggest about 2.87 pageviews per visit overall, or about 3.78 pageviews per non-bounce visit.

Alexa rank is separate from these counts and is relative, so higher pageviews do not automatically mean a better Alexa rank.

A VPS (virtual private server) gives you your own virtual machine with root access, but it still runs on shared physical hardware with other VPS customers.

Cloud hosting is a marketing term for hosting built on a pool of virtualized resources rather than one fixed physical server. In practice, it often behaves a lot like VPS hosting, but with more flexibility to move, scale, or balance resources.

So, the practical difference is:
- web hosting = simplest/shared hosting for basic websites
- VPS = more control and root access on shared hardware
- cloud hosting = similar to VPS in many cases, but usually marketed around flexibility and scaling

The closest guidance supported here is to use web hosting for basic needs, and use VPS if you want root access and more control. Performance can vary by provider, especially if they oversell resources.

Google is mainly interested in the page’s explicit description text, especially the meta description tag. If you want Google to use a description in results, add a `<meta name="description" ...>` tag in the HTML `<head>` with a concise page summary.

For example:

```html
<head>
  <meta name="description" content="Short summary of the page">
</head>
```

Google often uses that description in search results instead of generating one from the visible page content.

It doesn’t give a specific WordPress hosting provider recommendation, but it does indicate that offloading images to a separate host is a good approach for image-heavy sites.
