If the new domain just redirects to the main site, search engines will generally follow the redirect and index/update the preferred main page rather than the new domain itself.

The guidance here supports using a 301 redirect for that purpose. If the new domain only exists as a redirect, it’s not the normal way to get that new domain indexed as its own site.

If your goal is to have the main site recognized as the primary one, a 301 redirect is the supported approach, and rel=canonical can also help Google understand the preferred page. If you need already-indexed results updated, the supported method mentioned is Google Search Console’s URL removal tool.

If a domain only redirects to another site, search engines usually treat it as a move, not as a separate site to rank.

With a 301 redirect:
- the redirecting domain generally will not index as its own result
- the old URL is typically removed from search results
- the destination page is what search engines focus on
- value may be passed along to the main site

A 302 redirect can sometimes stay in search results longer, but that generally assumes the domain existed and was indexed first, and it may look suspicious and not rank well.

So the closest guidance is: a domain that only permanently redirects to another site usually won’t get SEO value as its own indexed result; the main site is the one that matters.

If the domain is just being forwarded or redirected, it will not give SEO benefit or make the old domain rank better for the new keyword.

The only case described that can help is when the redirected domain already had an established site, was indexed, and had backlinks. In that situation, a 301 permanent redirect can pass some SEO value.

So for a simple forward to a different site/domain, the closest guidance is that it generally does not help SEO.

The best-supported approach is to use 301 redirects from the alternate domain to the primary domain.

That way, search engines and users are sent to one canonical site instead of seeing the same content at multiple URLs, which can create duplicate content issues. Simply aliasing the domains or using rewrite rules to make them appear as separate domains is not recommended for SEO. Making them separate landing pages with slightly different content is also not a good SEO strategy, since those pages would have little SEO value and the links from them would be of little worth.

So, if you’re moving or pointing one domain to another, redirect it permanently with a 301 to the main site.

Set the custom domain to point at the host, and make the web server redirect that domain to the matching subdomain.

For example, if you want thisguy.com to go to blog1.mainsite.com, use a redirect rule like:

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^thisguy.com$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.thisguy.com$
RewriteRule ^/?$ "http\:\/\/blog1\.mainsite\.com" [R=301,L]

Then add a similar rule for any other domain, like thatguy.com pointing to blog2.mainsite.com.

If you want to redirect www to non-www, the supported options are:

1. Use two VirtualHost entries, one for the main domain and one for www, then redirect www:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot "/path/to/site"
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.example.com
    Redirect 301 / http://example.com/
</VirtualHost>

2. If you prefer .htaccess, put the redirect in the www site’s .htaccess:

Redirect 301 / http://example.com/

3. If you use one VirtualHost, set the main host plus ServerAlias and use rewrite rules in .htaccess:

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    ServerAlias www.example.com
    DocumentRoot "/path/to/site"
</VirtualHost>

Then in .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www.example.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://example.com/$1 [R=301,L]

The example you tried can lead to a redirect loop if the redirect is applied without a separate www host configuration.

Google may be skipping or changing the page title if the title tag is missing, repeated, or not set correctly in the page’s head section.

Make sure the page has a proper title tag in the HEAD, for example:

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<TITLE>This will be your site title</TITLE>
<META Name="Description" Content="This is the description of your site.">
</HEAD>

If Google shows something unexpected like “IIS7,” that can mean the title and description tags are missing or not configured correctly.

Google was likely not using your page’s actual title at the time it crawled the page. It may have fetched a temporary error response from your server, such as an HTTP 400 error page, and used that title instead.

So the supported explanation is that Google skipped your intended page title because it saw an error response or invalid request response when crawling. This can make the title shown in search results or the cached version differ from the real page title.

Websites can’t directly control that in Google results. Google’s search result formatting is determined by Google’s own ranking and display rules, so you can’t force extra information to appear or set rules like “only show at most 2 results from the same site.”

The closest supported option is to exclude specific pages or URLs in Google Custom Search, but not to control how many results appear per website or domain.

Websites can help Google show extra information by adding useful ancillary content such as location info through Google Places, meta information like ratings, price, and author details, and event information. This can make a result stand out more and may improve how it appears in Google search results, but Google still decides what to display.

Google can show extra information in results by using the page’s title and description for the displayed link text and snippet. It may also attach tracking parameters to result links so it can tell when a result is clicked for a particular search term.

What’s not fully covered here is how Google decides which links on a site are important overall. The closest supported guidance is that having titles and descriptions that match what searchers want can help those results get clicked.

Websites can improve the extra information Google may show by adding relevant details to the site or business listing, such as location information through Google Places, metadata like ratings, price, and author info, and event information.

Google gets the extra links it shows in results from the URLs it has crawled and indexed on your site. In other words, it uses the URLs it discovers while crawling your website, then may display some of those indexed links in search results.

If you want to check which URLs Google has indexed from your site, you can search with:

site:www.example.com

That will show results limited to your site.

You can’t force Google to show specific site sections under the search result description.

- an accurate summary of that page

Google may use either:
- the meta description tag
- relevant text from the page itself

Google doesn’t always show the meta description you set. The closest supported guidance is to make each page’s description a clear, natural summary of that page and avoid keyword stuffing, because Google may choose different text from the page if it thinks that content is a better match.

If you want sections to appear under the description, the best-supported approach is:

- make the page content relevant to those sections
- avoid stuffing the description with keywords

- .com / .org: generic, can rank worldwide
- country extension like .am: can help for local country targeting

- Google may be crawling your pages.
- Some pages may already be indexed.
- Keyword searches may still not show your site if Google does not trust it or sees it as irrelevant.

Closest guidance supported:
- Remove unrelated links.
- Keep the site focused on its actual topic.
- Improve the quality and relevance of each page.
- Give the site time, since new sites may take a while to build reputation.
